Socialism does not abolish it. It merely organizes those who have been divided into a social unity of distribution. That is much more terrifying.

Who, then, protects us from the distributors?

I found a fellow traveller for my campaign against law:

Father Dom Deschamps, a contemporary of Rousseau and Diderot.

Le vrai système ou le mot de l’énigme—The True System, or the Answer to the Riddle—first published in 1939 by Jean Thomas and Franco Venturi through the Société des textes français modernes.

From the état des lois, the state of laws, to the état des moeurs, the state of customs.

Utopia.

Anarchy.

Community.

Collectivity.

Freedom from needs.

Everything becomes self-evident as soon as this one final obstacle has been removed: law.

(Sent to Miss M. Stewens; at the same time I gave her the name Claude-Nicolas Ledoux, from Ledoux to Le Corbusier.)67

I keep thinking about utopia. For me, utopia means planning.

From the Five-Year Plan to the 50,000-Year Plan. Time, after all, is only money, and in an inflationary age it no longer matters.

What connects me with Erich Voegelin? He understood the central importance of Goethe, and understood it critically. If disaster has occurred, then from the standpoint of intellectual history it can only be traced back to the cult of Goethe. Above all, the specifically modern German idea of race can only be explained through that cult.

Everything else follows automatically once the idea spreads to the masses—once someone “dares to dare,” and the bêtes féroces, the wild beasts lurking behind every cult, are finally let loose.68

With Schiller, the turn toward Goethe has already taken place (Letter 9 of On the Aesthetic Education of Man): Goethe was the perfect human being (Voegelin, p. 140).

Carus: Goethe’s “noble birth,” the supposedly innate nobility of the man of genius and the demonic man. (We shall see what comes of that at the bicentenary celebrations in 1949!) This provides the basis for racial theory: Kommerell, The Poet as Leader, 1928, on Goethe’s role as leader.

Goethe also tolerated no one beside him who refused to take part in this cult. Hölderlin, Kleist, even Schubert were all pushed aside by him.

Goethe was simply such a great poet—the greatest poet—that he had to become the founder of a cult.

But he diverted this necessity into the individualistic world of educated culture, and everyone followed him there as well.

The final result: the beautiful animal, and the image presented by the self-conscious “elite” that came to power in Germany in 1936.69 That was the end of a road prepared, among others, by an honest Englishman, H. S. Chamberlain, and an honest Jew, Otto Weininger.

22 December 1947

To Gerhard Nebel:

I have often had the impression of a theogony—a theogony ab ovo, from the very beginning, so to speak.

There is no question that we are standing at the beginning of a theogonic age, an age in which new gods are being made. That is why there is such great anticipation surrounding your work on Prometheus. For my part, I still remain with my contemplation of the Christian Epimetheus:

The more that meaning seeks itself, The more the soul is led from dark captivity Out into the world. Do what you must! It has always already been done; You only give an answer.

(Alcaic.)

Gilles said in 1942: no longer Prometheus, whose reign is over, but a pure primal melody—Orpheus. We really are living through a theogony, provided we accept the concept of nihilism and refuse simply to stop there.

Däubler’s work is likewise a theogony.

Positivist science: an especially brazen theogony of “we shall make it ourselves.”

“The point is to change the world”: again, the makers of gods. And every time, this new theogony ends with a new elite.

Better, then, to stick with the old elites we already know!

Though of course these gentlemen of refined taste need protection themselves.70

23 December 1947

“Only when a majority loaded a minority with the full weight of its own repressed aggression could it regard itself as free from aggression, and therefore as good and just. Only then did it create a good conscience for itself and gain the moral upper hand, from which those parts of society that had remained at the level of primitive, unrepressed aggression could no longer escape.”

Paul Reiwald, The Conquest of Peace: Psychological Foundations of the New Society, Zurich and New York, Europa Verlag, 1944, pp. 99–100; quoted by Hans Wehberg in the essay “Peaceful and Aggressive States: The Problem of International Criminal Law” (Die Friedenswarte, 1944, p. 25).71

Reiwald:

Humanity’s enemy number one is the state of tension created by mass situations—not merely legal or political disputes. Such tensions can only be tamed. They cannot be eradicated.

Aggression is released against the criminal in order to redirect it toward another target.

Criminals are those who have achieved no repression at all, or only very little.

So the starting point is this:

Human beings are aggressive by nature. And the collective is even more so—the “great man,” the μάκρος ἄνθρωπος, humanity writ large.

On natural law:

I can tell from even the briefest and most casual discussion of natural law—and all the more from any serious and detailed discussion—whether the author knows Hegel’s essay “The Scientific Ways of Treating Natural Law” (1802/03).

If he does not, I recommend that he read it.

Unless, that is, the discussion itself reveals that the author is simply incapable of understanding Hegel.

In that unfortunately very common case, I stop reading.

Why is this young Hegel of 1802 so overwhelmingly great? And why is the old Hegel—for example, the Hegel of the 1828 essay on Hamann’s writings—so narrow, unfair, and determined to be right?

The parallel with Goethe is obvious.

Of course, the old Goethe played the role of cult image with more taste, with more effective means of cultivating the cult, and therefore with greater success than the old Hegel.

Strange how, only a few weeks ago, the thought of the Deus absconditus, the hidden God, tormented me (see 6 December 1947).

Today Bilfinger writes, in a letter dated 18 December:

“The Deus absconditus has lowered the Iron Curtain. Incidentally: the hidden God occupies me a great deal. I also have literature on the subject, probably connected with Persian religious ideas. But the Christmas message, our hymns, Beethoven, all of it—who can take that away from us?”

That is what he writes.

And while this mixture of religion with the comforts of cultivated culture still bothers me, I myself sit here playing the Meistersinger and committing the worst sins of cultivated culture.

I found this in Lucan, Book VII:

“We lie when we say Jupiter reigns.”72

And there too:

“No god cares for mortal affairs.”

Or:

German soil, which fate has held beneath perpetual tyrants. Among the peoples who endure kings, ours is the lowest lot, we who are ashamed to serve. Surely no gods watch over us, since the ages are swept away by blind chance. We lie when we say Jupiter reigns.73 Will freedom never return? This is the deeply moving lament of collapse. And from precisely this depth of nihilism, Christianity rises.

24 December 1947

Still thinking about the passage in Lucan, VII, 440–460. What does this mean:

“Civil wars will make gods equal to those above”?

(For a moment I thought it said divis rather than divos.)

Hans [actually: Paul] Reiwald:

Human beings are aggressive by nature.

Reiwald discovers that defence is the best form of attack. Only then does the dialectic of war reach its full intensity.

The idea that attack is the best defence now seems naïvely direct, almost unsophisticated.

To defend yourself, by contrast—to make the opponent appear to be the attacker—is rational and civilized. This dialectic of psychological repression produces the higher logic of higher imperialism.

Hans [actually: Paul] Reiwald:

The more disciplined the individual becomes, the more aggressive the collective becomes.

The reason is that the individual can now satisfy his own aggression indirectly, as a member of the mass. So the “great man”—the collective, the state—is also the great aggressor. It becomes the reservoir into which everything irrational flows.

Rational within, and therefore all the more irrational without.

Compare my Leviathan, p. 75, on relations between collective bodies. This is the unavoidable machinery created by the rationalization of the individual.

Meter belongs to magic. But there must remain a certain amount of open space between the meter and the thought or subject matter expressed by the poem.

Put crudely: between form and content there is still an empty space. And in that interval, in that space which remains empty, the numinous—the mysterious sense of sacred presence—begins to resonate.

Goethe’s poem “To the Moon” shows this beautifully.

In Däubler there is too much noise made by the sounds of words and by great clusters of words.

The numinous element in a poem is not the sound itself. It resonates in the empty space. It is not itself emptiness, τὸ κενόν. It moves within emptiness.

Everything moves in empty space.

Empty space is the condition that makes movement possible. But the numinous has a special relationship to emptiness.

The emptier the vessel, the purer it is.

Meter is the empty vessel not for the content, but for the magical vibration.

25 December 1947

To H. Bung, on the repeated confusion between me and my namesake in Tübingen:

I am still not sure whether these mix-ups help or hinder my great ambition to achieve perfect obscurité and complete self-effacement.

But, having learned from Reiwald, I can imagine that they have something usefully distracting about them.

Perhaps they disarm the most direct and primitive form of aggression.

(Then a question about Wehberg’s essay and its discussion of C. S.)

In any case, you must not imagine my situation as though I were rummaging around in the decaying printer’s ink of the past.

A great deal of it may be blown into my face, but I have not allowed my thoughts to be turned backward.

Most of what people are thinking today, insofar as it is new and interesting, we already thought in advance.

And whatever is worth thinking over afterward—in the manner of Epimetheus—we have thought over.

27 December 1947

To Mrs Jünger:

Mrs Schmitt really has managed to set up a home here.

Gilles’s fish, Nay’s Leviathan, Nay’s magnificent diamond—all of them surround me again.

Like a submarine that continually reassembles itself, I make my submarine, subterranean, sublunary journey through fire and water.

Three times the Leviathan has swallowed me and then spat me out again. Now I understand the three chapters of the Book of Jonah.

Strange, by contrast, how theogonic writings are flowing toward me from every direction:

G. Nebel; the Greek gods of Fr.[iedrich] G.[eorg] J.[ünger]; Däubler’s Hymns to Italy and the Attic Sonnets.

I look out at a magnificent mountain. Behind it lies another landscape, different from the Lennetal valley where I live.

The river outside my window is splendid in winter. It looks as though it has just come into existence, without a past and without a future: pure Heraclitean present.

I am reading Troeltsch’s The Social Teachings of the Christian Churches (1912), especially this sentence (p. 173):

“The Christian theory of natural law—in which the pure natural law of humanity’s original condition, the entirely opposite relative natural law of humanity’s fallen condition, positive law which often contains the most terrible atrocities, and theocratic supreme authority, which despite all natural law claims to communicate true goodness from itself, are constantly colliding—is pitiful and confused as a scientific theory. But as a practical doctrine it is of the highest importance in the history of culture and society. It is the Church’s true cultural dogma, and as such it is at least (!) as important as the dogma of the Trinity or the other major dogmas.”

This Troeltsch would have understood me, just as I understand him. How alone I am, then!

Non intelligor ulli.

No one understands me.

Poor Donoso.

The theological concept that truly corresponded to his political theory would have been the κατέχων, the katechon, the restraining power. Instead he wandered into this labyrinth of absolute and relative natural law!

There is a very simple sociological explanation for the hopelessness of Charles Péguy’s complaint that he could find no success among Catholics.

Perhaps the Jesuit order was the κατέχων. But what about after 1814?

A restored katechon?

28 December 1947

Refreshing to read Hobbes on the legal position of the prisoner.

In the state of nature there are no binding agreements. These really are the elements of law.

No one else has set them out with such elementary correctness.

Power in itself is evil, says the highly cultivated Swiss gentleman.

All I can say in reply is: and powerlessness is spiteful and malicious in itself.

29 December 1947

“The victor must not,” says Franz W. Jerusalem in the Frankfurter Hefte, December 1947, p. 1260, “rule the defeated country as occupied territory” on the pretext that the peace treaty has not yet been signed.74 So he still has not understood the doctrine of the discriminatory concept of war.

A just war is a bellum <infinitum>—an <infinite war>.

The doctrine of just war abolishes the <…> distinction between the enemy and the criminal.

The victor in a just war makes himself the judge of a criminal.

And depending on the scale of the crime, the judge may hang the criminal, imprison him for life, subject him to a regime of starvation and compulsory re-education, or do whatever else he considers just.

The naïveté of these jurists is unbelievable. They still refuse to see that the root of this entire problem lies in the doctrine of just war.

“The victor must not.”

Touching.

Like that Serene Highness speaking to the proletarians of 1848:

“But you are not allowed to do that.”

Only this time it is the <powerlessness> of the under-proletarians lecturing an all-powerful ruler about what one is allowed to do.75

Am I, as a layman and non-theologian, supposed to join in discussions of Catholic questions? So that I can be instructed, as Donoso Cortés was?

Ubi nihil vales, ibi nihil velis.

Where you have no power, desire nothing.

I, as a jurist—that is, as a scholar already one degree removed from theology?

Poor Donoso!

Flowing—the flowing of the river and of time—is Heraclitean passing-away.

Not so much becoming or coming into being as passing away.

In German, gehen, “to go,” is already contained in vergehen, “to pass away.”

To go is to go away. So the present is already the past. But nothing is said about the future. That is why Hegel’s philosophy had to become a historical view of the world.

The apparent paradox is that constant movement—that is, revolution—becomes so reactionary.

Always the same “paradox” again: the identity of opposites.

30 December 1947

Existentialism without Christianity: that really is a performance of Hamlet without the Prince of Denmark.

Compared with that, the Marxists have a major advantage.

31 December 1947

Tone does not merely make the music. It also makes language. Only angels sing, and only God speaks.

Since Beethoven, for us, in the beginning there is tone, no longer the Word.

(To Nette: glorification of the speaking race.)

Instrumental music solves the problem that sinful human beings should not sing, because only angels sing. Now the violins sing.

The flutes sing.

The horns sing.

PreviousWorks CitedNextBook II · 1948–1949

Book II

1 January 1948–31 May 1949

1 January 1948

“O brave new world, That has such people in’t.”

The Tempest, V.1.

A lovely line for New Year’s Eve 1947.

“O wonder! How many goodly creatures are there here!”

It is a touching confirmation of the year that has just ended, with a thousand threads running in every direction through an endlessly colourful fabric. It frees the words from the desperate irony of Aldous Huxley’s book title.

Not a bad beginning.

Omine auctus—strengthened by the omen.

“How beauteous mankind is!”

And yet, alas, I am being tormented by a hollow tooth: an oracle from the underworld.

On J. K. (to G. von Schmoller):

He is not a jurist but a logicist, someone devoted to pure logic, who happens to concern himself with legal problems and masters them effortlessly—schoolmasters them, in fact—because he does not suffer in the slightest from the problems that are specific to law.

Existentially, he is not a jurist. It is cheap nowadays to criticize a fashionable word like “existential.” But we should not forget what the word meant when it still had existential force of its own.

The real tests still lie ahead of us.

When they come, the foam of cleverness that has no connection with the substance of things will disappear by itself.

The logicist as theologian!

Of course he can do that too.

Until now, theology and jurisprudence were the “positive” sciences. They had something positively given to them: a revelation fixed in written form. Then came an enormous confusion.

Rules made by human beings for human beings were suddenly supposed to define the essence of positivism, while the supposedly assumption-free exact natural sciences claimed the word “positivism” for themselves.

Jurisprudence then shares the fate of theology. And now the abyss of the dilemma opens before it: theology or technology.

2 January 1948

Greater sensitivity means greater hostility and an enormous increase in the possibilities of hostility.

Kierkegaard’s very real hostility toward journalists.

No one has yet thought about the infinitely sensitive instrument—the sensorium—that must arise, along with an equally intensified sensitivity to the sound of words and language, once pure instrumental music exists.

Germany overdosed on the foreign element that was, in itself, necessary.

In the end came the great vomiting, after more than a hundred years in which the demand for purity had been overstimulated beyond endurance.

“You can’t go home again”?

You cannot return to the womb!

My present stay in Plettenberg: an arrow that has already been fired returns to the bowstring and seems to ask to be fired once again.

The somewhat naïve assumption is that the bowstring is still as tight and strong as it was fifty years ago.

Strangely, no one thinks about the archer.

5 January 1948

Good prospects for new forms of criminalization.

Enmity will be abolished by abolishing the distinction between enemy and criminal.

Samuel Butler, Erewhon (1872), Chapter XI, “Some Erewhonian Trials”:

“Misfortune is considered more or less criminal, but it admits of classification, and a court is assigned to each of the main heads under which it can be supposed to fall.”76

The judge then says:

“It is not my business to justify the law.”

Among the Erewhonians, being born to sick parents is a particularly serious crime.

Augustine’s Civitas Dei, the City of God, is certainly not a utopia.

Why not? Because its decisive orientation toward the world beyond rules utopia out.

So does utopia necessarily belong to this world?

What, then, happens to its satirical character?

The irony is directed only against the present order that is being rejected, never against the ideal condition being proposed.

Rational = activist.

Pan-interventionism.

Pan-criminalization.

Enemy and criminal, harmful creature and criminal, moral condemnation and crime: everything becomes a crime, with retroactive effect.

Anything that you cannot make “swerve” yourself, but which swerves by itself like an Epicurean atom, is treated as a crime.

Whatever does not belong to you, you must not tolerate.

So declare it criminal and destroy it!

Make sure you secure the position of prosecutor in good time!

6 January 1948

To R. Smend:

The year 1948 will give people many opportunities to look back and draw connections.

There seems to have been something in the soil of German Idealism after all. And the rubble left by the sceptical break with it now seems to be turning into a field of ambiguous, rumbling, theogonic beginnings.7778

(Smend’s wording in the essay “The Influence of Nineteenth-Century German Constitutional and Administrative Legal Theory,” Deutsche Rechtswissenschaft, January 1939, p. 39.)

But you know your own path.

And I sincerely hope that in the coming year too you will feel rewarded, through good results and worthwhile achievements, for work that has demanded so much sacrifice from you.

7 January 1948

Feelings, moods, situations, surroundings—the whole accompaniment that remains unspoken, unwritten, even unthought—clings to the apparently self-contained word. It clings to the sentence too, to the movement and gesture of a piece of writing that seems purely intellectual or purely inward. And it changes the interval between the tones for all time. It does so just as the harmonization of the passage “Sei Euch vertraut” in the Prize Song changes what would otherwise be a simple melodic movement through a triad. It is not only tone that makes the music. There is also the sequence of tones, different tones sounding at once, the changes in harmony, the changes of key.

The reply from Kluxen, my friend from youth, to my letter of 29 December.

First impression: childish.

The same juvenile arrogance and desire to dominate as ever.

Pity for poor Fritz Brust, who is dismissed as “unchanging.” He rejects the idea of creating any continuity with the Strasbourg years.

The self-satisfaction of the initiate who has managed to save himself from a catastrophe.

All that is missing is Switzerland—the mountains.

Then: the old friend who changes, who keeps moving on without end.

The feeling of an old bond contained in a friendship like this.

Respect for every other person, and for the path along which he too is travelling.

Finally:

You—I do not like to begin talking about it.

<…> there is talk of “space” <…>

to that extent it is a <…> first answer to your idea <…>.

I felt driven to send him Land and Sea, and to write with it:

As an acknowledgment of receipt, I am enclosing an attempt to introduce my child to world history.

You are of course not the intended reader of this little work. So you need not interrupt your own work for a single moment.

I merely wanted—good-natured as you know me to be, and as the least self-righteous person in the world—to give you the chance to listen in ad libitum, if you feel like it.

So, heartfelt thanks!

Always yours,

C. S.

Sent him Land and Sea on 10 January 1948, with the dedication:

καὶ ἡ θάλασσα οὐκ ἔστιν ἔτι—“and the sea was no more.”

I wanted to write as the dedication:

I have passed through all of this, and all of this has passed through me.

Finally:

Sors de l’enfance.

Come out of childhood.

Just wait.

Everything is coming toward you.

This too will pass through you.

It may be that he is still the same old ego-mad seeker after gods and fetishes, who only wants the right to find the god he has been seeking and then contemptuously throw him into a corner.79

8 January 1948

(To H. Barion:)

It helps understanding and conversation if we have a few common figures and model situations to which we can refer.

Benito Cereno, for example. Or the non-hero of Kafka’s Trial.

It did me good and strengthened me that you approach Kafka only from the satirical side, not from the side of tragic groaning that he himself intended. That is a sign of your still-unbroken health.

Perhaps it is also because you have not yet looked deeply enough into the secularized machinery of justice.

I carry a little more baggage in that respect.

When I was a young trainee lawyer in 1912, a famous attorney once revealed to me, late at night and in a state of complete honesty, the deepest secret of his existence. He gave me the final expression of his most intimate wish, and of his idea of the “rule-of-law state,” in a single sentence:

“There should be no court of last instance.”

(On W. Weber’s report:)

The very thing that excites my admiration—its exact and objective presentation—has the opposite effect on the typical committee man. This type, the type now sitting in judgment over us, can tolerate only a small dose of logical and factual rigor. It must be administered carefully.

A few notes from the heart are needed.

Joseph Kaiser’s dissertation showed me how automatically the opposition between state and Church now works.

Anyone who is not Church—not Curia—is immediately placed on the side of the state, and specifically of the totalitarian state. Yet the real problem is the totalitarian party. It is difficult to make this clear to people who have never been trained by Marxist thought.

The totalitarian state is something both unavoidable and capable of being made rational.

The problem is the totalitarian party.

One might have thought that people in Germany would gradually have understood this. But correct insights do not establish themselves so quickly.

Least of all among officials serving state institutions.80

9 January 1948

Identity: the identity of time and space at the moment when something is concretely located. That is the present. That is total presence.

Political restorations are no less utopian than ten-year or hundred-year plans. They are artificial attempts to make something present again: re-presentations, acts of making-present, re-presentifications, attempts to force continuity back into existence.

A brilliant and successful representation on the grand scale comes dangerously close to these manufactured acts of re-presenting.

10 January 1948

So now the people with the “cast-iron concepts” are arriving, as Dostoevsky called them. But the cast iron is already beginning to dissolve.

For:

11 January 1948

The products created by the breakdown of German Idealist philosophy are at work.

A theogony of rubble.

When I hear Max Planck or Heisenberg—or even C. F. von Weizsäcker—philosophizing today, I hear only an echo of G. F. Knapp or Heinrich Rickert.

The Protestant parsonage.81

Quantum physics is primarily metaphysics. It was born not only from the spirit of Neo-Kantianism, but even more from its concepts.

Reply to Pierre Linn, responding to his letter of 24 December:

You speak of “vagabondage,” and tell me that you “detest this style.”

You speak of Georges B.[ernanos], and I share your opinion. I have the slight impression that this concerns me personally as well. I believe it does, Mr Linn. I know it all too well to start offering apologies or evasions of that kind.

In an age of frank analysis and <…>.

But here, especially in my own case, we are dealing with a problem of situation.

The phenomenon, the problem, and even the very idea of “vagabondage” undergo existential changes, especially on soil where the opposing forces and tendencies of the world meet in a violent and chaotic collision.

In a country where opposing movements from West and East clash and penetrate one another;

in a region that is becoming more and more a “no man’s land” every day—that is, simple and pure nihilism—and at the same time an “everyman’s land”—that is, a complex field of theogonic forces released since 1840 by the breakdown of Protestantism and the philosophy of Idealism.82

I have thought a great deal about what you said in 1936 about the Idealist state.83

The confirmations I have seen since then are striking.

The missing link in the logical and systematic chain is the idea of the plan and the concept of utopia.

And so:

Brave New World!

Your conversation with me is not that of Boethius with the Visigothic king Theodoric. It seems to me much more like that of a senator in Aquitaine with Saint Severinus, the saint of 8 January, who lived in Noricum around the year 500.84

The historical parallel fits the parallel you draw with the age of Charlemagne.

The differences you speak of are only appearances.

Apart from two hundred years—1713 to 1914—Christian Europe has always been a pitiful thing, invaded from every side.

Christendom too was only a fleeting interval.

We are still—as in the year 500 or 800—inside the Christian aeon.

Still in agony.

And every essential event is, with much <pain> and <…>, nothing more than a matter of the Kat-echon:

“the one who holds back,”

qui tenet nunc,

“the one who now restrains,”

as in the Second Epistle of Saint Paul to the Thessalonians, chapter 2, verse 7.

You know my theory of the κατέχων, the katechon. It dates from 1932. I believe that in every century there is a concrete bearer of this restraining force, and that the task is to find him. I shall be very careful not to discuss this with theologians, because I know the miserable fate of the great and poor Donoso Cortés.

What we are dealing with is a total presence hidden beneath the veils of history.

Allow me85 one more personal word about my “vagabondage.”

I now find myself in Westphalia, in my father’s house, where in 1937 I attended my parents’ golden wedding anniversary.

I sleep in the room where my father slept, where he died in November 1945 at the age of ninety-two.

From my window I can see the Catholic cemetery where my parents lie, and where a grave has been reserved for my wife and me for twenty years.

I take the same walks I have taken for more than fifty years.

The economic situation has changed, of course.

We have been “dismantled,” and Mrs Schmitt is buried in the daily struggle to find enough bread.

Even so: this is a certain continuity of place, even a stabilitas loci, a stability of place, in a time of cataclysm, earthquakes, and universal nihilism.

As for existentialism, I find your diagnosis entirely correct and even—forgive me—very existentialist in itself.

Heidegger’s existentialism, with all its offshoots, is deeply atheistic. And yet Kierkegaard, a genuinely authentic Christian, a father of the invisible Church, remains the father, the great master, and the true source of all existentialism.

Kierkegaard’s existentialism is even more deeply Christian than Heidegger’s is atheistic.

Atheist existentialism seems to me like a profoundly Christian attack on Christianity.

Only the Marxists notice this and become alarmed by it.

Existentialism without Kierkegaard the Christian is nothing more than a performance of Hamlet without the Prince of Denmark.

Have you read The Concept of Anxiety, 1844 (!), and The Sickness Unto Death, 1849 (!)?

You are kind enough to ask whether there are any books that interest me.

My interest is very great. For example, I am looking—because of its title—for Lavelle’s La présence totale (Total Presence), published in 1930, I think. Then James Burnham, The Managerial Revolution, unless it merely repeats what we had already discovered in 1920–30. And also anything at all, book or pamphlet, by R. Capitant published after 1938.

Bernanos’s pronouncements no longer interest me.

(Mrs Schmitt asks whether the letter of August 1947 for Mrs Linn arrived, and also a small September gift—a little piece of Venetian lace <perhaps>.)

12 January 1948

What?

Walt Whitman?

We in twentieth-century Europe know boastful figures of a very different order from the <…> types of the nineteenth century.

I have defied the escapades of fate.

I have looked death by the executioner’s hand in the face.

Three times I sat in the belly of the fish.

I have tasted defeat in civil war.

Inflations and deflations.

Revolutions and restorations.

Changes of regime and burst water pipes.

Currency reform.

Bombing raids.

Interrogations.

Camps and barbed wire.

Hunger and cold.

Ragged clothes and hideous bunkers.

I was discriminated against, defamed, and dismantled.86

Terror from below and terror from above.

Terror on the ground and terror from the air.

Legal terror and illegal terror.

Terror from Nazis and <Jews>.

Brown terror, red terror, and mottled terror.

I passed through all of it, and all of it passed through me.

(So sings—or rather boasts—the Walt Whitman of the twentieth century.)

But part of the superiority of the present age is precisely that such boasting must now come to an end.

All that is missing is a Rilke-style conclusion:87

O happiness of the gnat that still jumps within!

O wool of every worm <…>.

Meanwhile I keep encountering the fatherly teacher of my brother Thomas Hobbes: the profound Francis Bacon.

His Sermones fideles, in the Leiden edition of 1644, have now become my devotional book.

Here are the basic political and philosophical insights from which Hobbes proceeds:

De invidia, on envy, Chapter IX, and De ira, on anger, Chapter LV, are the source of the psychology of competition.

And then: atheists as calmer citizens.

The conclusion: all the fox’s cunning and its many tricks are nothing beside the power of the one lion.

The fable of the fox and the lion.

“For a powerful and faithful friend gives more protection than countless arts and tricks,” etc.

I like that.

Hobbes as Bacon’s pupil.88

13 January 1948

An encounter with the grand style of German Idealism:

Hegel, Encyclopedia, § 248.

Again and again, the extraordinary position of Samuel Butler.

How can anyone write the intellectual history of the nineteenth century without knowing him?

How could Ernst Jünger write The Worker without knowing him?

The most intellectually superior treatment of the subject: technology and technocracy.

Irony and satire as elements of magic?

Irony is deadly serious.

Not the irony of the great English writers.

“The servant glides by imperceptible approaches into the master.”

“Is not machinery linked with animal life in an infinite variety of ways?”

This belongs with the Leviathan as the great machine.

15 January 1948

Visit from Günther Krauss.

Homo homini homunculus.

Man is a little man to man.

Homunculus homunculo Deus.

The little man becomes God to the little man.

And so on.

We shall have to drink this entire series of variations down to the dregs, until today’s humanism has driven itself ad absurdum and all the way down to Acheron.

No kneeling before this heartless god of global deception.

The small human being, the parvus homo, grows still smaller. He becomes a homunculus, a little manufactured man.

The great human being, the magnus homo, grows still greater. He becomes the superman.

That is:

Deus.

God.

Homo homini homo—man is simply man to man—is the zero point of pure indifference.89

In practice, that relationship cannot hold for even a second. It immediately divides again in order to create tension. It splits into polar opposites, like positively and negatively charged electrons.

One rises.

The other falls.

Illum oportet crescere, istum autem minui.

One must increase; the other must decrease.

The magnus homo, the great man, “reaches up toward divinity.” He becomes a manufacturer.

The parvus homo, the little man, becomes “more animal than an animal.” He becomes a manufactured product.

The wolf is really still a very human category.

Compared with the manufactured products of the brave new world, the wolf is still a creature.

Even the werewolf is.

The true intensifications, in the direction of both good and evil, arise only with the intervention of spirit.

The most astonishing document of the abyssal depth of German Idealism:

“But if spiritual contingency, arbitrary will, goes so far as evil, even this is infinitely higher than all of nature—higher than the lawful course of the stars or the innocence of the plant—for that which goes astray in this way is still spirit.”

Hegel, Encyclopedia, § 248.

That is magnificent.

The most evil, lowest wickedness of the human spirit is still greater than the starry heavens and the most beautiful flower. Because what goes astray in this way is still spirit.

What a sentence for our German situation in 1944!

The generation immediately after Hegel gave its answer:

Max Stirner.

Truly, the new products created by the breakdown of this philosophy will be stronger than every attempt to restore the old Churches. They will unleash theurgic forces—forces that try to make divine powers real in the world—that will make our miserable self-righteous people on both right and left shudder, along with all those who profit from the gigantic humiliation of the German people.

Instead of the renouveau catholique, the Catholic revival that took place between 1910 and 1933 and went unnoticed by official institutions, we shall now experience a fantastic retour offensif: a counterattack by the philosophy of German Idealism, armed with myth—which in reality means armed with theurgy.

Hegel above all. He will cease to be, in theory, a museum piece preserved by academic philosophy, and in practice, a weapon monopolized by Moscow Marxism.

16 January 1948

If Heidegger, with his acts of re-ontologizing, can produce such broad effects even in Gallia docens, teaching and learned France, what depth of effect will Konrad Weiss’s “Christian Epimetheus” have in Germany!

Werner Blischke was supposed to discover the identity of the I. K. who wrote an article on Sartre in issue no. 4 of Kurier, 6 January 1948:

“The Longing for Innocence.”

The idea was to verify the immanent existentialism of the article. But the author could not be identified.

All the better.

Alfred Döblin defines utopia:

“It is a human plan to interrupt history, in order to leap out of history and arrive at a stable perfection.”

That is illuminating for understanding Marx.

Marx’s claim to be “scientific” means claiming that one can change the world without leaping out of history.90

The machine is the instrument assigned to utopia. It is the weapon used to carry out the plan.

The machine differs from the tool because, within itself, it transcends the human being who operates the tool—the craftsman.

Utopia is already present in this transcendence.91

The machine dethrones the human being. It removes him from his place. That is the deeper meaning of Adolf Caspary’s The Machine Utopia (1930), which attacks the illusion that the machine could solve the problem created by the masses.

For Marx, the machine is the means of changing the world without leaping out of history.92

What does Revelation 21:1 mean:93

a new earth;

without a sea?

A utopia?

What does the destruction of the island of Heligoland in 1947/48 mean?

A piece of land is turned into sea. It is sunk into the sea.

Its population is evacuated as refugees. For the first time in history.

U-topia: the transformation of a place with an exceptionally strong sense of location into nothing.

Destruction.

17 January 1948

A summons.

The first in eight months.

The nervousness of a hunted animal when a shot is fired.

The objective powers that only yesterday seemed so interesting to me, so worthy of legal and theoretical construction, now reveal themselves as heartless enemies.

A constant shift between the subjective and the objective.

The heralds of subjectivity deceive one another, whether the name is Max Stirner or James Joyce. But objective greatness already means, in itself: a poor, deceived, plundered subject.

The landscape only appears objective.

A political complex of power is much more objective. But ultimately even that is nothing more than an état d’âme, a state of the soul.

A Hero’s Life in the style of Richard Strauss—with the hero’s companion perhaps thrown in as a finale in the style of Brother Straubinger—all of that has become foolish, cloudy foam.

Better, perhaps, the happiness of the gnat in the style of Rossini.

The happiness of the gnat.

The animals of the forest and the flowers of the field.

Life and creation arising directly from matter itself.

The blissfully accelerated circulation of the blood.

Life itself, without problems.

The removal of the barrier of nature so that we can have direct, unrestricted access to natural nature.

Deus sive natura.

God, or Nature.

To dissolve into nature.

To abolish all distance, and therefore every perspective.

Form without perspective.

Not even the giving of form: the unfolding of form.

Indeed—most paradoxically—the unleashing of form.

Theism.

Transcendence.

Even intelligence.

All of these still imply distance, perspective, difficulty, a falling-away from the pure immanence of the immediate, natural, unobstructed here-and-now and of bodily existence without problems.

So: down with distance!

Pure identity.

Do you see now which side the logic of pure democracy lies on? And who will find the absolution of the World Spirit for every atrocity, even the most inhuman ones?94

Now we Germans are everything at once.

We are the περισσόν, as the Pythagoreans called it: the excess that goes beyond equilibrium, disturbing and yet fertile. We are περισσόν and περίψημα—the excess and the refuse, the cast-off thing. And at the same time we are the ἄτοπον: the thing that has no proper place.

The point and moment when one opposite passes into the other, while itself being neither one.

The point of μεταβολή, of transformation.

The ἐναντίον, the opposite that participates in what is different from itself and yet remains independent.

The moment in which things are neither separated nor mixed—οὔτε διακρίνεται οὔτε συγκρίνεται—as Plato’s Parmenides puts it.

I am the ἄτοπον against utopia!!

No-place against U-topia?

The space I gain is the ἄτοπον!!

18 January 1948

To H. P. Ipsen:

From the intellectual side, I admired the cleanliness and precision.

From the moral side, I admired the patience and self-control with which you erected a systematically thought-out structure of legal argument while fully aware that beneath it opened a gaping abyss.

The gaping abyss is, of course, the unanswered question: whose authority are German courts and administrative authorities actually exercising today?

The concept of subjugation, which you deliberately avoid bringing to the foreground, serves as the legal vehicle for an intermediate condition.

The fundamental injustice of this condition seems to me to lie in the fact that the eternal connection between protection and obedience—a connection valid even in Hobbes’s state of nature—has been torn apart.

The person who has been subjugated obeys, and despite obeying is cast into misery.

19 January 1948

To H. Winckelmann:

Let me tell you at once, with surrealist openness, that the word—and still more the concept—Gesetz, “law,” fills me with horror and dread in every possible way: conceptually; intellectually; through psychological association; and, last but not least, even through its sound.

What horrifies me are the orgies of Setzen—of setting, positing, laying down—and the terror of the “positing of posits” into which we have been drawn since 1848 as though into the Maelstrom.

I am prepared to spend hours giving you examples and evidence: historical; linguistic and etymological; conceptual and systematic; constitutional; and from natural law.

Everything that is positively posited and posed is now struck by this curse.

Just as every “will to” anything whatsoever is now intellectually exhausted and condemned by history. And yet the positivist Walpurgis Night will continue to intensify for some time.

We shall have to drink the foul brew down to the dregs. So I suppress my horror and ask instead: do you think it is possible to repair the bankruptcy of the legislator by beginning from the judge?

Could one at least achieve something like a compulsory settlement?

Perhaps with the help of English methods which, in themselves, now seem like a luxury belonging to an old and wealthy country?

Do you want to create a new judicial estate?95

You will answer that you intend to write a work about method, and that once concepts have been honestly clarified, consequences will follow from them naturally.

Their strength and speed, you will say, can safely be left to those mysterious powers

qui mutant corda hominum et gentium—“who change the hearts of human beings and of nations.”

Good.

In that case I would begin—and indeed I did begin, in my lectures on “The Present Situation of European Legal Science”—with “law” in the full concreteness of its present problems.

I would begin from its existential bankruptcy.

Forgive the fashionable word “existential,” but it once had a very genuine meaning. That is why I prefer to start with the distinction between “legality and legitimacy.”

First I try to make clear to myself the many very different things that are called “laws” today. Then I ask: is the judiciary, in concreto, more “legitimate” than all legality? And truly, your faith proves to me that it could be. This also explains my reserve toward the word and concept “natural law.”

You want to return to the jungle of these difficulties.

Video vestigia ineuntium, non exeuntium!

I see the tracks of those who went in, but none of those who came out!

Compare the enclosed passage from Ernst Troeltsch.

Ever since that terrifying formula appeared—Deus sive (!) Natura,

God or (!) Nature—I have regarded the Babylonian confusion of language as incurable.

According to the last words left by poor Alfred Delp S. J.—hanged on 2 February 1945 together with our Popitz—the ordinary city-dweller is not “godless.” He is “incapable of God.” And so he slides quite naturally into your biological law of nature!

Irresistibly.

O brave new world!

(Then on the Max Weber edition and the cleaning of the Augean stables; the remark from New York about the “unbearable” Max Weber.)

This as a first reply from a monad reduced, even in the matter of typewriter and paper, to the status—or rather the situs, the physical situation—of an ordinary consumer.

In the morning, on the English plan to destroy Heligoland:

Here the outrage is directed immediately against the elements themselves.

Normally land was wrested from the sea.

Here land is pushed down into the sea.

Inhabited land.

The homeland of human beings.

Sacred land is deliberately destroyed.

Destroyed precisely as land. For military reasons.

Horrifying.

During the war we shuddered at the planned scelus infandum, the unspeakable crime, of forcing Leningrad back into the swamp.

Méchante et néfaste.

Wicked and disastrous.

“All joy wants eternity.”

Does it?

Joy wants nothing.

It is the total presence of the <…> present <…>.

It knows nothing else.

It understands nothing else.

It wants nothing else.

It wants nothing but itself, to enjoy itself.

It does not want eternity.

These <…> are kitsch formulations left behind by former theologians.96

“In German, one lies whenever one is polite.”

Not quite.

Unfortunately it is much worse.

In German, politeness turns too quickly into irony.

Into crude irony.

What is missing is the self-aware play of convention.

The slyness of a journeyman’s language corrupted by theologians.

The reservation of inwardness. For a hundred years now, since positivism, it has been malicious.

Its true poet is Wilhelm Busch: the humorist of malicious pleasure and envy.

22 January 1948

When I read what Edmund A. Walsh had written about me and my Concept of the Political in True Rather Than False Geopolitics for Germany (1946), the word Schafsnase escaped my lips.

“Sheep-nose.”

The word itself deserves analysis.

That is how deeply I remain trapped in a purely intellectual attitude.

Even toward someone already swinging the noose with which he intends to put it around my neck.97

Only afterward did it occur to me that this passage was an act of nastiness deliberately calculated for Schafsnasen. And that this nastiness in turn goes back to a crook, poor Gurian, who in his own way is trying to avenge himself for his own crookedness and uses a Jesuit to do it.

Here we see the chain of purposes and motives.

Chains and webs like this are what appear to us poor human beings when we try to understand the “connections” through which God’s providence supposedly “works.”

But God does not work. Only the crooks work.

The villains.

The sheep-noses.

So let them carry on working.

God had long since turned everything toward the good by the time [they] pulled the trigger and set their tools and projectiles in motion.

23 January 1948

A boundary has something magical about it.

Spatially magical. So says R. Kassner.

In time, what corresponds to the boundary is not another boundary but the “turn,” the moment of change.

Time corresponds not to magic but to freedom.

Will.

Mediation.

Tone, rather than word and myth.

Art.

With boyish seriousness, as an “ancient” man, I concern myself with the magic of space. I do not want to grasp it. Still less do I want to manufacture it. But I want to know it, and by knowing it preserve it for others.

A sole retriever.

Ancient.

I see the final space: my grave. I see it dissolving.

My homeland, the river—everything is being destroyed. But I hold on to it.

I go down with them.

And they go down with me.

The secret of my life. This is my property. I take it with me into the grave.

Property is only what one can take into the grave. So today there is no property left. Only the dead body. And that, apparently, is better burned. So the pacifists, the abortionists, and the advocates of cremation triumph.98

After reading Kant, Kleist told a friend: now there is nothing left that one can take into the grave.

Hegel: the Holy Sepulchre is empty.

The error of the Crusades. That is how they—and Däubler—interpret the resurrection of the flesh.

The only thing I inherit is my own body.

Truly, that is it.

Däubler: thinghood is dead; the word fills space!

No.

Tone fills spaces.

Indeed, tone abolishes them.

Däubler’s Northern Lights is not word. It is tone. It is tonality.

Every act of destruction necessarily produces so many attempts at restoration that the confusion becomes terrible.

Typical of the rubbish bin attached to every modern movement: all the anti-alcohol people; the anti-nicotine people; the anti-meat people; all the Bible Students; everyone joins in.

Naturally, the fellow-traveller is the only person who is truly guilty.

Making the sign of the cross produces greater world-spanning radiation than all the manufacturers of atomic bombs.

I make the sign of the cross over the chaos of my affects and emotions.

And behold:

Christ walks upon the sea.

24 January 1948

With Annette, the sign of the cross becomes only the “phosphorus plant,” the plant of life.

That is actually rather bad.

Her intensely scientific, determinist positivism.

Her tribute to her age. She paid it with feminine humility and honesty.

Equally deep and honest is her service in the “temple,” as she calls it. But why does she say “temple”? She is not ancient at all. There is nothing humanist or classical about her.99

30 January 1948

Meanwhile even Max Stirner, with his nihilism, has become nothing more than a boaster. He once seemed so irrefutably right.

What could be more immediate, more inalienable, more undeniable than my body and my ownership of it?100

Surely I take it into the grave with me?

Poor illusionist.

You do not take it into the grave. It goes into the crematorium.

Perhaps its ashes will be scattered to every wind.

Brother Straubinger practised this with a bad conscience. Those who followed as victors appear to have practised it with a good one.

Which is worse here: the good conscience or the bad?

A good conscience organized with the help of the justice system is the worst thing of all.

Excellent remark by Christian Wolff:

“The others did evil things with a good conscience; we do good things with a bad one.”

That is the situation which, both inwardly and outwardly, attracts every demon of revenge and every plunderer.

The vis attractiva of the bad conscience: its power of attraction.

Twice as powerful in the case of a fundamentally stupid and wretched devil whom German cultivated culture first summoned into existence and then abandoned.

The World Spirit grants absolution to the good conscience of those who are completely evil.

Naturally, anyone who has the opportunity to legalize his power simply by declaring it to be law will make use of that wonderful opportunity. He will not allow this <…> legal <…> surplus value to escape him.

No ruler has ever given up such an opportunity. This too belongs to the total phenomenon of legal “positivism” in the age of legality.

31 January 1948

I take nothing into the grave. Because the graves themselves are being destroyed, even if I still manage to reach my own private grave.

Today property is only what one takes into death.

Germany: put in brackets and at the same time bracketed out, inside a world splitting open.

On Nebel’s Tyranny and Freedom:

Now these intellectuals abuse the poor German people and list all its faults and disgraces.

The model is Luther abusing the poor peasants. Or the Anabaptists in 1535.

German cultivated culture itself shares in the guilt. It seems unable to escape this pattern.

The reverse case is fundamentally the same:

Goethe’s heroic poem about old Blücher—“conscious and great”!

1 February 1948

Measured by the standards that rule today, Kierkegaard was a dreadful reactionary and enemy of the people. He would have to be discriminated against, defamed, dismantled, and exterminated. And that is without even mentioning D.[onoso] C.[ortés].

My mistake was the good-naturedness of my attempts to adapt.

My inability to believe that human beings could really be as stupid and vulgar as they are, and as they prove to me every day.101

2 February 1948

It would be instructive—and necessary—to make a sociological comparison between the émigrés who returned to France in 1815 and those who returned to Germany in 1945.102 But even as a passing observation, that is probably already life-threatening and blasphemous.

“La Petite Cité”—the “Little City,” as distinct from the Grande Cité—the inner circle: this is what Augustin Cochin calls the specific formation103 for which I am trying to find a name: elite, political-criminal association, and so on. What matters is that he got his inspiration from Bryce and Ostrogorski—that is, from the “machine” of a political “party.” O Roberto Michels, come to our aid! “Petite Cité” is not good. But matière votante—“voting material”—is magnificent.

Again and again Cochin stresses the “social forces”: ces êtres inhumains, un Chalier, un Marat, un Carrier ne sont que les produits mécaniques du travail collectif—these inhuman beings, a Chalier, a Marat, a Carrier, are merely the mechanical products of collective activity. Calling it anarchy—or nihilism—explains nothing. Those are merely the rotting entrails from which, according to Aristotle, bees are born.

Do you now understand the full enormity of my crime? It is one of those crimes that can never be forgiven: curiosity about the true motives and the real driving forces behind organized indignation.

Augustin Cochin, Sociétés de pensée, p. 111: “The thesis of self-defense appears with democracy itself.”

Always the same thing: utopia—the product of abstract thought—against reality.

3 February 1948

My calendar of saints includes not only Jean Bodin and Thomas Hobbes, but also Donoso Cortés and Augustin Cochin, along with all those who were out of step with their age—provided they did not, like Nietzsche, turn their untimeliness into a publicity stunt—and all those who honestly despaired, provided they did not, like Kleist, solve the problem for themselves by suicide.

So what are you doing here now?

With boyish pride, you picked fights in the great world with truly great enemies. With Ra. and with great Jews. And now you are throwing yourself away on petty provincial brethren, you small-stakes player. You hide behind walls and pass your turn out of laziness and cowardly comfort.

You can’t go home.104

The genius of Villiers de l’Isle-Adam. Among the new mythic figures of our age—alongside Benito Cereno, the Chief Forester, and who else?—there belongs, above all, “Le Convive des dernières fêtes,” “The Guest at the Last Celebrations.”

Poe created mythic situations—the Maelstrom, the dungeon of the Inquisition—but no mythic figures. The beginning of one in Pym is too weak. This Convive, by contrast, is a mythic figure of extraordinary grandeur.

Annette breathed mythic symbolism into inherited images and situations: “a Helot who, grinding his teeth in the misery of slavery, gulped down the wine the tyrant gave him.” But she remained outside history.

Kleist found the bear in “The Puppet Theatre.”

Yet all of this—with the exception of Benito Cereno, of course—is surpassed by this Convive: the German baron who, while remaining perfectly acceptable in polite society, goes insane because he cannot legally satisfy his thirst for blood by holding an important public office, parce qu’il ne peut remplir légalement—because he cannot legally fulfill, and Villiers underlines legally!—l’office: the office of executioner and torturer. This Convive appears as “Baron Saturne” at the Paris carnival, at the Opera Ball, and is invited along with the others.

All those Germans in Paris from 1940 to 1944 were, after all, nothing but convives des dernières fêtes—guests at the final celebrations.

Compare the Chief Forester of 1939.

7 February 1948

Is there a parallel today with the “stillness” of 1938?105

Could it happen again that we Germans now carry out the communist revolution that was due in 1918—miserably, at foreign hands and after the proper historical moment has passed—just as, in the collapse of 1918–19,106 we belatedly carried out the bourgeois revolution that had been due in 1848? Or will we carry it out completely posthumously, in a utopian-romantic form and within an entirely different historical setting?

Just as we experienced the Peasants’ War of 1525 again in the form of the Reich Food Estate of 1933; the thirty-year Saxon revolt against Charlemagne as the Nordic Society in Bremen’s Böttcherstraße; or the Anabaptist scandal of 1534 as the defense of Berlin in 1945?

One ought to examine very carefully, and in concrete detail, the way different historians use contrary-to-fact conditional sentences. One would discover some very strange things.

I will begin with Gobineau’s On the Inequality of the Human Races: if, around 300 BC, there had been a strong nation of Aryan race in the West alongside the Romans, the Romans would never have been able to rise to power (II, 238).

Or, on the same page: the Romans could only have lost their supremacy if Indian or Germanic peoples had been their neighbors—but these did not arrive until the fifth century, and so on.

You can drive yourself quite mad following such unreal possibilities.

Why, incidentally, are these not utopias?

Uchronias?

Why are uchronias—imaginary versions of history—more ridiculous than utopias?

8 February 1948

Anxiety is the possibility of freedom. Whoever has learned how to be properly anxious has learned the highest thing of all. Reality is easier than possibility. We must not cheat the possibility that wants to teach us; we must not dishonestly reject the anxiety that wants to save us, and so on.

Read it again because of some trivial occasion.

Anxiety about this anxiety.107

The “pain-killing remedy”—what a strange phrase.

Where does the pain go when it has been “killed”? Martin Beheim-Schwarzbach asks this quite rightly. Where do all these pains go? They must remain somewhere. And where do the anxieties go when they are described away?

I am becoming very interested in this Martin Beheim-Schwarzbach. He is more reflective, and less clouded, than Thomas Mann.

9 February 1948

The discussion with Sartre in Berlin on 1 February 1948.

What he is amounts to the same thing as the solitary, critical, atheistic outsider Bruno Bauer.

Bauer was more of a constructor of history108—old versus new—but he already possessed the necessary “critique of the state”: including critique from within socialist Marxism, meaning criticism of one’s own state rather than somebody else’s, criticism of the state that grants your license to speak.

Anyone who appears publicly in Berlin today should not <…>.

The prophet and master of these <…> slave <…> can appear only with a great many permits, licenses, passports, approvals, and certificates. He will be very careful not to speak too critically about them. And yet this is precisely the existential, concrete reality of the whole discussion.

(Steiniger notices that Sartre’s The Flies, in France in 1944, worked against remorse, and that in Germany in 1948 it therefore works against denazification. He calls this an example of “dialectics.” It is nothing more than a change of situation while the wording stays the same—and a test of whether someone has any sense of reciprocity.)

Remorse dictated from above makes everyone complicit, says Sartre.

No one is free unless everyone is free. Hegel.

Who educates children for freedom?

The Christian or the atheist?

The very question of education already contains the limit of all freedom.

“Freedom” cannot possibly be the last word.

Libertas libertate perit: freedom is destroyed by freedom.

Always the same problem. Freedom can no more be the final principle than race can, or purity. And now, on top of everything else, “education for freedom.”

Just look at these heroes of freedom of the Ilya Ehrenburg type.

The brainwashers!

10 February 1948

What is a utopia? It is the abolition of humanity’s infinite possibilities by realizing one finite possibility: first imagined, then made real. Because every human thought eventually seeks fulfillment.

The sin of utopia lies in the belief that finite realization can abolish the anxiety contained in infinite possibility; that a finite achievement can free us from the sting of the infinite; that it can kill the bees of God that bother us, as though they were vermin.

Utopia is paradise located in a distant but still reachable future.

Our ability to think far into the distance is steadily declining. That is why the nineteenth-century utopian must eventually move from utopia to “positive science.” He must claim that paradise can begin tomorrow, if only we quickly and radically remove the final obstacle—the capitalists, the Jews, the Jesuits, or Hitler—and destroy it completely, eradicate it without leaving a trace.

Unfortunately, a few traces always remain.

Pauca tamen suberunt priscae vestigia fraudis: “Yet a few traces of the old corruption will remain.” So excuses remain as well, and there is still time to construct a new final enemy.

Erunt etiam altera bella: “There will also be other wars.”

But that is another question.

The subject of utopia is clear to me now. So is the utopian character of this whole complex of rationalism, Enlightenment, and positivism.109

What does Hobbes want?

Public peace and security. But he still knows: plena securitas in hac vita non expectanda—complete security is not to be expected in this life. So let us attempt what is possible. These are the modest utopians, the ones who are not yet intoxicated. They do not yet believe in global world peace.

Thomas More does not believe in it either. But the essential thing—the peccatum, the sin—is the organization of society for the purpose of abolishing anxiety: sécurité.

The only people who understood the peccatum, who recognized the sin, were the Lutherans.

Christian David, the builder of the first house in the Herrnhut settlement around 1730, says:

“And so we fight against our enemies: pride, lust, security, laziness, and idleness.”

But only the quiet people of the land thought like that.

The dominant tendency was activist and utopian.

At least give us some security.

The machine is not an instrument of happiness. It is an instrument of utopia. Yet machines do not appear in More—not yet. They do in Campanella.

The “unreal,” the irreal—something the French have felt very strongly—legality, meaning the state, and the machine: these are the two vehicles of this unreality and, in this sense, of the utopian.

Thomas More’s Utopia is not yet a scientific utopia. It is closer to a eutopia, a good place.

“More’s gay genius” was incapable of producing a machine-utopia.

And it is metaphysically, fatefully improbable that More—the man behind the great fourth scene of Act III of Richard III—could have meant the totalitarian planning inherent in the machine.

But what does it mean that he invented the name Utopia?

Does that not belong among the peccata, the sins, of neutralizing humanism, like Francisco de Vitoria’s Relectiones de Indis?

And Erasmus?

And the whole phenomenon of Erasmianism?

I ought to use this time to become much clearer about these humanist neutralizations. I should reread Konrad Weiß’s “The Present Problem of the Gothic” from 1927. I should analyze more carefully my enthusiasm for Christoph Steding’s non-book. I should bring fully to consciousness the deepest roots of my Barcelona lecture of October 1929. Only then would my interpretation of Vitoria be ready.

What is holding me back?

How did I myself formulate it, and write it down, on 21 July 1914, when the realization that I had been deceived was beginning to break through clearly?

“This is the feeling of the unchangeable. It is coming, and the wise man says nothing and does not resist.”

“How do you intend to defend yourself against death?”

Those exact words, more than thirty-three years ago.

Again and again I have fallen for the deception.

Again and again I have escaped it.

Again and again comes the realization “before which I remain still, as though I stood before a fate I had already accepted, like a man who is to be executed the next day and calmly awaits the terrible hour without really feeling its terror.” Those exact words, written down on 21 July 1914. That is the feeling of the unchangeable.

Both belong to death, which is itself the unchangeable—or, more precisely, they are a part of it, or merely an expression of it, one particular case of the unchangeable.

Read the diary entry of 12 October 1913:

“You can afford that,” the Privy Councillor remarked.

Touching to read that today.

It is also a formula for my life. I could afford many things, and I allowed myself many things.

Se payer quelque chose—perhaps that is how one should translate it: to treat oneself to something. It sounds less deluded that way, and it does not entirely forget the cost.

11 February 1948

My dislike of diaries and diary writers is too strong.

Most diary writers remind me of children sucking their fingers and sucking on everything else they can get their hands on. But there are magnificent diaries too, like Delacroix’s, and there are great accountants of the Absolute, like Léon Bloy.

The others, though—the well-read, literary Pepyses—really are no more than infants, even when they are terrible self-tormentors rather than Narcissuses like Samuel Pepys.110

The island in More is the dialectical atopos—the strange “non-place”—between the most solid possible location and utopian displacement from every location.

At this uncanny intermediate point stands Saint Thomas More with his island of Utopia, which in truth is a Eutopia, a good place.111

That is wonderful.

And with the deepest historical justice he was therefore made a saint—or, to put it more cautiously, absolved of the unintended consequences of his peccatum.

Vitoria will not be canonized, although he too is such a dialectical atopos.

12 February 1948

“The temptation of Francisco de Vitoria” did not consist in either defending the official doctrine—which did not exist—or remaining silent, as Verdross constructs the matter in his banal way, submitting himself to the official doctrine of today’s postwar world.

The temptation lay in neutralizing humanization.

Eritis sicut Logos: you shall become like the Logos. It lay in Erasmianism.

The Holy Spirit is not a skeptic.

More was not an ordained cleric but merely a clerc: a man of letters, a writer, not a priest. That is the secret of his great superiority—a superiority so quiet that it cannot even be heard or felt.

“The noble man remains in his room. If he forms his thoughts correctly, he does not need to publish them; they will find an echo more than a thousand miles away.” Confucius.

More is the mysterious Scrivener in Richard III, Act III, Scene 6:

“Enter a Scrivener.”

Almost immediately after the fabulous Scene 4 of the same act, which surely goes back to Thomas More—especially the portrayal of the tyrant’s fury over the word “if.”

Eureka!

The great clerc.

Bodin was one too.

Hobbes, by contrast, was a solitary wolf.

13 February 1948

What am I doing here?

I am not searching for the future, because I feel the powerlessness of both my inner and outer existence. I am discriminated against downward—and therefore upward as well. Nor am I searching for the past, because I do not want to survive myself by endlessly reflecting on myself.

So what am I doing? I am doing nothing. I am trying faithfully to cultivate the accidental reality of my own present in pure thought.

(A fine answer to put on a questionnaire from the employment office!)112

To Gerhard Nebel, thanking him for the dedication of Tyranny and Freedom: ξίφος ἐν μύρτου κλαδί—a sword in a myrtle branch.

The closing sentence of Bruno Bauer’s Christ and the Caesars:

“The sword of faith with which the princes of the Apostles opened a path for their congregation through the Roman imperial age, and then resisted the early medieval tendencies toward military dictatorship, was inherited by them from the Stoics, who, armed with the strength of conscience and conviction, threw themselves against the military triumphs of the Macedonians and Romans. The same sword will flash in the hands of the successors of the Stoics whenever a political power, amid the collapse of an obsolete world order, sees only a charter granting privilege rather than the work of universal liberation.”113

I wonder whether that good Nero scholar Gustav Würtenberg knows Bruno Bauer’s Christ and the Caesars. It is astonishing that he does not know L. Klages’s book on Alfred Schuler from 1941. That is the treasure house for the demonology of Nero that is, in fact, highly relevant today.

W. is no demonologist. He is a shuddering moralist, mocked by a dangerous and very specific demon: the diabolus ethicus, the ethical devil.

Hear, O man: Pan has awakened!

(Dedication of The Northern Light to Lothar Kreuz.)114

Wrote to Ernst Jünger, thanking him for the little booklet La salle d’attente:

I admired the impenetrable web of human destinies and book destinies.

Your name now stands in the light—or the shadow—of La Salette, and Léon Bloy has become a kind of godfather and neighbor to you!

Very strange.

News of Stülpnagel’s death:

formation dépendante du genre de mort—formation dependent on the manner of death.

The printed text omits the wonderful reflection that is essential not merely as an idea:

je cherchai alors à me souvenir des circonstances de ma mort—I then tried to remember the circumstances of my death. That sentence raises everything that follows above the merely dreamlike and gives the whole event its spiritual hyperreality. But I suppose the editor had his reasons.

While reading, I kept thinking of Drieu la Rochelle. I would have liked to ask him, in connection with this phosphorescent bath, about Villiers de l’Isle-Adam—not the fashionable, decadent, romantic Villiers tied to his period, but the initiate and occultist.

Villiers too would surely have regretted that the grands guerriers, the great warriors, are missing from the printed text.

So would Léon Bloy.

So would Drieu.

14 February 1948

Listen to this:

“I determine myself by subjecting myself to myself through action, and by thus bringing myself about, I constitute a world,” and so on.

I myself to myself.

Have we not been disgusted by this sort of thing for decades?

Did we run away from the honest private imperialist Fichte only to put up with these brazen insanities of the ego all over again? But because this comes to Germany under the protection of the victors, it is permitted here, and nobody dares to laugh.

I myself to myself.

A Buribunk straight out of the textbook of existentialism.

All he has to do is speak French and he receives every license.

I myself to myself.

“I am I, only I alone,” cried my namesake Carl Schmidt in 1845.

So this is what now enjoys the protection of the occupation powers, just as Roman law from 1939 to 1945 enjoyed the protection of the Axis.

An unexpected irony directed at the prosecution speech of the French prosecutor de Menthon at Nuremberg.

An unexpected revival of Max Stirner—especially his chapter on the relationship between the ego and the police.

Stirner’s “I,” too, refuses to become an object of thought.

15 February 1948

Carl Brinkmann considered it “unworthy of scholarship” not to mention my name in a bibliography.

I wrote to him:

I need only remember the situations in which the individual sentences of my note on Tocqueville were written, and I immediately fall silent whenever someone invokes the dignity of scholarship—a dignity that has been trampled underfoot in me and in my person.115

Careful: these “Radiations” might merely be reflections of oneself produced with a small pocket mirror.

What exactly did certain writers have against “space,” and why were they so strongly in favor of “time”?

Hausenstein, E. R. Curtius, and other humane, tasteful neutralizers? They still know intoxications of every kind, but no longer the intoxication of causality or the intoxication of finality; neither the intoxication of the abstract nor that of the concrete.

Gottfried Benn is the authentic German of the years 1919 to 1938, not the weak and ambitious fellow travelers.

Where does thirst go when it is quenched, and hunger when it is satisfied?

(See 8 February 1948.)

Where does the urge move to—the energy that was active in thirst and hunger?

16 February 1948

The secret:

“He” was, at the deepest level, compliant and obedient.

Oboedientia fecit hinc imperantem: obedience made him into the ruler. He was an imitator and absorber of cultivated ideas, but he took the concepts of his teachers more radically than the teachers themselves did. This kind of effectiveness made him great. But his teachers abandoned him. He wanted to be their executor: pure execution, a purely executive function. Yet the instructions he received from them were dishonest and full of reservations, like Luther’s instructions to the peasants. And so he became a ghost-horse.

Oboedientia fecit hinc imperantem.

The ruler is merely an executor.

The dictator only dictates the dicta that have been given to him.

The superiority of the so-called ideologues.

The dialectic of commanding and obeying—infinitely subtler than Hegel’s famous passage on master and servant, because here everything depends upon speaking and hearing. So man is a throw, a draft, a project: a preliminary design.

Strictly speaking, a planless plan without anyone who planned it.

Pan disappears; the plan enters the scene!

A beautiful example of the built-in oracular quality of the German language.

All you have to do is cultivate this sort of thing and you become a famous author.

17 February 1948

Early this morning, at six o’clock, Peterheinrich Kirchhoff gave me his Reclam copy of Max Stirner’s The Ego and Its Own. So Max is back with me.

Max, you faithful rogue, you always come back eventually, after you were so sadly lost to me in 1943/44 through Josef Wagner.

What do you want?

What are you plotting?

Listen to the first sentence of his that I read again:

“Ownness contains within itself everything that is one’s own and restores to honor what Christian language dishonored” (p. 201).

I am I. I am not an object of thought. I am I—not an idea and not a concept.

So Max has returned to me. He belongs to my schoolboy years in Attendorn and my youth in Plettenberg. I can hardly say “welcome” to him. And yet I feel it is an astonishing omen, an augury, that he is here again. I had not thought the muddled brother was so loyal.

Yes, it is you, Max.

Appear, Max.

Step into the self-conscious circle!

The dethroning of the Father through Auguste Comte’s positivistically altered, no longer Trinitarian sign of the cross—while still retaining the sign of the cross itself.

What takes the place of the Father?

Order, says Comte.

La loi—the law—says Michelet.

The sign of the cross performed in a name other than that of Father, Son, and Spirit.

Freud belongs within this same dethroning of the Father.

18 February 1948

The unbearable verbal sophistries of poor Karl Max.

One ought to operate on him existentially.

More than four hundred pages—that is too much. He drags along far too much foam from the philosophers’ bohemian tavern table.

Is there actually anything solid at the core, or is all of this merely deception?

A core?

Most of it is half-insane hairsplitting, interrupted here and there by individual grains of genuine existentialism.

19 February 1948

Some sentences from The Ego and Its Own remain with you. But you cannot tear them from the whole and line them up in isolation.

Not even as a chain of aphorisms.

What is this?

Something analogous to Donoso’s primal propositions?

Are they inseparable from the surrounding layer?

More important: their connection to the field of the historical situation.

(To Schelsky:)

“Primal positions”: they appear not in Fichte the father but in Fichte the son, in his metaphysics, where, as Eduard Zeller observes, “in substance they recall Böhme, as does his—Böhme’s or Fichte’s?—nature in God,” and so on.

Good old Zeller likes to lapse into Swabian.

I do not want to push biology so far that I import the son’s ideas into the father.

Nevertheless, your observation strikes me: in the later Fichte the father—whom the son consciously wished to continue—the act of positing by itself determines the basis of contemplation. For me, as a Christian Epimetheus, that is especially revealing. Then a reference to G. Nebel, On the Elements.

(In our present misery we occasionally need such stimulants.)

As for your essay, I naturally have no right to judge it quoad rem, on the substance itself. But perhaps I may at least enjoy encountering the spirit of Joseph Schumpeter again after so long, and observing that his power to stimulate thought has not weakened at all.

My last conversation with Schumpeter took place in 1926/27.

At the end of my Concept of the Political, published in 1927, you can still find an example of that influence.

Even after being refracted several times through translation and quotation, I can still recognize his voice. It is a great pleasure to argue with him.

One can feel that in your essay too.

(In a postscript I asked about Sauermann.)

Early this morning, around six, in the darkness and half asleep, I heard a factory siren and at the same moment saw the wide-open jaws of a large fish.

I would like to investigate this immediate simultaneity between an acoustic impression and a visual image. It would probably tell us more than research into radar problems. It would offer a glimpse into our inner sensory world.

People who no longer hear church bells but only factory sirens—are they supposed to believe in the God worshipped in churches? They are more likely to believe in a very hard iron Moloch, and to seek salvation in the melting process of a furnace. But as long as they hear both side by side—bells and wailing sirens—they will be helplessly torn between them. They will waver. They will be unable to decide. And they will hang steel bells in their churches.

20 February 1948

Stay with Hobbes and do not move on to Bacon, even if Bacon really did have a hand in Shakespeare’s finest plays.

(I read Ernst Lewalter’s Bacon, 1939, last night.)

How small Bacon’s end seems.

How comfortable his life!
