Read Nicolaus Sombart’s Capriccio. It reminds me of the young Walter Fuchs.

Not much comes of it.

A sad thought: this young man, whom I love, has gone over to the abortionists. He possessed a magnificent seed of genuine scholarly intuition—the existence of the person against the apparatus—and he aborted it in literature.

Out of impatience, laziness, hunger for pleasure, vanity, and the need to display his boyish mysteries of relations with girls.

Behind the question, so often posed in an abstract and general way, of whether only states or also individuals are subjects of international law, there lies a far more concrete, deeper, and more disturbing question:

Should the individual himself be able to decide independently on war and peace?

Does he possess his own jus ad bellum, his own right to go to war? That means the right, and even the duty, to resist.

Yes: a return to private war. And now there he stands, with his honourable subjectivity, helpless between the objective powers, which tear him to pieces.

28 June 1948

To Gerhard Günther:

Magic and space belong together.

Not magic and time.

I, here in Plettenberg, in the mountains beside the Lenne, lose my time and gain my space.

Time falls away from me.

Space approaches me and holds me in its embrace. It encloses and protects me.

Could you not come here sometime and question me as a “primitive,” and make me an object of your research into magical thinking?

Space is paradise.

Time is hell.

Boundary is magic. There is no empty space. But there is empty time.

Law is order, which means location.

See Corollary 1 to The Nomos of the Earth.

The two hunters on p. 23 of Land and Sea are mythical, and not merely mythology. For all the talk about myth that has gone on for years, I know only one man who truly realizes myth as a poet:

Theodor Däubler.

In him, the dissolution and self-dissolution of the great philosophy of German idealism releases theogonic transformations.

Thirty-two years ago I published a small book on Däubler’s Northern Lights, which I had pulped in 1925.

Today he confronts me again with immense power. And the little book contains completely different things from what I thought it contained at the time.

Däubler, incidentally, was the first to make use of the magic in the word “space,” long before the Expressionists and before Rilke.

But, however, and in spite of everything:

I know the dear Germans already, etc.236

29 June 1948

Further rules of Don Capisco:

Beware of every loudspeaker.237

Beware of every microphone that carries your voice into the wrong public sphere.

Every amplifier of sound is a falsifier of meaning.

World public opinion is the deception of the world.

What belongs to the world belongs to the devil. That is as true again today as it was in the year 63, in the time of Nero, Seneca, and the Apostle Paul.

Today the beautiful Christian forms of creaturely life developed by the Middle Ages have once again been completely abolished and assimilated away. But beware also of the false echo produced in the winding vaults of the catacombs.

Last night I almost succumbed again to the impatience of justice when I reread Francisco de Vitoria: the seven tituli idonei et non idonei, the valid and invalid titles,238 and once again recognized the horrifying abuse made of his doctrine of just war.

Especially the five Dubia circa justitiam belli, doubts concerning the justice of war, and the nine Dubiosa quantum liceat in bello justo, doubts concerning how much is permitted in a just war.239

Anyone who speaks of just war without showing that all these dubia and dubiosa have become part of his practical, moral, and historical consciousness no longer has any authority on his side.

The ideological fraud involved in exploiting and using all these doubts becomes all the clearer.

The trick is one that Francisco de Vitoria himself already employs:

omnia cedunt in favorem et jus justum bellum gerentium.

Everything gives way in favour of those who wage a just war and of the rights they claim through it.

With the help of this principle, even the otherwise so cautious Vitoria allows captured war booty not to be counted against claims for reparations and requisitions:

si licite sunt capta, puto quod non sunt obnoxia restitutioni.

If they were lawfully captured, I think they are not subject to restitution. So says the great theologian in De jure belli, second doubt concerning how much is permitted in a just war.

Tantum licet in bello justo!!

So much is permitted in a just war!!

Perhaps this sentence can help me identify my own peccatum, my own sin, and thereby answer the question that has tormented me for years:

Why does everything I say provoke such inexplicable hostility?

What terrible thing have I done?

J’ai montré la porte secrète de ce sanctuaire écarté où se jugent les perplexités de la justice et tous les problèmes, pour lesquels Thémis n’a pas de balance: car si on les montre, l’avide intérêt et tous les sophismes des passions forcent bientôt la porte et violent la conscience dans son dernier asile.240

I showed the secret door of that secluded sanctuary where the perplexities of justice are judged, together with all those problems for which Themis has no scales.

For once that door is shown, greedy self-interest and all the sophistries of passion soon force their way through it and violate conscience in its final refuge.

I am still thinking about Francisco de Vitoria.

About his seven tituli non idonei, invalid titles, and seven tituli idonei, valid titles.

About the five dubia circa justitiam belli, doubts concerning the justice of war. And the nine doubts concerning “how much is permitted in a just war.”

Then the impatience of justice takes hold of me for days at a time. This is the form of despair that comes with my profession as a jurist. But I do not want to die from it, as poor Max Weber did, whom I watched die from it in 1920.

At the time I thought it was very foolish to let oneself be consumed by such a thing and literally waste away from it.

Now I am receiving the lesson that has meanwhile become due.

To G. Krauss:

Do you consider it completely impossible to interest a Catholic moral theologian in the subject of “legality”?

Which religious order would even be suitable?

When I consider Vitoria’s attitude and his effect, I become frightened of the Dominicans.

I am now afraid that my chapter on Vitoria in the Nomos is far too gentle and considerate, almost concealing the issue, and that it therefore loses its force.

What I say there, very quietly, about Nys, James Brown Scott—and therefore about Jackson—is in substance every bit as serious as what Augustin Cochin, Valléry-Radot, and the earlier Bernanos, before he became weak, said and did.

But who hears it?

The Dominicans regard Vitoria as one of their household saints and as a matter of institutional prestige.

What is a layman supposed to do against that?

Ubi nihil vales, ibi nihil velis.

Where you have no power, desire nothing.

I could demonstrate from Vitoria—and from his own words, especially the five Dubia circa bellum justum and the nine doubts concerning “how much is permitted in a just war”—that the just war is total war.

But who is interested?

Have I already asked you about Höffner’s book on Vitoria, which bears the confidence-inspiring title Christianity and Human Dignity?

I do not know it yet.

In my experience so far, nine tenths of everything being written about Vitoria today is an outrageous fraud.

From a scholarly point of view, pure rubbish.

Nothing but the most miserable form of following the crowd.

Especially under the boom created by James Brown Scott.

It is a great disgrace.

I fear that even Gurian would be too intelligent to join in.

All the more eager, therefore, are our home-grown beneficiaries of the psychosis of 1945.

You compare my situation to Rossini being booed. That is not right. Today, the press pronounces the defamations and death sentences; the courts of the state merely carry them out.

My brother thinks Captiva Captivitas is far better and much more worth reading than Ernst Jünger’s Strahlungen, precisely because Jünger was never a prisoner. The Pour le Mérite has already found its new forms, and Kierkegaard said all of this clearly enough back in 1848.

1 July 1948

Since 1936241 I have been through terrible things, and several times I have been swallowed by the Leviathan that was already the object of my scholarly observation and research—and which, because of these experiences, became even more so. Being hunted for years as the quarry has made me somewhat tired.242 But I am still able to tell right from wrong, which my persecutors apparently can no longer do. I am also still able to classify my hunter in conceptual terms.

The ugly deception involved in my first attempt at marriage: is there a parallel between that and the self-deception involved in working with Frank? Or was the deception itself only a side effect of some secret desire to deceive myself? A desire to make myself cheap? An inability to deceive and disappoint other people? A helplessness against being steamrolled by people making brazen demands on me?

Was I too weak to find the courage to disappoint others? That false pity for the fraudster whose fraud I had already seen through? That terrible pity for an offer that nobody accepts?

Why do I feel such terrible pity for the little shopkeeper who waits in vain for a customer, while the customer who asks in vain for goods leaves me indifferent—even though we ourselves were always on the customer’s side?

Can this be a psychological accident, some lingering effect of the sad look I saw on the face of a small shopkeeper when I was a child? Or does it come from realizing that the merchant is now falling victim to the very risk he trusted in—from a deep sense that he is the victim of the supposed free market and its deceptions, that buying is better than selling, that money—until the next currency reform—is better than goods?

All of this shows just how many insights, experiences, diagnoses, calculations, and predictions can be packed into feelings of this kind.

2 July 1948

Theodor Haecker, Kierkegaard’s Hump, with a foreword by Richard Seewald, Zurich, Thomas Verlag, Anno Domini MCMXLVII. So that was the secret at the heart of it all!

Kierkegaard had a hump, and Theodor Haecker’s final word on Kierkegaard is about that hump—and about the spirit that the hump built for itself.

On top of this comes a clumsy introduction by the editor of this little book about the hump, Richard Seewald, a bad pseudo-modern painter who places Theodor Haecker’s broken nose beside Kierkegaard’s hump.

So at last we have the thorn in the flesh of these merciless spirits, these radical and demanding polemicists: the secret that was successfully kept quiet for a hundred years, the hidden engine behind this whole extraordinary intellectual existence, the secret motor of this existentialism!

Theodor Haecker’s last word concerns Kierkegaard’s hump!

Si tacuisset, magnus Ironicus mansisset: if he had kept silent, he would have remained a great ironist.

(But I have become so sensitive to polemics that, for me, every o si tacuisset—every “if only he had kept silent”—falls back on the person who says it to someone else. That was precisely the troubling thing about Kierkegaard: his silence never stopped talking.)

With this final word, Theodor Haecker meant only to strike at the non-Catholic—or not-yet-Catholic—Kierkegaard: the radical polemicist, the lover of the absurd, the intolerant Protestant. And Haecker meant well. He handled it tactfully. He was entirely right to qualify how much importance should be attached to the hump. But none of that helps him. He revealed the hump. An act like Ham exposing his father—here, his furious father.

Oh, if only he had kept silent.

I know my age. Simply naming this pudendum, this shameful bodily secret, destroys the Kierkegaard myth, which was already almost complete.

I know the spirit of this age.

With the best intentions, Haecker has tactlessly handed Kierkegaard over to his real enemy, the gutter press, for a second and even worse time. This time it will not be open mockery and ridicule. It will be the certain triumph not only of every psychoanalyst, but of every researcher of mind, body, and soul; every Nietzschean; every eugenicist and biologist; every believer in physical form—and above all that whole mass of educated people who can no longer look past the shape of the body.

And, speaking in Catholic terms, they are even right.

A hump does, after all, create an irregularitas ex defectu corporis propter deformitatem (Canon 984)—an irregularity arising from bodily defect because of deformity—though we need not argue over whether it was a gravior defectus, a more serious defect.

“Life draws strength from the spring of evil; better evil than the bourgeois middle ground”—that is Nietzsche, and Schubart agrees with him in Dostoevsky’s name.

The trick is clear to me now: make full use of every form of neutralization, while at the same time taking control of the point from which the decisive command is given. For example: introduce Gottgläubigkeit, “belief in God,” as an official creed.

As ideological content, this is about as neutral and as empty of any real decision as anything that exists in Europe today. At bottom, it can even remain neutral and non-committal in relation to the choice between theism and atheism. After all, Christians, Jews, pantheists, deists—all of them, in one way or another, believe in God. But now comes the decisive occupation of that neutral point:

I decide what counts as belief in God.

A devout Jew suddenly no longer counts as a believer in God, even though he may be as God-believing as anyone one can imagine.

Then comes the questionnaire:

Are you a believer in God or not? And so on.

The machinery of terror starts up.

Song of the Sixty-Year-Old

I have known the violent jerks of fate, Victories and defeats, revolutions and restorations, Inflations and deflations, being bombed out And being defamed, changes of regime and burst pipes, Hunger and cold, camps and solitary confinement. I have passed through all of it, And all of it has passed through me.

I know the many forms of terror, Terror from above and terror from below, Terror on land and terror from the air, Legal terror and terror outside the law, Brown terror, red terror, and mottled terror, And the worst terror of all, which no one dares to name. I know them all, and I know how they work.

I know the chanting choruses of power and law, The loudspeakers of regimes and their distorters of meaning, The blacklists filled with names And the card indexes of the persecutors.

What am I supposed to sing now? The hymn Placebo? Am I supposed to become free of problems and envy plants and animals? Tremble in panic among the little Pans? Share the happiness of the mosquito that jumps inward?

Three times I sat in the belly of the fish. I looked suicide by the executioner’s hand in the face. But the word of the sibylline poets wrapped itself protectively around me, And a saint from the East opened the gates and saved me.

Son of this consecration, you must not tremble! Listen and suffer!

What “line” lies behind the atomic bomb and the other bacteriological, biological, genocidal, and similar highly scientific, highly progressive, highly modern means of fighting a “just war” in the modern sense?

Not a Maginot Line, which still had something almost touchingly terrestrial about it.

Not a global line in the sense of the Raya, the Amity Line, or the line of the Western Hemisphere. Those still imagined the globe in terms of its surface.

No line at all.

Instead, a space. And before that space can be filled with the proper content—cuius economia, eius regio—it must first be emptied completely and turned into a tabula rasa.

Don Capisco’s pocket oracle:255

Only the elite matter. So always keep yourself close to whatever happens to be the elite.

But remember:

  1. Today’s elite are not yesterday’s elite, still less tomorrow’s or the day after tomorrow’s.

  2. The elite are those who, while receiving the highest incomes, pay the lowest taxes.

  3. The elite are those who can require other people to fill in questionnaires. The elite are those who can demand full and generous compensation for their own sacrifice.

  4. The elite are those who do not have to go to the courts to obtain their rights, and who do not have to fear the courts because of their wrongs.

  5. The elite are those who, if they have passports, do not have to collect them from the police.

  6. The elite are those whose sociology nobody dares to write. The elite are those who can accuse others without having to fear being accused themselves.

  7. The elite are those who are allowed to reject the tu quoque: “You did it too.”

If, at a mass meeting, you hear someone shout to general applause:

“Not butter, but guns!”

do not laugh.

Instead, practise sociology in Pareto’s style and tell yourself:

“Guns,” sociologically speaking, means the military and the arms industry.

So the sentence has a simple and very obvious sociological meaning:

You are living in a country where only soldiers and arms manufacturers still have butter to eat.

If you hear:

“Not gold, but work!”

then know this: you live in a country where people are required to hand over their gold and are not paid for their work in gold.

If you hear someone call for “burden equalization” at a public meeting, then know this: it is good business to be officially recognized as a victim.

23 July 1948

I read in Rilke:

“The meteor leaves your hands and races into its spaces.”

There is nothing like this kind of kitsch in Theodor Däubler. And the famous passage about Christianity in the letter from Córdoba, written to the Princess on 7 December 1912, is vulgar: a sudden, almost obscene dropping of the gentle mask worn by a delicate race.256

Most of what I have thought and said over the past several years, and some of what I have even written, has not been published. It resembles Beethoven’s variations on a theme by Diabelli—variations written for no instrument that has ever existed up to now.

Here lies my existential kinship with Vilfredo Pareto.

“Suicide by the executioner’s hand” has many different levels and phases of meaning:

  1. The outward, banal meaning: a cheap death, practically free, administered without any special expense for a doctor or funeral. Though even that is not always true, because the heirs can be held liable. But today the property is usually confiscated anyway.

  2. The Göring case.

  3. A sublime Stoic experiment: treating the executioner as the freely accepted means of one’s own suicide.

  4. The Christian meaning: receiving the executioner as a welcome messenger, like an illness or any other cause of death.

Nebel claimed that the phrase appeared in Ernst Jünger.

I have not found it there.

I did, however, encounter it years ago in the work of a Viennese lawyer who was a friend of Franz Blei.

The phrase itself is legal in character.

24 July 1948

In response to a disappointing letter congratulating me, the following verses began whirling around in the lower part of my brain:

Do not linger in the mass grave, Cast this mistake away from you.

Deep insights often do their work through bad rhymes.

25 July 1948

A pure interval holds me.

Machiavelli is nowhere near as Machiavellian as Francis Bacon.

Machiavelli never gave advice like the advice Bacon gives, for example, in his essay On Anger:

cum subtristes homines sunt, aut aliquantulum morosi, tempus est iram incendendi—when people are somewhat sad or gloomy, that is the time to inflame their anger.

26 July 1948

The person who sets out to break new ground quickly becomes a criminal when the others refuse to come with him and refuse to follow. Then he becomes a criminal, and finally a ghost horse.

This much I can say about myself:

I have not fallen into the mortal sin of feeling secure.257 For more than forty years I have lived ready to be called away at any moment.

Ever since I first became conscious of myself, ever since my school years as a teenager, I have been ready to leave everything lying where it is and answer the summons. That is why people never trusted me.

Infamous: trahison des clercs, the “betrayal of the intellectuals.”

What it really means is placing the intellectuals into particular political fronts instead of preserving the natural solidarity of the intellectuals, which should remain above every front—and certainly above the miserable fraud of dividing everything into Right and Left. It means placing them in the front of the Left. It means granting the absolution of the World Spirit to every crime committed on the Left, while mobilizing the just war against the Right.

27 July 1948

Notes on the concept of the political.

Hobbes says:

Human weapons—swords and guns—surpass the weapons of animals—horns, teeth, and stings. And by exactly the same measure, man surpasses wolves, bears, and snakes in greed and cruelty. Those animals are not ravenous beyond their hunger and do not become savage unless provoked; man can be hungry even for a hunger that is still to come.

(De homine, in Molesworth IV, p. 91.)

One part of this statement expresses a very exact relationship: human beings are more cruel than predatory animals by precisely the same degree that human weapons are more powerful than the weapons of animals. That applies to swords. It applies far more strongly to modern weapons of annihilation.

Think for a moment about what that means.

I will be careful not to say any more.

30 July 1948258

The fate of the lawyer and of the legal profession on the European continent:

Since the French Revolution, from 1789 to 1848, law has split into legality and legitimacy.

[It]259 ends with the lawyer sinking down into mere legality. That was “positivism.”

Since 1848, this division has been followed by a division within legitimacy itself.

At first, during the Restoration from 1815 to 1830, legitimacy appeared as purely historical, dynastic, and restorative legitimacy. Then a new revolutionary legitimacy arose against it and finally won.

The test is this: having a clear conscience about legality and illegality.

The great manifesto of this victory is Lenin’s work on legality and illegality as nothing more than different methods—Left-Wing Communism: An Infantile Disorder.

Its authentic philosophy of law rests on a philosophy of history: Georg Lukács, History and Class Consciousness, 1923.

Now there is only revolutionary legitimacy. This legitimacy is capable of justifying any cruelty. It can give every imperialism the character of an act of liberation. It can give every inhuman act the character of a measure taken in the service of a higher humanity. And for everything—for wars and civil wars, for the liquidation of entire classes and peoples—it can guarantee the absolution of the World Spirit.

Today this legitimacy has been monopolized in the East.260

The West has not even noticed the split between legality and legitimacy.

The Anglo-Saxons and the Catholic Church <…> still do not make this distinction. <…>

1 August 1948

Romanticism, according to the Schlegel brothers, is the Middle Ages.

Both are mixtures of the Romance and the Germanic.

Both are identical with Europe.

Well, if that is so, then the English language—and with it the English spirit—is, in concrete reality, the most Romantic, the most medieval, and the most European thing there is. But in that case the German claim that began with Fichte was an attack on this Europe.

Its only result was to clear the way for the East. It was not Robespierre but Metternich who destroyed the monarchical crown.

There is only self-destruction.

Only suicide.

Restorations are a specific method of finishing off and destroying whatever is supposedly being restored.

Why? Because they are acts of self-destruction.

So: no restorations!

Not of the Church or the state.

Not of monarchy or democracy.

Not of throne or altar.

Not of past forms of freedom, nor of past forms of obligation and authority.

We put it in order. It falls apart. We put it in order again, and fall apart ourselves.

(Eighth Duino Elegy.)

My reply to a German who wanted to be angry about the NZZ [Neue Zürcher Zeitung]:

Are we perhaps supposed to be angry at the distinguished tone of the NZZ, at Werner Kaegi’s call for resistance, or at the refined Monsieur Béguin?

Are we even supposed to start talking about Phariseeism?

2 August 1948

No!

Let us instead remember, in a spirit of universal kindness, the beautiful story of the distinguished Swiss gentleman.

A distinguished Swiss gentleman was sitting on the shore of the Swabian Sea. Then he heard the desperate cries of a drowning man:

“I can’t swim! I can’t swim!”

The distinguished Swiss gentleman looked away indignantly and said:

“I can’t swim either, but you don’t hear me making such a fuss about it!”

Deeply moving: the young Hellingrath discovered Hölderlin around 1910, against Goethe. He discovered the hidden German—which is to say, the true German, the non-public German.

Today I discovered §247 in Hegel’s Philosophy of Right.

I am drawn to the hopeless, to those who fail, to the condemned.

There is no hidden Marxist motive behind this, or any other kind of hidden motive.

No revolutionary purpose.

No desire to change the world.

3 August 1948

French: sécurité.

German, until now: Gemütlichkeit.

The certainty of grace internalized, moved into the private interior, and yet at the same time secularized.

The end of fear and trembling over a good cup of coffee and a pipe of fragrant tobacco.

The return of a well-disguised sensual pleasure, after Luther and the Moravians had attacked security so fiercely as the true form of sensual pleasure.

“Where now is your pleasure?” asks the prophet of the miserable man who has been thrown out of his security.

“Where now is your trembling?” I ask this Quaker who has become a billionaire.

The date on the birth certificate of the modern just war, and of the union between its particular kind of justice and weapons of annihilation,261 the birthplace of the modern Bethlehem where the storms of steel are prepared, and at the same time the beginning of that era of international law which organized its four-year Epiphany at Nuremberg beginning in October 1945:

14 December 1910.

How tactful that the date was not 24 December 1910.

A letter from Mr Andrew Carnegie to the trustees of the Carnegie Endowment:

Literally:

“I have transferred to you, as trustees of the Carnegie Peace Foundation, ten million dollars in mortgage-secured five-percent bonds, worth eleven and a half million dollars.

“You will use the income to abolish war, this stain upon our civilization.

“We no longer eat our fellow human beings; we no longer torture prisoners; we no longer plunder cities and destroy their inhabitants. And yet we still make war like barbarians.

“Only among wild beasts could this be excused in the twentieth century of the Christian era, because war is by its very nature criminal—la guerre est essentiellement criminelle.”

So not merely aggressive war!

Why is war essentially criminal?

Answer: because it gives victory not to right, but to power. It is a crime—another new crime!—for a people to refuse arbitration.

(But the same text also contains the sentence: Le juge qui siège dans une cause où il est intéressé est discrédité jusqu’à sa mort: the judge who sits in a case in which he himself has an interest is discredited until his death.)

And the Secretary-General of this foundation for the criminalization of war was James Brown Scott! So in any case: here stands the cradle of the new fame of Francisco de Vitoria.

Here is the source of the new, modern doctrine of the just war.

Here, in the steelworks of Bethlehem.

No shepherds sang here.

I, in the loneliness of the man who runs ahead of everyone else, make discoveries of this kind at the risk of my life.

I find the polarity between the superman and the “non-human,” and the modern concept of an enemy who must be exterminated, in Karl Marx in 1844, in the introduction to the Critique of Hegel’s Philosophy of Right:

Criticism, when directed against Germany, “is not an anatomical knife; it is a weapon. Its object is its enemy, which it does not want to refute, but to destroy.”

Sic.

Literally.

Karl Marx at the age of twenty-six!

So: the destruction of the justus hostis, the legitimate enemy, from both sides.

From Bethlehem as well as from Moscow.

And in between them, a German fool receiving injections from the West who thought he could fight both a two-front war and two different kinds of war: a non-discriminating war in the West, and a discriminating war in the East.

The transition to the sea as the new element:

Hegel, Philosophy of Right, §246.262

K. Marx, Riazanov I, p. 131: turning points in the development of philosophy.

When a divided world is confronted by a total philosophy, there is no reduction of its claims.

Instead there is a transition into another element.

Just as Themistocles, when Athens was devastated, persuaded the Athenians to abandon it completely and found a new Athens at sea, in another element.

I was the only one who demanded this for Germany and Europe: the conclusion of Land and Sea.

A transition to fire? Or to air?

(Sound waves?)

5 August 1948

In one of Alain’s Propos I found the following quotation: space is the image of our power, and time is the image of our powerlessness.

Whether the part about time is true, I leave open. But space is power. That is why the word Großraum—“great space”—caught on immediately, whereas we can speak of a “great time” but not of a Großzeit.

The essence of being is spatial being: location, space, and power. It is not temporal succession. It is presence—that is, space.

The fact that bodies could not pass through one another was space and power. That is precisely what is coming to an end.

The unlimited ability of waves to pass through everything is no longer power but influence.

“God is dead” means: space is dead.

Physical embodiment is dead.

(That is why the masses, despite all their fear for their own lives, display such incomprehensible indifference toward physical death and toward the destruction of their bodily form.)

In its place comes submission to forces.

Space is power made present, not force.

Time is neither one nor the other.

Forces are powers that have not yet been located.

Powers are forces that have been given a location.

6 August 1948

Virgil, Horace—all of it littérature dirigée, directed literature; all of it engagée, committed literature.

Even the Eclogues are a hymn to Caesar.

What do those who call us traitors actually demand from us?

Trahison des clercs as the slogan of a supposedly existing pouvoir spirituel, a spiritual power.

Has nobody yet noticed the sheer arrogance of such slogans, and the brazen claim to a monopoly over humanity,263 which means the right to brand one’s opponent as inhuman and strip him of his rights?

How could “natural law” possibly fail to attract eager believers again and again?264

Natural law: a few dozen completely contradictory demands; a heap of vague general clauses; basic concepts that are simply assumed—the concept of nature and the concept of law above all—without ever being clearly defined; a picture with a hundred different faces and a hundred wax noses.

How could something like that not win universal approval?

9 August 1948

Again—as last week, on 3 August 1948—I am horrified by Karl Marx.

Fourth Thesis on Feuerbach, The German Ideology, p. 534: the self-division, the self-contradiction of the worldly foundation must itself be understood in its contradiction and therefore revolutionized in practice.

“So, for example, once the earthly family has been discovered as the secret of the holy family, the former must itself be destroyed in theory and in practice.”

Sic.

Destroyed in theory and in practice.265 He wants to change things. And that means, first of all, destroying them.

Destroying them in theory and in practice.

Horrifying.

Consolation: the destroyer destroys only himself. This is true above all of the destroyer of destroyers.

Look clearly at the company you were keeping in the spring of 1933:

Carl Eschweiler, Konrad Weiß (see Schildgenossen, vol. 13, 1), Gottfried Benn, Martin Heidegger, W. Ahlmann.

What an ecstatic new beginning!

Oh, you poor men setting out to break new ground! It was not difficult for your enemy to brand you as criminals.266

10 August 1948

A bone-note rattles inside the dress.

(That was my dream from March 1918 in Planegg, about the skeleton with pink ribbons.)267

Notice whom you are alienating yourself from.

(Did you notice anything in the spring of 1933?)

Feel whom you are winning over.

(Did you win even one single person in the spring of 1933?)

You boy who blindly puts himself forward.

Can a person who throws himself into the creative struggle pay attention to this noticing and this feeling?268

How animal-like this cautious noticing is, sniffing the air before quietly moving away.

How panic-stricken, plant-like, and passive is the feeling that leads someone cautiously to attach himself to something. It is heliotropic, geotropic, hydrotropic, aerotropic—and at the same time monarch-tropic, aristocracy-tropic, and power-tropic.

A Pan-orama and a Pan-tropama in one.

11 August 1948

The positivist stays safely in the calculable middle and avoids dialectics.

The dialectician moves toward the edges of concepts, toward their boundaries, toward the abyss.

By doing so, he is driven beyond the boundaries, into the abyss, and then through the abyss into a new world. He accepts the risk of the abyss in exchange for the reward of discovering that new world.

The most magnificent picture the human mind can see of its own human greatness is the intellectual and historical picture formed by the opposition between Hegel’s dialectics and Comte’s positivism. This completely undialectical positivism won a provisional victory in the nineteenth century. But it too can only be understood as a dialectical stage, and today dialectical thought is once again lifting it off its hinges.

Comte’s positivism is undialectical despite its three stages—the theological, the metaphysical, and the positive—because it treats the first two merely as preliminary stages leading toward positivism. It does not understand them as the parents that generated and gave birth to positivism itself.

Meanwhile I am struck by a sentence from Maurice Barrès’s Cahiers:

On n’aime rien tant que ceux que l’on a vus humiliés269—we love no one so much as those we have seen humiliated.

(Quoted in Duhourcau, La voix intérieure de Maurice Barrès d’après ses cahiers, 1929.) This concerns the trauma of seeing the victorious Prussians in Charmes during the winter of 1870–71.

And what, then, about us!!

Me:

The positivism that begins around 1840 means a transition from dialectical thought to annihilation.

Bruno Bauer remains a dialectician.

Marx attacks this as “theology.”

Karl Marx is not a dialectician but someone who crosses things out and destroys them—the notes of 3 and 9 August.

To that extent, he is the true positivist.

The great transformation took place around 1840: the turn toward positivism, which by dialectical necessity becomes negativism—that is, nihilism.

Bruno Bauer, despite all the leaps and convulsions of the years 1840–48, always remained a dialectician. That is the basis of his relevance today.

How could I fail to love my enemy when I myself have produced him! And once I have even a little self-awareness, I must soon realize that he produces me in turn for as long as I make him real as my enemy. But the annihilation of the enemy is a claim to creatio ex nihilo, creation from nothing: a new world built on a tabula rasa.

Someone who wants to annihilate me is not my enemy. He is my satanic persecutor.

The question of how I should behave toward him can no longer be answered politically. It can only be answered theologically.

A dialectical theology of the most concrete kind arises when the destroyer claims that all he wants is to destroy the destroyer.

13 August 1948

Something never seen before? That is not much.

Something that cannot be repeated—that is the thing.

Something that cannot be reproduced?

Something nobody can imitate from us?

No!

Everyone imitates everything about us. But no one must be allowed to catch up with us, or worse: repeat us.

14 August 1948

My invulnerability does not come from having a hardened skin. It comes from the fact that I cannot be fixed in place.

From the fact that I cannot be caught up with.

The enemy who fires at me can, at best, hit the point where I was standing one second earlier.

The persecutor who wants to arrest me can, at most, seize and comprehend my corpse. He can then test his hatred on it by burning it and giving the ashes back to the elements.

“The ashes will not stop; they blow through every land.”

15 August 1948

I cannot be caught because I am moving at great speed, but I am certainly not fleeing from my enemies.

How could they possibly catch me? It follows naturally from the very nature of enmity: the hostilities that cannot be explained are the most revealing ones—and the easiest to explain.270

Genitum, non factum: begotten, not made.

Given, not posited. And positum, what is merely “posited,” is even less than factum, what is made.

The people who operate today’s machinery of legality are not even legislators. They are merely setters of laws—in the worst sense of that ugly expression.

17 August 1948

Freitod: voluntary death.

Freizeit: free time.

Organizing one’s free time by organizing one’s voluntary death.

League for the Organization of Voluntary Death in a Manner Appropriate to Free Time. And many other contemporary forms of freedom.

League of Purely Human Human Beings for the Immediate Destruction of All Non-Humans, Superhumans, and Subhumans.271

Behind every neutralization stands an unavoidable decisionism.

Behind every humanitarianism stands the claim:

I decide who counts as human.

18 August 1948

L’homme passe infiniment l’homme.

Man infinitely surpasses man.

Apply that sentence for a moment to the foolish homo homini homo—“man is man to man”—and you will see how completely evasive that formula is.272

Freedom and humanity: these seem to be two names under which particular kinds of crime can be committed.

Hitler’s bungling becomes obvious at this point.

Hitler committed great crimes. But for the greatest crimes, the World Spirit reserved instruments other than Hitler.

When it comes to the atomic bomb and the retroactive criminalization of aggressive war, Hitler is no longer even relevant.

What would happen if, in a liberal-democratic constitution, we added another sentence to the usual formula:

“The representative is answerable only to his conscience”?

Suppose we added:

“Coercion by political parties and parliamentary groups is unconstitutional and constitutes a crime against the people.”

What would happen if we inserted that sentence into the constitution of a one-party state?

With retroactive effect, naturally.273

20 August 1948

“The distance between a creative spirit and a virtuoso must always remain sacred to us.”

Rudolf Pannwitz wrote that to Herbert Nette after Nette had mentioned Nietzsche and Ernst Jünger in the same breath.274

I immediately applied the sentence to the relationship between Theodor Däubler and R. M. Rilke.

When H. Nette saw a picture of Däubler, he said that Rilke, by comparison, had the face of a ferret.

The slaughter of the children in Egypt, which Moses escaped, and the slaughter of the children in Bethlehem, which Jesus Christ escaped, form a perfect parallel.

To me, that is a sign of truth.

To the critical positivist, it is evidence of forgery.

The people of the region of the Gerasenes ask Christ to leave their country (Matthew 8:34; Mark 5:17). That is the same thing as the Grand Inquisitor asking Christ to leave us and never return.

Is this sameness a sign of truth or of falsification?

The whole tradition of German “criticism” enters its critical stage around 1840 and turns into naked positivism.

Bruno Bauer is the model of this process.

At its core, this critical attitude comes from the deep feeling of having been deceived. And so it discovers forgery everywhere.

Especially in the Gospel of John, in the “Fourth Gospel.”

The Jew then becomes, for Bauer, the original symbol of forgery and deception. This lies at the heart of the whole metaphysical and anti-metaphysical suspicion of ideology.

A later, less important but still revealing form of the same process is linguistic purism. It grows out of anxiety, fear, and concern for oneself—for one’s own unique and supposedly true being—and consists of a fear of being deceived by what is foreign.

The fear of being deceived by others becomes a source of self-deception.

The result and punishment of armouring the self.

A magnificent insight: for a time, the new regimes of freedom, liberated from the old helmsman, continue to live from the reserves accumulated by the authority they have removed.

Plato, Statesman 273c:

χωριζόμενος του κυβερνήτου—separated from the helmsman. That is the brief festival of pure liberalism.

The quickly vanishing moment that Röpke would like to make permanent. So Berlin lies on the straight air line between New York and Moscow.

On that line, East and West meet in Berlin. But such lines produce neither location nor order. And showing precisely that is the whole point of my Nomos of the Earth.

To Ernst Jünger:

While reflecting on the things that naturally come to mind as one enters the seventh decade of life, I came across the passage in the little Rivarol volume you gave me in Paris seven years ago (compare 17 July 1948, Riv. II 66). It touches one of the secrets of my life. And because you showed me so much understanding and fairness in your Strahlungen, I must thank you again for that today.

If you had been sitting at the table with us, I could have explained it to you more fully than I can now in writing.

At the time, I read my guests the Song of the Sixty-Year-Old. It would be wrong of me to withhold it from you. But harmless expressions of this kind of personal subjectivity, alongside the attraction of being open with oneself and one’s friends, also have the disadvantage of being obscure and easily misunderstood by an outsider who does not know all the references.

And so the enormous advantage of a suspended, hovering intonation can become a disadvantage: in the mouth of a stranger, the song can turn into a parody. That is how it is with all esoteric things.

Even the Christian Eucharistic formula Hoc est Corpus becomes “Hocus Pocus” in the mouth of an outsider.

Then, about your wonderful sentence:

“Style is, at the deepest level, founded on justice.”

And about the cup with the inscription:

“To justice—always.”

Positivist natural science is incapable of this kind of justice.

The atomic bomb, on the other hand, requires the just war.

Connections of this kind occupy me greatly, and I am tormented by the impatience of justice.

About the printed copy of the essay on peace:

I do not like the introduction. It is not fair to introduce you as a client of Ernst N.[iekisch]. And if today’s public knows no other grounds on which to recognize your standing, then that public is simply unworthy of you and incapable of judging you properly.

You are right when you say that N. (Cellaris) could have become important for German history.

I know that very well. But today, when Berlin has become the model for the entire German situation, that earlier possibility is no longer enough.

A man who is now nothing more than an old fighter and a victim of fascism cannot provide your legitimacy.275

Kniébolo was a criminal. But he was neither the greatest criminal—for the greater crimes, the World Spirit chooses other instruments—nor the last one. And today no one can continue living off the struggle against the dead Kniébolo.

Doing so only produces surprising increases in his value, until eventually the performances of Tristan over these last few months—in London, Lisbon, and Milan—become posthumous triumphs for Kniébolo.

(Then about Niebel, who came instead of Nebel.)

23 August 1948

The law governing every great Conquista of a New World: a Reconquista must come first.

An example of historical dialectics: first defeat. Then the victory of the defeated.

Only that gives the momentum for the leap into the great world.

Spain, 1492.

Russia, 1942.

Even today, only the defeated could make this leap into the new.

Not England in 1588: there the movement was into a new element, and from there into industrialism.

Industrialism belongs to the sea, no longer to the land.

The unique, the fantastic, the utopian.

Is the next step supposed to lead still higher into the utopian?

25 August 1948

Many people have lived through a sleepless night. And many have read the poem “Sleepless Night” and perhaps even understood it. But Annette’s Spiritual Year is a whole life kept awake. And not many people have kept watch through their lives as through one long night. So one should not expect too much success for a book of poems like that.

Surely it cannot be an accident that Protagoras, the very man who declares man to be the measure of all things, also defends the right of the stronger.

Qui veut faire l’ange fait la bête.

Whoever tries to make himself an angel makes himself a beast. That applied to an age that still believed in angels.

Today the formula is:

Qui veut faire l’homme fait la bête.

Whoever tries to make himself “the human being” makes himself a beast.

The enemy sitting as judge in a war-guilt trial against the defeated.

He becomes an even more horrifying figure if he simultaneously declares the defeated party to be his debtor, and now, as creditor, also plays the judge in a debt case against that same defeated party—while he himself has established the “foundations” of the case, namely guilt and debt, and declared them beyond challenge.

D.[on] Cap.[isco]:

Look carefully at the author Who speaks so beautifully of silence. For as long as he speaks of silence, He is, of course, not silent. They do not merely steal words, slogans, mottoes, and concepts. They also steal flags and colours, songs and sacraments.

In the end, they even steal the wreaths from the grave of the defeated enemy.

31 August 1948

Often I am crushed by the loneliness of knowing about a scelus infandum—an unspeakable crime.276

1 September 1948

“Natural law” is a misleading and outdated expression in an age of natural science and of rule by the concrete results produced by natural science.277

But after the development of legality and legitimacy, law today has found refuge only in legal scholarship, no longer in legislation.

There will therefore be only as much law as legal scholarship is able to recognize, grasp, and bring to life. But legal scholarship, as in similarly chaotic periods in earlier centuries, follows its own path and finds its own people to carry it forward. That is the great process of selection taking place today.

Let us be glad that we are no longer held back by having to show consideration for people like Radbruch.

(To G. Dahm:)

You have been given a task more magnificent than anything you could possibly have accomplished before, even with the best will in the world.

As a teacher of criminal law, you are being drawn into a process of criminalization on an enormous scale—including retroactive criminalization of a kind that legal history has never known before.

You need do no more, for example, than read Friedrich von Spee’s Cautio Criminalis of 1642 and replace the word “witch” with “Nazi” to find countless points of inspiration. Or think about vehicles of criminalization such as “piracy” or “conspiracy.”278

I do not intend to parade my colleagues before you one by one.

I am speaking only about the astonishing moment in legal history in which your discipline suddenly finds itself “placed.”

Don Capisco:279

The inhabitants of Mars are warlike.

Their very name tells us that. It follows that there <…> ultimately wage war against war.

Are the inhabitants of Mars beginning <to deliberate>? For a moment it seemed that we might be allowed to hope so. For without question they have become Germany’s <…>, namely Germany’s war. But several complications have arisen.

Utopia on Mars:

How beautiful the Earth is.

The inhabitants of Mars are quarrelsome and argumentative. But there are also success[ful] pacifist <people> among them.

As a result, the only wars they fight are just wars. They therefore also know what it means to be defeated in a <…> just war. They have read about this in the great teacher of international law, Vitoria, whose name has a very homely appeal to them, since every <…> hopes to win.

Vitoria is their great authority.

In books they read <…>, <…> what is <permitted> in a just war:

quantum liceat in bello justo. But now a controversy has broken out among the scholars of Mars concerning Germany. They have obtained a copy of the latest German constitutions and imagine how beautiful life must be on Earth in general and in Germany in particular: property is guaranteed; everyone has the right to a healthy home; dictatorship is forbidden.280

The pacifists claim that the Earth has actually been living in a condition of perpetual peace for a long time already, and that Germany is simply a normal example of the general condition of the Earth.

The others,281 however, claim that Germany won the just war and therefore finds itself in the paradisiacal condition reflected in its constitutions.

2 September 1948

Versari in re illicita: being involved in an unlawful matter.

An art dealer is exposed as a black-market trader and criminal.

The monster is even said to have abused small children.

In his shop, investigators discover paintings by a certain Rembrandt.

The responsible prosecuting authority therefore places Rembrandt on the blacklist and orders the immediate destruction of every work produced by this disgusting accomplice.

4 September 1948

The present constitution of Germany is determined by the retroactive criminalization of aggressive war.

The true constitutional principles of present-day Germany are:

  1. Omnia cedent in favorem gerentibus bellum justum.

    Everything gives way in favour of those who wage a just war.

  2. Versanti (or versato) in re illicita omnia nocent. Victo bello justo omnia nocent. Bello justo victus versatur in re illicita, cui omnia nocent.

    For anyone involved in an unlawful act, everything counts against him. For anyone defeated in a just war, everything counts against him. Whoever is defeated in a just war is treated as someone involved in an unlawful act—and everything counts against him.

5 September 1948

I will lay The Nomos of the Earth on the grave of European international law, like a flowering branch grown from my own discrimination.282

8 September 1948

“In a monarchy, anyone who wishes to remain unnoticed is safe, no matter who happens to rule.” So Hobbes, De Cive, X § 7.283

“Citizens are less often unjustly condemned when one man rules than when the people rule.” Ibid.

Those are sentences that speak directly to the heart of someone being persecuted today.

14 September 1948

In the bleak world of total planning, new forms of collective emotion arise.

The worst is the rage that can so easily be stirred up against anyone who disrupts the plan, gets in its way, or sabotages it.

The saboteur is not merely someone who disturbs the peace, a perturbateur. Ideologically, he is the final obstacle standing between us and paradise. In practice, he is an obstruction blocking traffic.

If he is relatively small, he gets run over like a dog on the motorway.

If he is a larger obstacle, he gets blown up.

Nobel’s dynamite and the Nobel Prize are simply two sides of the same reality, just as the atomic bomb and the just war are.

The competitive impulse Thomas Hobbes had in mind is harmless compared with the will to plan that drives the technological mind.

Again and again, the Hobbesian uncertainty relation.

16 September 1948

Ne quid ex contagione incommodi accipiant—“so that they suffer no harm through contact with him.” That appears in Caesar’s Gallic War (VI, 13), in the chapter dealing with the social boycott that the Druids could impose.

The chapter sounds so modern that one immediately wonders:

Was it inserted later? That is the modern positivist’s obsession with forgery and fraud. Or were things then simply the same as they are today, and as they have always been? That is the disillusioned person’s nothing-new-under-the-sun complex. Then there is the historical envy of new peoples and new social classes.

America’s existential history begins in 1775.

Soviet Russia’s begins in 1917.

Rudolf Smend’s begins in 1517, with the Hussites as a prelude.

Hannes Schneider’s begins with the Great Elector.

The great Yes-men of 1933.

Theologians such as Karl Eschweiler—what a historical legitimation!

Poets such as Konrad Weiß and Gottfried Benn—what tension between the widest possible poles!

Philosophers such as Martin Heidegger—what an existential document for both sides! And on top of all that, Konrad Weiß’s poem “1933” standing at the head of The Christian Epimetheus!284

The complexio oppositorum—the bringing together of opposites—as a symptom of old age. But it can also be a sign of youth.

Life is simply that complex.

Then come all those balancing compromises, the carefully balanced formulas about original sin: original sin merely wounds man, it does not kill him. But no one says whether the wound is only a graze or a bullet through the brain. In any case, it must supposedly be possible to bandage him up. Then there is the balancing of subject and object. That produces the type of the trimmer, the man forever adjusting himself to both sides. But it is still a very long way from producing a Don Capisco.

In German, you lie when you express admiration.

German envy, together with its offspring—the German demand for absolute purity—makes honest admiration impossible.

Every expression of praise immediately becomes ironic.

Wilhelm Busch is the German national poet.

There is the malice of the journeyman craftsman, of the three just combmakers. They know every trick of the trade. Even when they describe a work as “successful,” the jargon of the journeyman still hangs around the word, because for him “successful” also carries the sense of something comic or ridiculous.285

There are still many New Worlds to discover. They simply no longer lie on the surface of the earth we know today.

18 September 1948

There is something bad about combining setting and giving in the German compound Gesetz-Geber—law-giver.

First he sets the law, and then he gives us what he himself has set.

German is not a legal language.

The real and most terrible trahison des clercs—the betrayal of the intellectuals—is this:

According to Saint-Simon, Comte, Taine, and that whole tradition of scientism, the natural sciences were supposed to represent the true pouvoir spirituel, the true spiritual authority.

Yet it was precisely these sciences that handed the new weapons they had discovered—culminating in the atomic bomb—over to political rulers.

Scelus infandum.

An unspeakable crime. And these scientists were not fascists.

No. They were antifascists—militant antifascists, practicing antifascists, antifascists who had gone into exile.

Do you finally understand what that antifascist slogan about the trahison des clercs really means?

Written on the morning when the news came that Count Bernadotte had been murdered.

On Rudolf Sohm:

His opposition between love and law, spirit and world, charisma and office is probably not as purely Lutheran as it first appears. It has itself been purified—and purified by the German Idealist idea of purity: idea and reality.

To realize the idea is both duty and guilt at the same time.

Sohm is the father of the doctrine of the charismatic leader.

This is not about Max Weber. It is about Rudolf Sohm.

Leader, guide, helmsman, director, The list goes on and on; Director, leader, guide, helmsman, And the whole thing grows more costly. Helmsman, director, leader, guide, Here even the sharpest thinker fails; Guide, helmsman, director, leader, What guardians! What fire-stokers! Charisma in any case.

21 September 1948

It drives me deeper into the depression of powerlessness when, in my helplessness, I realize:

Anyone without power needs plenty of sweets. But another thought gives me protection—the thought of powerlessness as something that can make a person stronger.

My powerlessness is really nothing more than my refusal to take part in the power politics of terror.

From the viewpoint of this non-participation, it appears as lack of power. But seen from beyond this world, it becomes a counter-power: exemption from the terror of this world, and an increase in my claim upon history.

Michelet, la loi:

“The philosophers of France, in their eagerness to escape from what they deemed a superstition of the priests, flung themselves headlong into a superstition of the lawyers.”

Sir Henry James Sumner Maine, Ancient Law, 1861, in the chapter “Law of Nature.”

Quite right. But surely the priests are not the legal problem here.

23 September 1948

I will not die, because my enemy is still alive.

I have found the only concrete category of existentialism: friend and enemy.

The cycles of the cyclical writers—F. G. Jünger, for example—seem to me like that rather small glass dome into which the horizon contracts when you are far out at sea and can see nothing but water, without even a thin line of land.286

F. G. Jünger’s verses are language, but not Word.

Even when they become completely simple, they still do not become element or sacrament.

Their simplicity remains within the world of “noble simplicity and quiet grandeur.” For Däubler, the whole world becomes radiation.

The earth becomes the Northern Lights—that is, cosmic radiation.

Poems such as “The Night Wanderer” or “Listener on a Blue Meadow” should not be isolated from this larger setting. They would have to be read together with the dozen other poems of the “Flaming Stream of Lava.”

And from mere experiments, miraculous flowers would bloom.

28 September 1948

Since 1945, we Germans have been undergoing an education at the hands of four great educators, who beat us hard and work us over thoroughly.

We stare in amazement at these authorized guardians and at their methods of education.

According to Vitoria, the victor in a just war is allowed to sell the defeated enemy’s children into slavery.

Wonderful. There is something impressive about that.

What a beautiful task that must have been; <…> of duty <…> and if that duty is violated <…> magnificent.287 But then the opponent of a power waging a just war is, by that very fact, acting in legitimate self-defense. Or is he perhaps under a duty to lose the war?

Homo homini homo—man is man to man.

No, thank you.

I would rather deal with honest wolves than with this mixture of fox and marten.288

Flaubert, 1853:

The eighteenth century denied the soul.

The task of the nineteenth century will be to kill man.

Quite so.

Peacefully, in the manner of Aldous Huxley’s Brave New World. Or in a just war, with atomic bombs and radiation.

Bacteriological warfare is always a just war.

Otherwise it would not be allowed to take place. And whoever wins it will leave no one alive who doubts its justice.

The alternative was <…>.

A beautiful definition of law in the young Hegel:

Law is a fragment of human nature.

Before the law, the criminal is nothing but the criminal. But law itself is only a fragment of human nature, and it therefore reaches only fragments of the human being.

(The Spirit of Christianity, p. 288.)

30 September 1948

There is historical proof—more than proof, in fact.

There is a fully valid and, both in form and substance, definitive model showing that there is no escape from the alternative:

homo homini deus—man is a god to man,

or

homo homini lupus—man is a wolf to man. And that also proves that we cannot remain at the neutral zero point of

homo homini homo—man is simply man to man.

The proof is the fate of the Roman Caesars.

From Hadrian onward—and according to Mommsen even earlier—the Roman Senate faced an unavoidable choice whenever a Caesar died: either declare the dead Caesar a god, or declare him an enemy, a princeps hostis.

There was no third possibility.

The moment man tries to rise above himself—and he has to, because l’homme surpasse l’homme, man surpasses man—this alternative appears and the abyss opens.

3 October 1948

The lukewarm and neutralized become agitated about atheism and nihilism without noticing that one much admired and endlessly quoted remark by Jakob Burckhardt contains infinitely more atheism and nihilism than all of Bakunin’s writings.

I mean the sentence:

Power is evil in itself.

Who today understands that this sentence means the same thing as:

God is dead.

5 October 1948

Bernanos’s polemic in La France contre les Robots (1946) is thoroughly old-fashioned and ineffective.

Its manner is the same polemical hissing we find in Theodor Haecker’s Satire and Polemic, which could still make an impression thirty years ago.

As for its substance, it is a critique of the technological age of a kind we in Germany have known since the beginning of the century through Max Weber, Troeltsch, and Rathenau.

And in the end the author reveals himself as a respectable anti-Vichy man, which means he can be certain of a license from the present regime. He spits on the poor French policeman of 1940, who behaved in a perfectly ordinary way. It is embarrassing: the excited polemic of a man who emigrated in good time and in complete comfort, who never spent a single day in prison and never lived through a bombing raid, and who now comes back to beat us Europeans over the head with his standards.

6 October 1948

The old ghosts that cannot die are happy to forgive. But they cannot forget.

To be unable to die means: to be unable to forget.

An inability to grant amnesty. They want to go on living. They do not even want merely to survive.

7 October 1948

This Karl Barth really has no more to do with the Christ of the reborn human being than any pope—or, for that matter, Pope Joan.

8 October 1948

“If I had the misfortune to be German, I freely admit that at Munich, standing before Daladier and Chamberlain, the two Big Men of that time, I would have been tempted to think myself not merely a lord, but God.”

So says Georges Bernanos in La France contre les Robots—robot = machine!!—1946, p. 173.

10 October 1948

We poor Chaopolitans—citizens of chaos.

In chaos, nothing remains to us except the discernment of spirits.

How else could a cosmos ever arise? But to discern the spirits already means distinguishing friend from enemy.

Anything else would be a joke.

16 October 1948

From Henri Murger to Henry Miller.

Henry Miller’s Tropic of Cancer is Henri Murger’s Bohemia all over again.

Instead of Alsatians, we now have Americans, and the whole thing is filled with global human types.

The Priapism is open. So is the despair. It no longer ties a little pink ribbon289 around itself. It shamelessly admits what it is and even manages to draw a certain spiritual impulse from that shamelessness.

“The whole earth staggering with crime and distress.”

“Man has been betrayed because he calls upon the best part of his nature, and that is all” (p. 121).

We heard this back in 1840 as well. But only now, after the Second World War, is it finally being carried through consistently—and globally.

The line of development from 1848 to 1948 runs from the proletariat to the peripsēma—the cast-off refuse. That is the whole of progress.

I said that despair no longer ties a little pink ribbon around itself.

I spoke too soon.

In the second half of Henry Miller’s book, a hymn to humanity appears.

More precisely, it is a hymn to the art of Matisse, in which the flesh breathes so beautifully.

A tremendous relief: from the variété de la pâture sexuelle, the variety of sexual fodder, to the variété de la pâture culturelle et humanitaire, the variety of cultural and humanitarian fodder.

The paralyzing legend: the white gods who come from the East.

Salus ex Judaeis.

Salvation comes from the Jews.

Bes uswika: wordless.

The line from 1848 to 1948 is the development and intensification of nothingness and nihilism.

Put in concrete sociological terms: from the proletariat to the peripsēma.

Existentialist chatter accompanies the crossing over into the shamelessness of nothingness.

The Christian peripsēma seems to have been used up.

Who was it who said:

The German would rather be a criminal than a citizen?

Beautiful.

But he did not want to be a proletarian either. So instead he flew into a rage and became a Hitlerian.

I fear that he will fly into an even worse rage once he grasps the idea of the peripsēma.

Only then will we really see the Antichrist.

Compared with the peripsēma, the proletarian is merely an ambitious climber on the ladder of historical development.

The enemy is nothingness?

No.

Today the enemy is the non-nothing. And that is precisely the Christian.

In W. Grewe’s publications on occupation law, the basic fact always remains the same: the situation of the defeated party in a discriminatory world war.

May Herbert Krüger’s excellent essay in Gegenwart (September 1948) help the Third World War return to a human concept of the enemy. But the Furies of the just war have now been unleashed, and they will probably not be so easy to tame again.

Until that happens, everything constructed as “law” must end up serving the right and advantage of the side that wages the just war, as one can already read in Vitoria. And our entire situation—constitution, Basic Law, occupation statute—remains one gigantic versari in re illicita: existence within an unlawful situation.

Nevertheless:

At last time makes Saul Too weak and tired to persecute.

After four years of occupation, the animus hostilis—the hostile intention—must surely have worn itself down somewhat, and the provisional arrangement must surely begin to stabilize in one direction or another.

Perhaps even the tu quoque—“you did it too”—will eventually gain a little room for use against our guardians and educators.

In any case, Grewe’s scholarly achievement in international law is extraordinary.290 He is now Germany’s leading teacher of international law. That is not merely an achievement and a task. It is also a situation.

May every good spirit assist him in it. These victors are not even capable of establishing a clear spatial order for the earth.

18 October 1948

At last, another new enemy.

Henry Miller has discovered him and sounded the alarm: the friends of classical education, the lovers of the past.

“There is something obscene in this love of the past,” he says.

“Something obscene in all this spiritual commotion that allows a cretin to sprinkle holy water on Big Berthas, dreadnoughts, and explosives.”

And now it comes, on p. 303—the great killing potential of a new persecution:

“Anyone with a belly full of the classics is an enemy of the human race!”

The phrase enemy of the human race has by now become more explosive than any atomic bomb or biological weapon, even if it begins merely as a slogan.

Someone will always come along who takes it seriously.

Someone will carry it out.

“The world looks more and more like an entomologist’s dream.”

The freezing over of the earth.

No Catholic heart.

Obscene Christian gibberish.

At the end, looking at the Seine flowing quietly, he writes:

“Human beings make up a strange fauna and flora. More than anything else they need enough space—space even more than time.”

So, in the end: space after all.

American.

Taken as a whole: rotten flesh prepared with literary nonchalance.

Spirit serves as seasoning so that one can swallow the stinking flesh.

The result is a myth of blood and excrement whose potential for killing is considerable.

21 October 1948

“In the face of the field of ruins.”

That is how the Bavarian Constitution of 26 October 1946 begins, documenting the fact that even the Bavarians, standing before a landscape of ruins, could think of nothing better than cheap, moldy banalities left over from the good old age of constitutionalism.

Perhaps the relationship between cat and mouse is itself only the outcome of a very long war.

Perhaps it is simply the permanent fixing of that war’s result.

As Heraclitus says: war makes some free and others slaves.

In this way it has made some beings <gods> and others mice. It reveals nature—physis—and at the same time fixes it in place. That is the justice of war. That is natural law.

War between human beings still has its honor. It is not just.

Only war between natural beings is just. It ends by revealing that some are free and others slaves, some cats and others mice.

Law is the final distribution of space.

Law is first of all division and distribution—and specifically the division and distribution of land.

Law is the clear distribution of freedom and subjection.

We jurists, after all, are only scribes. We do not possess the Word directly. We do not possess the image directly. We possess only writing.

We can count ourselves lucky if we are at least the first to write something down ourselves—as with so-called customary law—instead of being forced to rewrite a law that has already been written.

27 October 1948

On Annie Kraus’s book On Stupidity (Carolus Verlag Knecht, Frankfurt):

On p. 38 of Annie Kraus’s “stupidity,” one comes across my name.

Carl with a C.

Schmitt with two t’s.

Identity and continuity cannot be disputed, so the recommendation to the prosecutors—on p. 42 I am called “co-responsible”—lands concretely enough.

What I now read in print from Annie Kraus—while remembering, with some emotion, her doe-eyed look—is much the same as what I heard from Kempner’s own mouth. But Kempner and I managed to have a conversation.

I have no desire to engage with Annie Kraus’s many words about “humility.”291

We poor goyim are simply stupid. That has now been settled for the next thousand years and established with full legal force by an international military tribunal.

Res judicata.

A decided matter.

Military tribunals are the highest <…>.

And reading so much “On Stupidity,” dedicated with reverence to Gertrud von Le Fort, genuinely hurts me for Annie Kraus’s sake. She behaves like a little throttling angel. Yet she does not really belong in the company of the prosecutors and accusers. And if I was responsible for her somehow ending up among them, then I regret it. So now I see her riding toward me on the high horse of Christian humility without being able to change so much as a single line of The Concept of the Political. Because I still have not discovered whether enemies really exist or whether there are only fools. And despite all these years of talk about existence and existentialism, I have still never found any existential category other than the distinction between friend and enemy.

One rather striking conclusion of The Concept of the Political might be this: treating the enemy as a criminal can itself become just as criminal as treating him as a bottomless fool is foolish. Or am I to be held responsible because Germans have a tendency to substitute their distinction between I and non-I for the distinction between friend and enemy?

A fine dedication between Germans:

Con-versanti in re illicita Co-existentibus in re illicita.

To one involved in an unlawful situation. To those co-existing in an unlawful situation.

5 November 1948

Today “natural law” is nothing more than the phosphorescent product of decay left behind after two thousand years of talking the subject to death.

The mere possibility that a thought might someday be communicated—even if that possibility remains completely unconscious—already falsifies the result of thinking. So what are we supposed to make of everything that has been spoken?

Or, worse, written?

Or, worse still, printed? And what are we supposed to make of diaries that were already intended for publication at the moment they were written?

The height of madness: a just war combined with a liberum veto for the great powers on the World Security Council!

What an order!

The unrestricted veto places the great power above the peace order. It makes the great power the final authority on questions of peace and therefore also on the justice of war.

7 November 1948

Anthropology since Pascal:

grandeur et misère.

Man is enormously great and enormously small, very much and very little.

In short: an oversized giant-dwarf.

Situation.

Recognize the situation!

Existentialist imperative No. 1.292

  1. European legal scholarship is the last refuge of law.

  2. European legal scholarship is in exile.

  3. We belong to the government-in-exile.

11 November 1948

At the deepest level: the terrible drive to live, the terror of the instincts, the compulsion to go on living— the élan vital is a criminal arrogance— that is the Leviathan.

Julien Green described it well.

Hobbes and Rousseau both seek protection from it.

Hobbes does so by intensifying the problem.

Rousseau does so by removing the problem.

Hobbes turns Leviathan into a machine, an apparatus, a collective.

By doing so he opens the technological age: protection and security through technology.

Rousseau turns Leviathan into a rabbit with poison in its tail, venenum in cauda.

What concerns me most deeply is the transformation of the beast of prey into a machine: the connection between technology and Leviathan—that is, between technology and a predatory sea-creature.

Hegel’s genius shows itself in the fact that he saw the connection between the sea and industrial technology (Philosophy of Right, § 247). But Hobbes’s genius is greater still. It shows itself in the fact that he symbolized all of this in his Leviathan.

Son of this consecration, son of this knowledge, son of this transformation—always son.

How beautiful. It even leaves open whether I am the son of a father or of a mother.

Probably the father is meant rather than the mother. But this cannot be decided either on the father’s side or the mother’s side.

Least of all can the two be combined in some gynandrous mixture. It must remain unspoken.

The scientific word for this is: result.

15 November 1948

From presence to presentation, and from there to representation.

Why is there no re-presence?

Why only representation? Yet we do have re-education.

All of these are suspicious re-volutions.

Artificial beginnings.

Forgeries produced by making something “genuine.”

Things “made good again.”

Artificial virginity.

Re-presentification.

30 November 1948

This world unleashed.

Machine: the unleashed activism of a world unleashed.

2 December 1948

They issue emergency-contribution stamps—that is, tax stamps—and require people to stick them onto letters before those letters can be sent.

The post office refuses to carry letters and other mail if the tax stamp is missing.

The postal service is transformed into a tax-enforcement agency.

The postal monopoly is used to collect taxes.293

A blatant détournement de pouvoir—misuse of power. It is a simple method of forcing obedience: exclude people from the positive services provided by the administrative system.

Why not use the same method to obtain money for residences suitable to the rank of the new ministers?

Here we have a dangerous gateway into the total administrative state.

“The serpent, it is said, can cause its whole body to enter at the opening through which its head will pass: with regard to legal tyranny, it is against this subtle head that we should guard.”

That is what defenders of the rule of law—Bentham among them—were saying more than a hundred years ago.

Today they have become helpless. They have lost even their instincts.

“Beings destined to perish are in agreement with their enemies.”

Their clouded intellect is no longer capable of recognizing the nature of an administrative state. But if I were to say these simple truths aloud today, a pack of my colleagues would immediately reopen the hunt against me and shout:

The characterless scoundrel is stabbing the brave people of Berlin in the back while they are fighting!

So it is better to remain silent.

Christ died the death of the person stripped of rights: the death of a slave.

Christ’s crucifixion took place hors la loi—outside the law.

The Jews and pagans acted together.

Who placed the Holy One outside the law?294

Pilate did not act as a judge toward Christ. He did not sentence him to death.

At the urging of the Jews, he simply handed him over to the administrative measure of crucifixion.295

I can find no formal wording of a death sentence in the Gospel text.

Rex Judaeorum—King of the Jews—is not the wording of a judgment.

Pilate was not a judge.

How could a judge who, acting as a judge, sentenced an innocent man to death say at the same time:

I am innocent of the death of this man whom I myself have sentenced to death? That would be a completely meaningless and useless protestatio factis et actis contraria—a declaration contradicted by one’s own deeds and actions.

We cannot reasonably attribute that to an educated Roman of the period.

4 December 1948

How sad and hopeless.

I say:

l’obscurité protège mieux que la loi—obscurity protects better than the law. And at best people find it clever.

People think in concepts, not in situations.

Unfortunately, “situation” itself has become an especially interesting concept.296 That explains the many disappointments one experiences precisely with those people by whom one initially felt so well understood.

How can someone who has never been defamed understand someone who has?

Where do these conceptual footbridges lead, the bridges that appear to span the abyss?

On this narrow bridge we are merely dragging the stolen calf with us, like the knight Tondalus, and in the end we meet only ourselves on the thin plank stretched over the abyss.

Advent in the Lenne Mountains is overwhelming: the total presence of pure waiting and expectation.

12 December 1948

Here is a Thomist or neo-Thomist in 1948 who fears the world will be “de-spiritualized” unless we remain Thomists.

O God.

I know spiritualization.

I know the ending in spirit, in the Northern Lights.

I know the return to blood and soil, which Michelet was already preaching in his Bible of Humanity.

I know the chthonic thinkers and the followers of Pan.

Is contemporary Thomism now supposed to offer itself as a juste milieu, a comfortable middle way between spiritualism and materialism?

As the golden mean between blood and brain?

The Yogi and the Commissar?

No: the Martyr and the Grand Inquisitor!

14 December 1948

My rejection of positivism came with age.

Would it have made more sense in my youth?

Compare this with the young Hegel’s rejection of “positivity.”

Positivity = legality = Judaism = despotism = the cramp of the “ought” and of the norm.297

Hegel polemically opposes a non-positive religiosity to positive Christianity.
