Damned liar!

And then “values”—which this valuer drives into your back out of duty!!

(Der Monat, no. 87, December 1955, p. 48.)

We Christian folk now rejoice.

26 December 1955

Self-assertion—self-definition.

Who are you?

Tu quis es?

I am a man of the Moselle who can never, for all eternity, be canalized—and who is therefore cursed by the Pope with every ban and anathema.547

30 December 1955

They took the chalice away from the laity, and in doing so they lost control over the intoxicants. Now they are dying miserably because of it. And they need the wretched Adolf as a bogeyman so that they can fraternize with the Jews, who for their part have needed such bogeymen for two thousand years in order to raise their own moral standing and collect compensation as victims—provided they can find fools to pay it: reparations, that is.

Inside Germany this is comparatively easy. Outside Germany it is difficult. And for that they need Germany again. Hence this compulsion.548

4 January 1956

The first greeting of the New Year was miching mallecho: a radio talk by Hermann Heimpel on NWDR calling on us to repent and make reparations, and warning us not to forget that we are criminals while the others, who are entitled to compensation, are the victims of our crimes.

A quotation from [Franz] Böhm revealed the heart of the matter.

Keep stirring up our sense of guilt, and paying will become easier for us!

Joyfully we pay our billions as we hear repentance’s minstrels.

Before this Shylock greeting came my reading of the new Catholic catechism for West Germany. It is no longer “the Jews” who crucified our Lord and Savior. That no longer appears in the Roman catechism. Instead it was:

“the leaders of the chosen people.”

What exactly is worse for us now?

Sovereign is he who decides on the state of exception.

How cheerfully I crowed that definition of sovereignty out into the world back in 1921!

And how right I turned out to be.

Today everyone quotes it who suffers under somebody else’s sovereignty, while everyone who exercises sovereignty himself suppresses it and keeps silent about it.

Today I know that Hans Freyer is right when he says, in his Theory of the Present Age of 1955:

Exceptions do not count; they are charged against the person who points them out.

That is a magnificent sentence.

Does anyone apart from me have any idea how magnificent it is?

Anyone apart from me, the victim of precisely this reality?

For that reason alone I want to travel to Wiesbaden tomorrow to speak with Hans Freyer.

The concrete exception can arise in two opposite directions and from two opposite impulses.

Grace comes from an abundance of security and gives its goodness without needing a reason.

Dictatorship comes from a lack of security and can no longer be good, because it feels threatened by a dangerous enemy. That is the polarity between grace and dictatorship.

No one thinks about this. Even Wilhelm Grewe failed to recognize the passage from 1921 in the introductory note to my book on dictatorship, p. IX.

That would probably have been asking too much.

The one drips like heaven’s gentle rain; The other drops hydrogen-bomb blessings.

The difference between goodness and anxiety.

Agnosticism produces anxiety rather than fear; means of annihilation rather than weapons.

12 January 1956

The great man, the magnus homo, is a great father, or a great brother, or else a great beast—namely Leviathan.

We cannot do without such enlargements.

Question: is the great mother still the great human being?

Or must greatness take the form of a great man?

Only in the masculine does this upward intensification lead to the hero, to the lord, and to rule.

The great mother is only a great womb.

The great man drops bombs upon the small; Thus mankind makes itself one whole. It need only negate the other’s No, And everyone will think the same.

31 January 1956

In January 1956 the GDR—the German Democratic Republic—introduced a criminal prohibition, a law threatening with death the crime of Abwerbung, enticing or recruiting people away.

Magnificent.

A new offense.

Criminalization on the modern level.

Automobilism; car traps; alcohol consumption; aggressive war; and now: enticing people away.549

They have my blessing.

After all, a manufacturer once poached my cleaning woman.

Young Paris poached beautiful Helen from old Menelaus. And the Russians poached several Nobel Prize winners and atomic physicists from the Americans, and they were certainly no Helens.

Naturally these are all crimes for which the abolished death penalty must immediately be brought back.

Newspaper clippings pasted in.

Left: FAZ, 22 November 1955.

To the right of the right-hand clipping:

“I thought: against every.”

1 February 1956

And here, ladies and gentlemen, you have one-hundred-percent potestas indirecta, indirect power, to which nothing can ever happen because it will certainly end up on the side of the victor, no matter what that victor looks like. For the Christian-social ideal is the victorious war won by other people, after which one joins the victor. And if, while exercising our divine right to political error, we should happen to bet even slightly on the wrong side, we afterwards swing ourselves all the more energetically onto the victor’s side. There are victors, and there are those who belong with the victors.

We, at any rate, always belong to those who belong.

So listen <…> to this supremely legitimized representative of potestas indirecta:

Newspaper clipping pasted in.

On it:

“Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung, 23 November 1955.”

Above it:

“23 November 1955.”

Below it:

“The Pope too has a right to a private life; and the public has a right to learn about this private life—insofar as it is edifying.”

Who are you?

I am what I do!

What do you do?

I bless!

I am blessing!

What do you bless?

I am blessing the temporal!

What is the temporal?

I will be very careful not to tell you.

Besides, you should be ashamed of yourself for asking me.

All your questions and questionnaires are overflowing with time and temporality.

Answer to my persecutors E. Kaufmann, Fr. Böhm, Küster, W. Strauss, and Ebenstein:

Rabies is the accusation the dog brings against its master.

Do you know who said that?

But how could these poor dogs know such a thing?!

Shame on you for asking them.

2 February 1956

Hail to me that I saw the great departures and those who broke them open!

1914 and 1933.

The German language keeps releasing new ironic creations from the abyss of its profundity.

The latest examples: the European civil servant; the integration employee; the Western senior government councillor.

One only has to ask what all of this is called in French, and then in English, and the whole West is exposed as a piece of suburban Bonn magic.

Meanwhile, of course—as for me, in the old way—meanwhile several solid bourgeois families have thoroughly “consolidated” themselves. That is: they have scraped together something “under their feet,” some real estate, and had it entered in the land register. And so, if anyone dares to challenge this profit—their strictly legal profit—the matter becomes a problem of the constitutional state itself: first, law; second, state.

So, for the sake of dear peace, let us grant the whole Holy Family all its plots of land, buildings, investments, shares, securities, and pensions that it carried away as the final result of its heroic struggle against the miserable criminal Hitler.

May they have them forever!

May they live on them for a long time!

Well and long!

Every grandson!

Every son-in-law!

Long may he live!

Down with this Hitler—dead for ten years anyway!

He has been dead for ten years, but we intend to live off him for another thousand!

He deserves no better, that gigantic pig!

That gigantic roast of repentance!

When gigantic pigs are slaughtered, the thousand-year banquet of Leviathan begins.

We are gradually beginning to notice that today.

Adolf and his champions wanted to live for a thousand years off the filthy business of the November crimes of 1918.

That was a mistake.

The people of 1945 want to live off the oversized gigantic pig Adolf for at least as long.

As an old loyal defeated man, all I can say is:

Very well.

Then bon appétit, and ad multos annos—may it last for many years!

In any case, the end is always nothing more than the great banquet of the slaughtered Leviathan. That is: the gigantic pig concerned at that particular moment is slaughtered and eaten.

That is eschatologia concreta—concrete eschatology.

At the end, when the pig has been slaughtered, every Piefke who ended up on the correct side can stuff himself with the chops and schnitzels that will then exist in enormous quantities.

Apparently the Christian age is supposed to end in the same way.

Compared with this, I find Buddhism, which has no eschatology, noble and infinitely superior. This swinish expectation of the end—the slaughtered Leviathan toward which everything leads in the practical Christianity I have experienced so far—this concrete eschatology was something we recognized in 1945 through Romano Guardini and through Gustav Radbruch.

Back then, in 1945, the German pig was slaughtered.

That was the grace of the zero point.

That—and greed added suddenly afterward.550

Today they are looking for the next pig.

Permanent eschatology.

Reparations, again and again!

The main thing is to make sure the pig is slaughtered kosher.

The theologians will see to that.

4 February 1956

For a long time now:

Moral = Anti-fascist.

Much as, for the ancient Egyptians:

South = upstream. And then this is proved with the help of some material or substantive natural law—in any case, always a materialist natural law. For me, the entire present-day discussion of so-called natural law means nothing more than a dead end built out of questions belonging to a situation that has long ceased to exist, and defended by a stubborn scholastic establishment.551

Do not keep digging here for nothing!

Do not let yourself be drawn into this Augean stable by an invitation to participate.

Not even by the urgent demand that you help with the supposedly necessary cleaning of the Augean stable.

Not even on the grounds that doing so is surely the ethical duty of every decent Hercules.

15 February 1956

A new crime—in the Eastern Zone, punishable by death since January 1956:

Abwerbung, enticing or recruiting people away.552

In Norway, harpooners who hire themselves out to foreign whaling companies are punished by loss of citizenship and confiscation of property. But they are not punished if they betray the foreign whaling company’s trade secrets to the Norwegians.

New crimes.

New legal definitions of offenses.

New grounds for exemption from punishment.

New criminal law.

The world history of humanity develops: from land-taking through sea-taking to industrial-taking; and beyond that to space-taking.

Nightmare under the heading:

Looting in the Castle.

I try to prevent the looting. I give a good speech. And a gentleman with an aristocratic appearance betrays me to the looters with a wink.

So be careful with your theory of taking.

The great takers do not like people talking about them while they are still taking—or while they still hope to inherit what has already been taken.

Later, later, my brave professor of constitutional law!!

16 February 1956

For weeks—from 20 January to 12 February—I was in love with the title:

Hamlet or Hecuba.

Only Peter Diederichs advised me against it.

I had won over most of the others. But it turned out that nobody knew who Hecuba was.553

Presumably because, in Germany today, Hecuba means nothing to anyone anyway.

A well-educated and well-read Protestant pastor from Bielefeld, fifty years old, thought Hecuba was a name from the Old Testament.

At that point I surrendered. Now I am obsessed with the title:

Time Breaks into the Play: An Interpretation of Hamlet by Carl Schmitt.

I think it is very good. But it still does not hit hard enough. And everybody wants a title that hits.

Everybody wants nothing but hitting now.

Quick-hitting, sudden-hitting, hard-hitting—they apparently want to be hit.

Not beaten dead.

Beaten alive.

Millions of heads and one record;

millions of hearts and one beat from the fist of the great Schlagintweit.

Strike, poet, strike with force; Strike the reader to the core.

18 February 1956

Modern conversation:

How many languages do you actually speak?554

Two dead languages, Greek and Latin, I can read well. I speak five national, which is to say half-dead, languages reasonably well: German, French, English, Spanish, and Italian. And I have mastered at least seven living languages—that is, ideological, effective, international languages: humanist, liberal-democratic, fascist, Marxist, Roman Catholic, Protestant Christian, and also positivist and Hegelian. That makes fourteen languages altogether whose vocabulary, grammar, and syntax my brain has to keep immediately available. Otherwise I would long ago have been absorbed and ground under. But as it is, I am still alive and enjoy the freedom of my mind.

A new answer to the question:

Who are you?

In the age of interrogations and of everything being called into question.

I am the polyglot who understands Polyphemus and no longer cares to make himself understandable—that is, understandable enough to be heard, interrogated, and finally taken in and appropriated.

1 March 1956

Three premiums, three premiums, I planted upon my grave. They are the three premiums attached to the legal possession of power:

obéissance préalable—obedience in advance;

the presumption of legality;

the execution of general clauses.

Children, just picture that for yourselves and you will recognize the stupidity of the Totalitarians!

There is no need to claim totality in order to be total. Totality emerges all by itself. Those three premiums, without which no system can function at all, contain everything needed. They contain it—that is, they contain a genuine totality without ever having to expose themselves as totality. The poor fool who openly wrote “totality” on his banner was therefore almost harmless compared with the implication contained in a power that exercises totality indirectly, through the back door, and all the more effectively: the holders of power and law.

5 March 1956

When I read yesterday afternoon the diary notes from April, May, and June 1945, it became clear to me that every word spoken by a human being is filled with content and meaning by the particular space in which that person presently exists, and that the word retains its unique tone.

Typewritten report from the German Time Archive pasted in; concerning the report in the FAZ of 23 March 1956.

What is it that is being preserved there?

Time that exists.

We are located within it, and every word we speak is located within it. But what, then, does it mean that only a few hours later my eagerness to write books and publish things seemed to me like the behavior of an eager little boy placing paper boats on a raging river in competition with other boys doing the same thing? That was probably an image produced by exhaustion and despair.

Words and sentences are not paper boats. They are more like buds and fruit, vibrating branches and leaves of a tree; a kind of divination through vibration for our mysterious self and the selves of our friends; creationes ex nihilo per verbum: creation out of nothing through the word.

16 March 1956

Everything is determined by the first imprint, the first ray of light that reaches the newborn child. The murderers try to seize control of this first imprint. The fathers try to defend themselves against them. There is no escaping the jus primae noctis, the right of the first night. The struggle over the school and the kindergarten becomes the struggle over the jus primae noctis. No constitution, no social order, no system of law, and no religion can escape this central problem of the prima nox.

30 March 1956, Good Friday

Christianity is Judaism for the people.

“The people” are those who do not rule; who do not know Latin; who receive no wine at Communion; who do not ride on horseback but walk; who do not drive a Mercedes; who do not belong to the elite; who—in Germany today—are not entitled to reparations.555

Religion is opium for the people. An intoxicant. But the people had the wine taken away from them long ago. Prohibition at Communion exists in the Roman priestly Church just as much as it does in the Puritan-Methodist-Pietist universal priesthood. “The people” are those from whom the chalice has been taken. In return they are given a substitute. Or they simply take one for themselves—the first cheap rotgut liquor they can find.

A delightful Biedermeier joke: instead of saying “it is high time,” say “it is high railway.”

Today even that is outdated. But it is an unconscious expression of the recognition that the railway brought a different kind of time into existence: the time of the timetable; a stricter time than the one before it.

The joke ceases to be a joke and becomes the objective expression of a gallows situation with gallows humor. It becomes a surrealist work of art: a lightning flash of recognition in a single instant.556

The simplest, most obvious practical logic: If I read in the constitution of a country the sentence,

“He who does not work shall not eat,”

then I know that I am dealing with a country in which the person whom they want to starve is not allowed to work. And if he is nevertheless forced to work, then that work is punishment and coercion, for which he receives not food but an input of fuel. Meanwhile the chatter of the ruling class counts as “work,” for which they receive especially good food and an expense allowance.

The backwardness of the bourgeois expression:

“expense allowance” (Aufwandsentschädigung), Article 48 of the Bonn Basic Law.

“Compensation” is good.

Apparently it is compensation for sacrifice. They make sacrifices. They sacrifice themselves. A sacrifice is something for which one can demand compensation. New definition of the elite: the elite are those whose work counts as sacrifice; as self-sacrifice.

The difference between concrete and abstract arises from the difference between intoxicants. The European intoxicants—wine and beer, perhaps spirits too?—what is called alcohol, put me into the concrete situation and sharpen my knowledge of reality. In vino veritas means: I see myself and other people more clearly and more truthfully. It sharpens my sense for what is actually present in the moment. Then it exaggerates this clarity of vision and finally simply knocks me to the ground. But it is always a concrete insight. That is the effect of good wine.

The other drugs work in a magical and abstract way. Christian wine worked concretely for as long as it had not yet been taken away from the laity. For as long as that remained true, it cured people of anthropophagy.

Mescaline, by contrast, produces abstract utopias.

Hashish produces an abstract feeling of happiness and utopian visions;

anthropophagy;

cannibalism.

Wine does not create utopias. On the contrary: it immunizes against them. There was not a single utopia for as long as the Christian sacrament of bread and wine remained intact—that is, for as long as the layman still took the chalice.

1 April 1956, Easter Sunday557

Caduca culmina vagi saeculi contemnens.

Scorning the crumbling heights of this wandering age.

Good Arator.

Now you have reached that point.

There is a higher law: the people from whom a universal impulse goes out must themselves perish, while the impulse passes beyond them.558 Hegel discovered this higher law.

(Positions and Concepts, p. 113, note.)

I.

He was probably thinking of Jews and Greeks. These are the small peoples from whom the great impulses went out.

II.

These peoples are not eternal. The great empires, by contrast, establish themselves for eternity.

The great model for us is Roma aeterna, eternal Rome.

It cannot and will not die.

It goes on living as a ghost.

It becomes the vampire of its own unending past.

It sits on its own grave—the grave of its own empire.

Terrible, these empires that have fallen and yet cannot die!

Kill the dead at last!

More terrible still, however, are the empires that are dying now before our eyes.

We watch them with horror. They do not want to die. The older they become, the more tenaciously they cling on. They cling to their vanishing power.

Like Moloch, they devour millions of human lives. They drink rivers of blood merely to remain in this world for one single hour longer. They have Niehans-style fresh-cell injections administered to themselves, made from the blood of sacrificed hecatombs.

Just ten more years.

Just one more year.

Just one more day.

Just one more hour of life—which means: one more hour in power.

That, then, is what stands behind Roma aeterna: the ghost sitting on the grave.

Immortal because it has long been dead.

Fools are impressed by it.

Clever people know how to profit from it.

Weaklings convert in order to profit from it.

Poor little gnats who are not even Italianos hope to raise their status by turning themselves into Romans.

Self-valorization here too.

Hausenstein becomes German ambassador in Paris.

III.

What follows from this?

An alliance of failures!

Where do we Germans belong?

Compare Positions and Concepts, note on p. 113, the essay on Beckerath’s book about fascism.

Where do the French belong?

The English, from whom the Industrial Revolution came?

Insights born from the intuition of decline, in the hour of death;

superiority over the fraud of eternity represented by this Roma aeterna.

Newspaper clipping.

On it:

“End of March 1956.”

Below it:

“Atheism of the non-academic Stoics; compare Lucan (sed victa Catoni).”

2 April 1956, Easter Monday

In Henri Lévy-Bruhl I found the following contrast (in an article from 29 March 1956 in Le Monde): socialism is the opposite of paternalism. The rule of law—de la loi—was also opposed to paternalism: law against the father, loi contre le père. This was already there in Michelet. So socialism = rejection of inheritance rights.

Property without inheritance.

The only thing I inherit is my own body. But who did you inherit it from?

In the age of fertilization at a distance.

4 April 1956

Who are you?

I am a layman in whom the millions of cartloads of wine are still fermenting that the Roman priests took away from the laity.

5 April 1956

What? You want to become a Christian?

Christianity is in safe hands.

Yes, indeed, I want to become a Christian.

A Christian in the abstract, or a Christian in concrete reality?

I should think: in concrete reality. So that means: a Christian in 1956. CDU, or where exactly?

My dear friend, Christianity is in safe hands!

If you want to become a Christian, you will be packed straight into an extremely concrete system.

7 April 1956

I would like to compare the sociology behind Pascal’s “human condition” (fragment 139) with Hobbes’s sociology of competition.

How suspicious Pascal’s longing for repos and chambre—rest and a room—looks beside Hobbes.

How boldly and openly Hobbes looks at reality.

How centered on the individual Pascal is; how sober and masculine Hobbes is.

How completely Hobbes sees through everyone, including himself, in their hunger for social prestige. And how painfully cramped and repressed poor Pascal becomes as he slips away into another world!

No. Give me Hobbes instead.

If all human unhappiness comes from our inability to remain quietly “in a room”—dans une chambre—then surely the first thing to do is give people rest and a room, as Pascal himself had. But too many of us have been driven out of our rooms too many times.

10 April 1956

There is a good, German, true, genuine, wonderfully cozy translation of the word “social.”

It is: folksy and affable—leutselig. And so our bigwigs are all wonderfully leutselig.

Stalin was leutselig.

Hitler was leutselig—and how!

The Yankees cannot possibly be leutselig, because they come from Calvinist stock.

The Puritan is not leutselig. But he keeps smiling and shouts, “Hello!”

12 April 1956

Forms of asceticism.

Henry VIII’s break from his marriage and from the Church led to a world empire, to the seizure of the world’s seas.

Magnificent.

No sexual asceticism, and no asceticism of property.

On the European continent, the break takes the form of opposition to the celibate bureaucracy—that is, opposition to sexual asceticism. Once sexual asceticism loses its value, property asceticism becomes overvalued.

The real world conflict today is between Moscow and Rome: property asceticism—the abolition of private property—against sexual asceticism, preached by a celibate bureaucracy. But the heroes of asceticism are weakening on both sides.

Their successors and beneficiaries are willing to negotiate.

The result: coexistence of the two asceticisms.

The development of technology seems to be working in favor of property asceticism—against private property—and against sexual asceticism, which is becoming ridiculous and uninteresting.

6 May 1956

How sad and hopeless it is to put one more note on paper while knowing that nobody has any time left to read or think about anything.

How strange: ever since human beings invented machines to save time, they have had no time.

General relativity ends in the absolutization of nothingness.

Space is destroyed by the perspective of space.

Time is destroyed by the perspective of time—that is, by the relativity of systems of motion.

Public opinion ends in front of the little buzzing box of a radio: in front of the isolated, blind listener. There were times when a person could escape into public life. Today it is better to escape into obscurity.

But all these perspectives and relativities shatter against one fact: time cannot be repeated.

Time is irreversible. And so people flee into the future—which is destroyed by that very flight—and into the cosmos—which is destroyed in exactly the same way.

10 May 1956

I do not need to travel to Russia or America.

The Russians and Americans came to me.

They came looking for me in Berlin.

They even wanted to liberate me there—by arresting me.

Strange visitors who turn into persecutors.

Strange persecutors who turn into visitors.

Everything that is coming to you comes to you.

And whatever comes to you is also what is due to you—as I already wrote on 18 September 1947.559

And so they all come into my room on the radio waves of the great broadcasting stations:

Roosevelt and Hitler, statesmen and rulers. They come into my attic room and pay me a personal visit.

More persecutors than visitors, these great frauds.

Whoever says “God” wants to deceive.

Whoever has power must deceive.

13 May 1956

The Concept—that is it.

The seriousness of the Concept, as it marches across these figures and smashes them to pieces.

The people sense it, and they get to see how badly their celebrated gods fare when they dare to step onto the ground where the Concept rules.560

The Concept—that is it;

18 May 1956561

The development of democracy: the increase and deepening of equality.

  1. Stage One: From political equality to social equality; first stage of the industrial revolution.

  2. Stage Two: From social equality to nuclear equality.562

Every human being has a basic right to at least one atomic bomb.

Only when we are all equally armed are we truly equal.

Only then—according to Rousseau—will we once again be in the state of nature.

Only then can everyone kill everyone else.

Only then will concrete equality prevail.

But how are we supposed to provide everyone with an atomic bomb?

Well, that industrious little tribe of Nobel Prize winners will solve this problem too.

So forward!

With ruthlessly humanitarian commitment!

Forward to nuclear democracy!!

22 May 1956

I appeared in this world in July 1888. It came as a complete surprise to me, because I had not planned myself. I had not designed myself. So I suppose I was thrown.

Ejaculated.

Dear good Papa, by now already a grandfather.

Please forgive me.

29 May 1956

The Loss of the Center: that is the withholding of the chalice. The destruction of the sacrament of everyday life. The destruction of bread and wine—that is, of the Eucharist.

Horrifying.

But Mr. von Sedlmayr says nothing about that. Here the art historian’s politeness falls silent.

31 May 1956

God is dead and Reaction keeps marching anyway—and now it is only the marching that matters, in the spirit of Forward Everywhere. But whatever it may be—God dead or alive, Reaction or Revolution, whatever it may be—sociology will hunt all these foxes out of their holes, reactionary and revolutionary alike, and drive them into the open. In the end, Reaction and Revolution will form a coalition and coexist, if only to exterminate this kind of sociology as a form of fascism.

Corpus Christi, evening

Entirely unsuspecting, on the evening of Corpus Christi 1956, I am sitting in my attic room wanting to read something about Hegel. In a situation like this, the best people to read are the officially approved Marxist Hegelians. So I read Ernst Bloch, Subject-Object: Explanations of Hegel.563

Yes indeed. Explanations of Hegel. Something we can certainly use today.

I read about the fourteen stages of the road that Spirit passes through, one after another. They are, of course, the—of all numbers, precisely fourteen—Stations of the Cross prayed by the Catholic Christian people.

Mr. Ernst Bloch knows quite a lot.

Extremely exciting.

Extremely edifying.

Thrilling reading.

I sit there reading, astonished by this terrifyingly well-informed Ernst Bloch.564 I read his account of the fourteen stages. I check Hegel. I read from a Stations of the Cross prayer book that belonged to my good parents, who many times in their lives walked and prayed the fourteen Stations of the Cross.

Everything fits.

Fourteen stations.

Extraordinary parallels.

But suddenly—someone comes up behind me and smashes me over the head with an iron bar.

I reach page 229 of Ernst Bloch’s book: the fascist Carl Schmitt in complete agreement with reactionary fraud.

Ecco.

There you have it.

Serves you right, you poor little fool, letting officially approved Marxists teach you about Hegel.

You got exactly what you deserved.

Mr. Ernst Bloch, meanwhile, fulfills his quota.

Fulfills his quota. Quota-fills his full. And gets a professorship for it.565

7 June 1956

Everything is really so terribly simple. Whenever you run into some enormous difficulty, whenever something absolutely horrible does not suit you, simply become moral. Become highly moral. Become indignant. Set yourself up as the prosecutor. Raise the question of guilt. Put yourself in the role of accuser and turn the whole thing into a moral problem. Raise the question of guilt. But remember the first rule:

  1. Make sure that you are the one who asks the question of guilt.

Then nothing can happen to you. You automatically—eo ipso—become the morally superior person. As the accuser, which means as the persecutor, you are recognized as such. The person who asks the question is master of the answer. The person who asks who is guilty is master of the situation. So make sure that you are the one who asks the question of guilt.

And remember the second rule:

  1. Make sure that among the guilty there is at least one person who has something worth taking.

Perhaps he has a fine office, a fine house, ox and donkey, shares, and all sorts of other pleasant things. Once he has been declared guilty, these things can be taken away from him. He has forfeited them. They can be removed from him once you have secured recognition as his persecutor. Once you have legally obtained that position, you can take whatever he has. And your taking is then recognized as good and just.

You may enjoy what you have taken in complete security. So make sure that you are in the right, so that things may go well for you and you may live long upon the earth.

6 July 1956

My copy of Leo Strauss’s book on Spinoza (1930) has recently fallen into the hands of Karl Löwith. He threw himself on it like a persecutor finding a trail, like a detective discovering the evidence of a crime, like a fortune hunter finding a will written in his favor. But I can think only of the strange destinies of books and of individual copies of books.

Without Strauss’s book, my own book on the Leviathan (1938) would never have been written. From 1932 to 1945 it stayed with me. In the summer of 1945 I was still making many notes in it and writing remarks in the margins. Then, in October 1945, the Americans confiscated it along with my other books and carried it away. It was among the books returned to me in 1952, which had most recently been stored in Mainz. From there, in a fit of despair and taedium fugae—weariness of flight—I sold the whole collection cheaply to the Kerst antiquarian bookshop in Frankfurt am Main. Now the library in Heidelberg has acquired it, and Löwith has traded in his own bound copy so that he can possess my marginal notes.566

Obviously, it is not only our actions that follow us. Our glosses follow us too!

Do not worry about finding readers, you good and faithful writers!

The smallest note, the most unintended pencil mark, reaches its proper destination at exactly the right moment.

Should that make us cautious?

On the contrary!

It should encourage us to do everything without intention. Unintentionally. And only faithfully.

10 July 1956

Listen to this prophecy from the year 1904:567

I tremble at my power! Is what I bring the truth—or night? Do I obey the call of Heaven … or of Hell? Was I created by law—or arbitrary will? Am I a god? A fool … one just like you? Am I myself—or merely a sign?

Who could have written that? It is prophetic enough. Naturally, it comes from Vienna—the Vienna of 1904. Hitler was living there at the time, a fifteen-year-old adolescent tough. And the antennae of a Jewish writer sensed him and his destiny, in connection with the Great Wurstel, with whom a whole century of beautiful appearances and pure play had to come to an end.

11 July 1956

Hieroglyph of the Western world:568

1848: Germany is Hamlet. 1918: Europe is Hamlet. 1958: the entire Western world is Hamlet.

Compare the illustration for Gelimer’s laughter: 24 March 1955 (IV, p. 104).

12 July 1956

The speech given by CDU member Nellen in the Bonn Bundestag on Friday evening, 6 July 1956 (159th session, report pp. 8840 ff.)569 appeals to the concrete judgment of conscience in each concrete situation, and wants the state to recognize this judgment of the situation in cases of conscientious objection to military service. The Social Democrats, especially Arndt, applaud.

And nobody shouts:

Situation ethics!

That is how deeply these normativists have themselves sunk into the very situation ethics they reject. Hermann Heller’s cry of “situation!” during the Leipzig trial in October 1932570 is still ringing in my ears today.

Carlo Schmid called out:

Quis iudicabit?

Who will judge?

And with that he wanted to make the conscience of the individual the final court of appeal. But conscience is not a court. It is an abyss.

16 July 1956

Ernst Jünger counts himself, with justified pride, among the Order of the Shandyists. We, however, belong to the race of Rameau’s nephews.571 Only someone who belongs to this race has been initiated into reality.

No fascist and no antifascist belongs to it. No persecutor and no believer in restitution belongs to it. But Mr. von Goethe certainly belongs to our brotherhood, at least as an honorary member, because it was he who introduced this Nephew into Germany.

Hegel belongs to it, because he raised the Nephew to the rank of his chief witness. So too does the magnificent gang that wrote Shakespeare’s plays in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. For a long time Marxism was able to live off this genuine membership in the brotherhood of Rameau’s Nephew.

Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels were brothers of the Nephew.

Lenin and his Russian comrades were already exploiters of him. And with exploitation begins surplus value. With surplus value begins high politics. And everything after that is merely what follows with time.

But we carry on the race of Rameau’s nephews in its pure form.

Do not worry, brothers!

Do not let giant bigwigs and state philosophers in the style of Georg Lukács confuse you!

The race lives.

The Order flourishes.

The brotherhood remains—impossible to exterminate.

No massacre of the children of Bethlehem, no gassing operation, no Katyn, no Hiroshima bomb, no Morgenthau Plan, and no invention by Nobel Prize winners can destroy us.

5 August 1956

A beautiful parallel:

Shylock stands to Nathan the Wise as Caliban stands to Papageno. This is an example of a whole series of parallels = implications.

Careful!

Danger of automatic operation!

Parallel automation!

Musil’s Parallel Action turns into an automatically parallel reaction!

How grotesque this European nineteenth century was!

What a miserable elite it must have had—a miserable elite in state, Church, and society! They let Russian professional revolutionaries scare them out of their wits.572

Conservatism in the face of genuine professional revolutionaries is passivism and masochism.

Fortunately, however, the Russian professional revolutionaries died out with Stalin’s death in March 1953.

De-Stalinization is the active form of conservatism.

Anyone who has already taken what he wanted now blesses himself and what he owns. He declares the taking finished and makes security the foundation of the existing order.

The Taking is over.

Long live the legitimacy of the new status quo!

Look around and see what has become of your coexistent people—your fellow-takers and fellow-travelers.

Coexistence means status quo.

In every case, after it all, the status quo wins in the Augean stall.

17 August 1956

There is only one Shakespeare play that is Christian through and through—and Christian even in a thoroughly medieval sense:

The Merchant of Venice.

It is the old Christian theme of the Jew who is cheated and the Devil who is finally cheated too.

Naturally, that can only produce a comedy. There simply cannot be a Christian tragedy.

At most, there can be a tragedy about the hidden God of the Jansenists, as in Racine.

Hamlet is tragedy and is therefore essentially non-Christian.

Where things are Christian, comedy is the superior form.

You can still see this in Hegel’s placing of comedy—with its humor and irony—above tragedy, and above all in his association of present reality with comedy.

Lessing’s Nathan is, as Kommerell says, the “tragedy” of reconciliation and neutralization. So it is not a tragedy at all.

The neutralization is carried not by the state, in the European sense, but by one wise individual. So from comedy we move onward to neutralization. Comedy itself is not yet neutralization.

That is very important.

From Shylock the rough to Nathan the sly. But how can even the wisest man carry the burden of neutralization?

A play about compromise!

Max Kommerell is right to make fun of it. Even from the Jewish point of view, I would prefer Shylock.

The parable of the counterfeit rings could only have been invented in the brain of a counterfeiter and believed by harmless idealists.

25 August 1956

Consumption is the continuation of production by other means. That is the splendid definition Jürgen Habermas gave at the “Bund” conference in Wuppertal in October 1955.573 The subject was: cultural consumption and consumer culture.

Back in 1925, as a joke, I defined consumption as: service to the producer. But Habermas’s definition is much better and has far greater potential. First, it can be reversed any way one likes. Second, it can be applied generally to our present stage of development. For example:

Defense is the continuation of attack by other means—and vice versa. Leisure is the continuation of working time by other means. Adultery is the continuation of marriage by other means. Drinking beer is the continuation of university study by other means—and vice versa. And finally—if we think about the history of the wars of religion, the Inquisition, and the persecution of heretics—even the Devil is only the continuation of God by other means. The opus Dei, the work of God, passes over into the opus Diaboli, the work of the Devil, until in the end the two become interchangeable. Nathan the Wise becomes the continuation of Shylock by other means. Their interchangeability shows that “by other means” really means nothing more than “in other words.”

So, for example:

God—in other words, the Devil.

Or:

Nathan—in other words, Shylock.

Shylock becomes a tragic hero. For roughly fifty years now, the theaters have played him that way.

Karl Marx, in Capital, Book I, p. 279, in the discussion of the struggle over the normal working day, still treats Shylock as the symbol of exploitative capital. Now the exploiter and usurer becomes a tragic hero.

What magnificent progress in the development of capitalism!

The usurer as a hero who brings us to tears!

He inspires fear and pity!!

You see, my son, here in 1956, very clearly what in 1946 you still had not guessed, although it stood directly under your nose and sat on your very skin: the Wholly Other is the continuation of the Wholly Similar by other means— though, admittedly, by wholly other means.

26 September 1956, Wednesday

Eleven years ago today, on 26 September 1945 at ten in the morning, the officers of my persecutors appeared at my home in Schlachtensee and threw me for a year into what they called “automatic arrest.”

This is my memorial day.

4 October 1956

When I was asked to comment on the tenth anniversary of the Nuremberg judgment:

Ask Mr. Kranzbühler. He can do it much more beautifully.574

For me, the matter is different.

I have to tell myself: in the house of the hanged man, one does not speak of the rope. But in the house of the executioner, people talk all the more about law and justice.

9 November 1956

Ceasefire in Egypt.

A great victory for the idea of peace.

The world is on its way toward law and nonviolence.

The United Nations is marching forward.

And what is really happening?

Two Very Strong powers—the USA and the Soviet Union—are teaching two Half-Strong powers—Britain and France—about the true balance of strength in today’s world.

At the beginning stands the Taking.

At the end stands the exception and the state of exception.

What good is all this de-Nazification or de-Stalinization if the most important de- of all never happens: the de-Lincolnization of the Americans?

I remember the conversation with Nicolaus.

The German is a monad. He reflects the universe, but he has no windows. A new type now growing up believes he can acquire windows by tearing down his house.

Becoming houseless as a form of clearing out the clutter. The atomic bomb as the specific instrument of clearing out the clutter.

18 November 1956

The Greek popular assembly sat.

The Roman one stood!

The difference between democracy and republic!

And now one step further: from standing to walking!

From status to movement!

From statesman to gangster!

Irresistible progress!

23 November 1956

Creation out of nothing.

Creatio ex nihilo.

Sociologically, this means: the conquerors come out of the desert;575 and then: Taking / Dividing / Grazing. But no conquerors of the non-Paradise ever come out of Paradise.

From Paradise one can only be expelled.

The monad has no windows.

Then perhaps it should try making the sign of the Cross.

Perhaps a few windows would open.

28 November 1956

All human beings are equal.

Indeed: equal in a way that inspires pity.

“Christianity is Judaism for the people,” Disraeli said.

And Ludendorff and Hitler, as honest ex-Christians—Disraelites—enthusiastically repeated it after him.

Christendom is humanity freed from the Jew.

Remember the ambiguity:

“freed by the Jew” or “freed from the Jew.”

Using this style, you can construct whole series of definitions:

Psychoanalysis, when it is not simply de-ghettoization, is Judaism for intellectuals = ex-Puritans.

The theory of relativity is Judaism for Nobel Prize winners with no education in the humanities.

Darwinism is a doctrine of salvation and a system of education for social climbers and Manchester men.

And so on and so on.

5 December 1956

Take care.

Your persecutors are trying to drive you into persecution mania. Only when they have robbed you of your reason and taken away your mind have they truly won.

They want to make you nervous.

They want to throw you into a panic.

They want you to tremble in fear at every sound.

Every blast of a car horn is supposed to feel like an attack directed personally at you. Every sound that disturbs you is supposed to become their ally. So be careful and remain normal!

Every exaggeration harms you. But so does every understatement through irony, sarcasm, or parody. Nobody must be allowed to push you off the path of reason.

Listen and suffer, suffer and listen!

And leave aside the silly pleasure of artistic jokes, no matter how witty they may be.

That includes amusing exercises in rhetorical forms such as tmesis: the Suez—oh my God—Canal; or: the science—good heavens—of law. Every sharpening of the point harms your case.

Suffer and listen, listen and suffer!

End of the year 1956

At Christmas 1912 I wrote to Fritz Eisler:

The time is ripe for dictatorship.

At Christmas 1956 I write in my diary:

The time is ripe for every kind of hydrogen bomb.

Dictatorship is obsolete.

Compared with the means of destruction invented by Nobel Prize winners, it has become an old-fashioned instrument.

Humanity had need of them, Hegel says—and immediately they appeared.

The hour of consumer society has arrived.

The essence of the human being ceases to be work and becomes play. But the atomic bomb enters as the violent intrusion of time into play. And so—is this still play?—Meyerbeer and Offenbach sit themselves down on top of the system of tonal music that patient monks worked out over a thousand years of Christianity.

17 January 1957576

I asked Kojève:

What did humanity need when the atomic bomb was invented?

And I asked him for an authentically Hegelian answer. He replied:

Humanity needed a moral alibi, an excuse that would allow it to stop fighting wars.577 Because a new humanity is beginning: without war, without play, without heroism, without risk.

Total welfare begins.

We are not standing at the end of all security.

We are standing at the beginning of total security.

That was Kojève’s apparently optimistic answer. He added that this new Paradise would not be his Paradise.

The Anglo-Saxons have a simple answer to my question: humanity needs the atomic bomb so that, if necessary, it can use force to stop the senseless overpopulation of the underdeveloped regions. That is the meaning of what people such as Julian Huxley say. It grows out of Malthusianism, itself a product of island anxiety. But the simplest and most popular answer remains simple criminalization: humanity needs such a weapon of destruction in order to eliminate my enemy—the final obstacle standing in the way of world peace.

With these reflections I continue the final paragraph of my Nomos of the Earth, which suddenly breaks off, quickly drops the curtain, and makes itself invisible to the persecutors.

No human being has ever spoken more calmly or more consciously to his persecutors in the middle of a danger to the world than I did.

You can see this both in the preface and at the end of The Nomos of the Earth.

Will another person ever be found who understands it?

18 January 1957

Konrad Kaletsch told me about the incident involving Flick, de Menthon, and Armengaud during the visit of the delegates from the Coal and Steel Community to the Maxhütte works.

In the end, the furious accuser and criminalizer was satisfied when the old Friedrich Flick, now seventy-five, agreed not to give a welcoming speech. So the two men sat silently at the same table.

I must ask Kaletsch sometime whether they shook hands.

In Flick’s case, that is how the matter ended.

In my case it cannot end like that.

I am defenseless and Flick is powerful. But I am bound to conscious language and speech. Even so, I felt deep sympathy for the capable old Flick, and as a jurist I was ashamed of the legal criminalizer who becomes trapped in his own constructions and can no longer make peace.

21 January 1957

There the diary appears as a small institution. But the great beneficiaries of inherited institutions are much more watchful than the little people who keep diaries. They do not simply beat these little, honest book-keepers to death.

Beat them to death?

Certainly not.

Out of the question.

Simply dead?

Oh, no!!

Excuse me—why not simply dead?

Enemies of humanity may surely simply be beaten to death!

Oh no!

Not with us!578

Oh no!

Not with us!

Then what are we supposed to do with them?

Well, we can always question them.

What a language this German language is.

What bottomless hidden meaning:

vernehmen—to question, to interrogate, but still containing nehmen, “to take.”

There will be no more taking, only questioning!

That is enough to make a human being harmless.

Simply prescribe for these diary-keepers the questions they must answer in their diaries. Then the diary becomes the most useful institution of the new Paradise. Then you will have statistics unlike anything any previous social order has ever possessed.

I already sensed this during the First World War and described it in my essay “The Buribunks” (Summa, 1917/18). But at the time I knew nothing yet of the questionnaire—invented by the Anglo-Saxons—or of all its later refinements.

3 February 1957

In his lecture on European colonialism, delivered in Düsseldorf on 16 January 1957, Kojève avoided every word that might sound directly topical. And yet the explosive relevance of the subject was bursting out at every corner. For me, it was an unbelievable and completely unexpected gain that the specific meaning of the Großraum became visible.

The Großraum—the “large space”—is a provisional name for the scale of the space of development, now that the earth is divided between developed and underdeveloped peoples and territories.

Point Four of the Truman Doctrine as today’s Nomos of the Earth.

We established, unfortunately, that the magnificent formula

Taking / Dividing / Grazing

is extremely difficult to translate into French.

The greatest difficulty is the wonderful word Weiden—grazing—which raises production and consumption into the higher unity of consumption itself.

How helpless the Spanish attempts at translation are:

toma de tierra, presa de tierra, ocupación, instalación for Landnahme—taking possession of land;

apacentamiento for Weiden—grazing!

It is enough to drive one to despair!

The greatest difficulty is that Western capitalism and colonialism, which supposedly give, have no name.

“No one can baptize this child,” Kojève said, word for word.

Socialism is an accepted name. But “giving capitalism” and “giving colonialism”? Nobody will believe those. There is no such thing as purely giving capitalism—that is, capitalism that takes nothing.

That would be absurd.

To give without taking is not human. That would be God’s affair. And specifically the affair of a God who can create the world out of nothing.

What can the taker give?

The name.

And that is exactly what is missing.

Nobody can baptize this strange child, this capitalist who develops purchasing power.

“Fordism” is not really a name either.

Socialism, by contrast, as I said, still has a certain ring to it despite everything. And that gives it a historical legitimacy powerful enough to make 200 million Russians, practicing ascetic renunciation of their own consumption, “develop” more than 600 million Chinese, Indonesians, and other peoples!

I read the chapter “Plotnoi” in Mutius’s Katorgan and became suspicious because it smelled too much like Ernst Jünger’s Forest Passage.

How does one undermine today’s world domination?

The way early Christianity undermined the Roman Empire?

That would be the problem of asceticism.

Anyone practicing asceticism today is sabotaging the pure consumer society.

Keynes already said that.

The Russians can justify being ascetics today only by claiming that they are organizing an even more comfortable consumer society for tomorrow. Otherwise they would be the saboteurs of the new Paradise.

Nicolaus asked about the patriot.

I answered:

The patriot, as such, is neither a producer nor a consumer. So what exactly does he want?

He must go on strike. But even the strike, if properly organized, can become an institution of the pure consumer society.

I do not know how Nicolaus ended up with a subject like this.

Bavarian Radio probably hung it around his neck.

I would rather give a lecture on the Bavarian Party and the electoral threshold.

28 February 1957

“Those bells were never yours, and they are no longer mine.”

These are extraordinary lines.

You must know them if you want to understand my life.579 They stand at the beginning of the German twentieth century.

At the time they were written, I was a naive thirteen-year-old country boy madly infatuated with a Jewish girl named Meta Gutmann.

I could never have guessed that a poet from the generation before mine, with deeper knowledge, was writing lines like these. And it would have done no good if someone had quoted them to me and explained them when I was thirteen.

Everything would have disappeared beneath my completely Catholic upbringing and my rebellion against it.

How astonishing these lines are!

Yet I have never found them quoted, much less interpreted.

People passed over them then and continue to pass over them today. And how easily they can be extended:

Those were never your myths, and they are no longer mine.

Or, just as importantly:

Those were never your wines, and they are no longer mine.

Or:

Those were never your poets, and they are no longer mine.

Here, admittedly, the extension seems to fail. But this remains:

Those were never your saints, and I cannot part from them.

17 March 1957

Peter Schneider’s book State of Exception and Norm: A Study of the Legal Theory of C. S. has finally appeared.

It is presumably intended to de-Schmittize German jurisprudence.580

A Swiss man who went through none of it summons me, who went through all of it, before his tribunal.

A neutral man without a fate of his own passes judgment on my fate.

At bottom it is completely incompetent. But it is symptomatic and symbolic. And that is how I want to accept it, without irony or polemic, as one part of the general fate, like everything else: without submitting, but also without defending myself. It would be contrary to the style and the esprit de mon âge—the spirit of my age in life—to raise questions of jurisdiction, standing, or legal authority to bring the case.

Today anyone can kill anyone.

That is total jurisdiction.

18 March 1957

Walter Warnach thinks, rightly, that Catholics are more restrained in their speech than Protestants.

That is understandable.

Since Catholicism stopped being a religion of the people, with whom can a Catholic speak freely and without concern?

Priests cannot speak freely among themselves.

Laypeople cannot speak freely among themselves.

Priests cannot speak freely with laypeople.

Laypeople cannot speak freely with priests.

Secularized priests and secularized laypeople continue this habit for generations.

25 March 1957

Polla ta deina—many are the terrible things.581

Yes indeed.

Many terrible things I have seen.

Of many terrible things I have heard.

Six million murdered Jews.

Twelve million persecuted Germans.

But the most terrible—but the most terrible—is and remains—nobody understands it;

nobody can grasp it: the most terrible thing is and remains the celibate bureaucracy that finds itself facing a reality—which it has itself helped create—in which Christianity is not even “Judaism for the people” anymore; and which now, in this admittedly precarious situation, looks around for new sources of strength—and of money.

27 March 1957582

This book by Peter Schneider has no form. It is a cancerous growth of extensive excerpts from a few of my writings, with my life’s work slobbered over by bland C. G. Jung ideas.

The book has no form because it has no fate. But not fate-less like Hölderlin’s sleeping infant. Fate-less like a Swiss man whose country has been neutral for more than a hundred years.

How was this author supposed to digest a life’s work such as mine? And how was he allowed to appear before the German public while suffering from such obvious digestive problems?

30 March 1957

Meanwhile Hans Zehrer blows a tremendous trumpet blast into empty space by publishing an article on the permanent state of exception in Die Welt of 30 March 1957. It is a magnificent, though anonymous, German answer to the Swiss book’s complete lack of connection with reality. Zehrer dares to say openly that atomic power—which by its nature depends on secrecy—and democracy—which demands complete publicity—are incompatible.

Today, when a small sworn circle decides matters concerning the atom, we live under a permanent state of exception that more or less suspends democracy.

Faced with concrete realities like these, our Swiss ostrich prefers to stick his head into a bowl of whipped cream.

10 April 1957

Behind my work on the state of exception lies the problem of the limits of what our modern, highly divided social machinery calls “law.” It is the problem of the limits of the courts and of judicial procedure.

The limit of what a modern legislator can turn into a statutory rule.

The limits of norms and normativity as such.

Naturally, asking about these limits brings one directly up against the territory of secrets and taboos.

As a young, inexperienced jurist, guided by no genuine teacher of constitutional or international law, I made a number of mistakes and violated more than one taboo.583

That was serious and deserves correction. If Peter Schneider had asked and answered the question in that way, his book would have been magnificent, even if it had not been exhaustive.

Instead, as he calls it, he approaches the matter “anthropologically,” using a thin infusion of C. G. Jung’s categories, and asks about my personal secret—my Arcanum—on p. 96 of his book and elsewhere. And he ignores—with what right, exactly?—the passage in Ex Captivitate Salus, p. [75], where I formally deposited that Arcanum. He would have done better to consider my reference to the connection between dictatorship, sovereignty, and grace in the preface to Dictatorship, p. IX. And he should have remembered Rivarol’s warning not to betray the “perplexity of justice” and not to deal with problems “for which Themis has no scales.”584

Peter Schneider’s book pushes me further into the problem of the judicial process itself:

  1. Each of the three peoples that shaped European thought—the Greeks, the Romans, and the Jews—had one man who, for us Europeans, was their greatest.

    The Greeks had Socrates.

    The Romans had Julius Caesar.

    The Jews had Jesus Christ.

    Each of these three peoples killed its greatest man.

    But only the people with the strongest sense of law and legal procedure—the Romans—did not kill their Julius Caesar judicially.

    They murdered him.585

  2. Queen Elizabeth of England sensed in 1585/86, through the instinct of royal blood, that it would have been less dangerous to the principle of monarchy to have Mary Stuart killed informally than to subject her to a formal trial before judges and an executioner appointed and authorized by Elizabeth herself.

    She sensed the great precedent that would later lead to Cromwell’s trial and judicial killing of her successor Charles I in 1649.

    And finally to the death blow against European monarchy: the judicial killing of Louis XVI by the Jacobins in 1793.

    Compare J. E. Neale, Elizabeth and Her Parliaments 1584–1601, London, Jonathan Cape, 1957, pp. 140 ff.

  3. The killing of Wallenstein in 1634, according to Pekař.

  4. Under the impact of the judicial killing of Louis XVI, Kant wrote in his Doctrine of Right, Part II, General Remark, Meiner edition pp. 142 ff.:

    “Even the murder of the monarch is not yet the worst thing—for one can still imagine that it was done out of fear—because it does not claim to be an act of punitive justice but an act of self-preservation.

    It is the formal execution that fills a soul imbued with the rights of man with horror…”

    The “complete overturning of all concepts of right”—Charles I, Louis XVI.

    “That is the crimen mortale, inexpiabile—the mortal, unatonable crime—at bottom inexplicable because the criminal knowingly acts against the law,” and so on.

    The reversal of the relationship between sovereign and people.

  5. Yalta, February 1945:

    Stalin proposes simply liquidating 50,000 German [officers].

    Ch[urchill] demands a trial.586

  6. Nuremberg, 1945/46.

    My opinion of 25 August 1945 on the scelus infandum—the unspeakable crime.

13 April 1957

Listen to this Ernst Bloch:

The country building socialism—that is, today’s Soviet Union—has used all its immense power for one purpose only: to bring power over human beings to an end! So says Ernst Bloch in The Principle of Hope, 1953, vol. 2, p. 490!!

All this so that “instead of the so-called constitutional state, which because of its rotten class content has become completely a state of injustice”—Ernst Bloch should never have touched this rickety contrast between Russia and the “state of injustice”; it is beneath him—so that, in the end, “no state at all will be necessary.” And in this way the monstrous super-state called the Soviet Union is justified!

Such faith I have found nowhere but in Israel!

Such justification by the final end I have not found even among the Jesuits!

24 April 1957

In the spring of 1948 the famous atomic physicist Niels Bohr solemnly declared:

“Humanity will face decisive decisions five years from now. If by then it succeeds in avoiding war, the world will be saved.”

Those were his exact words. And he continued:

“By the end of those five years, natural science will have advanced so far that war will be impossible.”

That was the prediction in 1948.

What actually happened?

At the end of those five years, natural science invented the hydrogen bomb.

That was the colossal advance that arrived.

This, and nothing else, is how natural science honors its predictions of progress and world peace.

To all these Nobel Prize winners who now warn us so impressively and lament so loudly—including the good, dear, brave Albert Schweitzer, who spoke so beautifully on the radio about radioactive radiation—to every one of these accusers and mourners I answer with Lucan’s lines from the Pharsalia IV.183–184:

Why beat your breast? Why, madman, do you groan? Why pour out useless tears, instead of admitting that of your own free will you obey the crime and fall into line the moment things become serious?

28 April 1957

Lucan also gives us the most brilliant example of how a sense of law, in a situation of civil war, must lead to disaster—and all the more disastrously the better justified it is.

This is the story of Petreius. He stands on the just side, the side of the Senate, and warns against fraternization and betrayal (Pharsalia IV.212–235):

trahimur sub nomine pacis—we are being dragged along under the name of peace.

Everything can be applied to the present world situation.587

The Roman is the man of law precisely because he knows the limits of law.

22 May 1957

Everyone screams about Hitler’s violation of the principles of the constitutional state when he crushed the Röhm putsch.

Today they all scream in moral outrage: even the Reichswehr stained itself by taking part in Röhm’s murder.

Dachau trial, April/May 1957; Der Spiegel, no. 20, 15 May 1957.

So poor noble Röhm and the four million good SA men, infiltrated by Communists, were supposed to receive a proper constitutional-state trial—that is, a judicial trial!

How exactly are we supposed to imagine that in the situation of June 1934?

Would every single one of them presumably have had to receive a defense lawyer?

What these killers were capable of had been shown shortly before in the Potempa trial!

Is all this shouting about the constitutional state not grotesque if people seriously mean it as a description of what should have happened in 1934?

And if they do not seriously mean it for Röhm and the situation of 1934, and only use it to stir up general outrage, is it anything more than the lowest kind of preaching for a purpose?

Lucan’s knowledge of civil war remains simply admirable here too, as it does in the problem of Elizabeth and judicial procedure discussed above in the note of 28 April 1957. It is a sign of Victorian-aesthetic stupidity when Robert Graves tries to dismiss the magnificent Lucan as rhetorical cardboard kitsch. He is rhetorical. Thomas Hobbes already knew that and said so. But the rhetoric expresses his real situation.

It is not unreality.

The opposition between the rhetorical and the lyrical dominated the nineteenth century because politics had become fraud and ideology, while reality withdrew as truth into lyric poetry.

There, for one moment in Expressionism, it became politically explosive again.

Just listen to this line from Lucan about the informal murder of Pompey and compare it with Elizabeth’s occasional hope that someone would be found to murder Mary Stuart and spare her the trouble of legal proceedings.

Pompey’s murderer presents the victorious Caesar with the murdered Pompey’s head and says:

si scelus est plus te nobis debere fatere quod scelus hoc non ipse facis.

Pharsalia IX.1031

If this is a crime, then admit that you owe us all the more gratitude because we took it off your hands and you did not have to commit the crime yourself.588

Hitler could have said that to the bourgeoisie in 1934 if he had possessed as much sense for law as he possessed for the situation.

But he was clever enough to hold on to legality instead and have the Reichstag give him a certificate clearing him by passing a law. He had boasted that at the time he had been the supreme judge of the nation. But to him that was merely a phrase. He would have found it extremely unpleasant if someone had taken him literally. That is what I naively tried to do in my essay “The Führer Protects the Law,” an essay whose boldness—indeed recklessness—nobody understood at the time.

The Nazi jurists, including press chief Du Prel and Minister Frank, were completely baffled when they read it. They called it “liberal.”

Fortunately for me, Hitler himself never saw it. He would have sensed what it meant: to take the tried-and-tested trick of legality out of his hands and force him into legal responsibility. He would once again have staged one of his fits of rage against the jurists. There is only one way for the philosopher or jurist to deal with the ruler: take him at his word. That too is a form of Taking.

Compare the story in Funck-Brentano, Le Roi (1907):

“Your Majesty will decide the case personally.”

1 June 1957

The editors of the Rheinischer Merkur—Roegele—deleted my name from an article by Walter Warnach about Spain and Calvo Serer.589 So I still have a guardian angel after all. He guides the hand of these people who strike my name out. They intend evil, and the guardian angel turns it into good.

I would have been very embarrassed if my name had appeared in that article.

10 June 1957, Whit Monday

At the end of May I wrote to Peter Schneider to acknowledge receipt of his book:

“for me, as the object of this vivisection—or better: this Arcanoscopy.”

I thought the coinage “Arcanoscopy”—an inspection of my secret—was especially witty. But neither Rüdiger Altmann nor Johannes Groß reacted to it.

Apparently my contacts and my antennae are failing.

I am already too old.

What am I still doing in the world? Do you see how the lightning falls over there?

Or rather: the H-bomb?

A delightful conversation with George Schwab about homo homini homo—man is man to man.590

I asked him:

In what concrete situation is that true?

He said:

On a bus, surely, homo homini homo applies.

Man is man to man, and neither God nor wolf.

I replied:

But in a philosophical discussion, homo homini homo means nothing other than:

homo homini alibi.

Man is an alibi for man. For whom?

For man!

For what?

For being human!

An alibi for the God and an alibi for the Wolf.

An alibi before whom?

Before another human being!

11 June 1957

You pray to false gods.

You use the wrong intoxicant. You take opium instead of drinking wine.591 Religion becomes the opium of the people when the laity has its wine taken away. Naturally they have to run to foreign gods once they start taking foreign intoxicants.

12 June 1957

The priest has stolen away the wine. We have a great deal to make up for.

17 June 1957

The surest way to abolish the priesthood is the universal priesthood. If all laypeople are supposed to become priests, then all priests are more likely to become laypeople than all laypeople are to become priests. The level at which the two sides finally meet will be the lowest and most comfortable one: universal lay status. Not universal priesthood. That is the path of democracy.

Democracy is universal kingship.

Everyone his own sovereign.

The democratic way of life. It is the road forced upon us by the logic of concepts of this kind.

20 June 1957

The final result of a jurist’s existence:

I do not want to have power.

But I want even less to be in the right.

So my heartfelt condolences on your constitutional state!

1 July 1957

The steel bells that call a person to church in this country—those are no longer my bells. Everything else follows by itself: those are no longer my songs; those are no longer my wines; not even my schnapps anymore. It is Coca-Cola-coalition music.

21 July 1957

In Heidelberg I quoted to Carl-Joachim Friedrich the line:

Those bells were never yours, and they are no longer mine.

At that very moment the bells for Vespers were ringing.

He said:

In America you rarely hear church bells ringing.

30 July 1957

In Wiesbaden, at Hans Freyer’s seventieth birthday, we laughed at Adorno’s revealing remark about Hegel’s “grandiose peasant cunning.”

In that remark you can see a cloven hoof that may turn into a boomerang and, as Hans Barion added, strike an Achilles heel.

How amusing these self-revelations of the great revealers are.

10 August 1957

How disgusting the whole philosophy of work then becomes: with its servant undermining the master, its serva padrona—the servant who becomes mistress, its successful private tutor, and all the social climbers who marry aristocratic girls and eventually create in Darwinism their grand myths of the ambitious survivor who compensates for his physical weakness through intelligence.

So that was the European nineteenth century.

Perhaps I will live to see its end.

How magnificent, by contrast, was Hans Freyer’s reply to Arnold Gehlen’s birthday speech:

What we have gained is: progress in the mode of failure.

The defeated man writes history.

The infiltrator writes sociology. And Samuel Pepys crawls into his diary.

Switzerland is certainly no katechon.

12 August 1957

When I was talking with A. Kojève about the falsification of the sacrament and complained about the withholding of the wine, he replied:

The layman has too much blood anyway.

At that moment I noticed that he was a cleric and I was a layman. And yet no Iron Curtain fell between us. Nor did the speaking grille of a confessional.

17 August 1957

In Wiesbaden, in his speech for Hans Freyer’s seventieth birthday, Arnold Gehlen declared: we are passing from one age, the age of history, into another—the age of sociology.

The age of history is over.

According to Kojève’s interpretation, Hegel had already said the same thing. But Hegel did not yet know what Gehlen knows: that the age—one presumably must no longer say time—of sociology is now beginning.

Excellent.

And how pleasant to hear and believe.

The end of time has arrived.

History was never the ground of happiness.

But now sociology is coming.

And the social is coming.

The pure consumer society.

That, presumably, will be the ground of happiness.

Wars will cease.

Class struggles will cease.

Socialism ends in sociology.592

21 August 1957

The real explosive force of the atomic bomb strikes the very concept of the human being. It drives homo homini homo out of its comfortable hiding place and blows apart the threefold neutrality of this threefold tautology.

Human beings drop atomic bombs made by human beings onto the heads of other human beings.

That is the reality of homo homini homo. Here human beings are completely among themselves. So where is the true human being?

And what becomes of the other person, who by consequence is no longer a true human being?

I really ought to start thinking about a Song of the Seventy-Year-Old, an antistrophe to my Song of the Sixty-Year-Old.

Perhaps like this:

Listen and suffer! Listen and suffer?

That is still too grand.

I listen and hear nothing anymore. I suffer and feel nothing anymore. What am I still doing in the world? Waiting until the atomic bomb is hurled?

Spare yourself the death of an insect that threatens from Nobel Prize clouds.

Leave this establishment before the brothel owner throws you out and has his police arrest you as an enemy of the constitutional state.

Should I sing like that?

Or rather with the cheerfulness of an all-knowing old man who knows that he has passed beyond the line and nothing can happen to him anymore, because neither a declaration of enmity nor the decoration of some order can still reach him?

Vedremos.

We shall see.

Perhaps you should sing of progress?

Yes indeed!

2 September 1957

Yes indeed!

Progress of every kind:

Progress in the consciousness of freedom, with Hegel.

Progress in the consciousness of the distinction between friend and enemy.

Progress in the consciousness of defeat.

Progress from taking land to taking sea, and from there to taking industry,

taking space,

taking the world.

Progress in the methods used to liquidate whoever disturbs the cleansing.

Progress in the mode of failure.

Come into your own where you inherit your failure!!

And carry out progress in the mode of failure!

That would make a fine antistrophe to the many forms of terror in the Song of the Sixty-Year-Old!

13 September 1957

The Catholic lay intellectual who speaks publicly is normally a comic figure—and in great cases, such as Donoso, a tragicomic one.

Who exactly is he talking to?

Inside the domain of the celibate bureaucracy he has nothing to say.

Outside it, people must take him for an altar boy.

A just punishment for this idiot of an intellectual layman.

Why does he insist on speaking when all he is allowed to say is Yes and Amen?

A naked, unclothed intellectual standing among prelates decked out in pomp!

A very comic role.

One cannot ignore the saying

Ubi nihil vales, ibi nihil velis

—where you have no power, desire nothing—without being punished for it.

If a person starts preaching instead of dutifully acclaiming—that is, instead of saying Yes and Amen—he merely causes embarrassing attention.593 But look: atheist rationalists and Marxists such as Georg Lukács suddenly find themselves in exactly the same tragicomic situation and are instructed by their own headquarters about their true function. So perhaps we could all quite happily philosophize together about knowledge and power, sagesse et tyrannie—wisdom and tyranny—without insulting one another and criminalizing one another as traitors to the spirit.

4 October 1957

By creating the world out of nothing, God thereby made Nothing into Something it had not been before: Something from which a world can be created.594

And that is quite something.

What?

This whole beautiful world was created out of nothing?

Out of nothing?

Ex nihilo?

Ex nihilo, yes indeed!

Well, it certainly looks like it.

Yes indeed.

It certainly looks like it.

Which only makes this Nothing from which it was created more and more interesting.

5 October 1957

The problem of the order: wine—woman—song.

Material for a new world war.

I find it unbelievable that wine comes before woman.

Woman is the first stage.

6 October 1957

Carl Schmitt—connaisseur of Chaos.

Tu quis es?

Who are you?

To my friend George Schwab:

The identity formula homo homini homo lies at the core of the identity between rulers and ruled—that is, at the core of democracy itself.595

Anyone who denies it cannot be a democrat.

Yesterday I became agitated for a moment when George Schwab read the note at the end of my opinion of 25 August 1945 on aggressive war:

How can Hitler’s scelus infandum—his unspeakable crime—be atoned for?

Surely not through a judicial process!

That would strip it of its unbelievable character and standardize it. It would turn the crime into a procedure, into a precedent, and place it inside the realm of what can be foreseen—and reviewed afterward.

Hugo Ball criticized my Political Romanticism with the remark:

To hunt one rabbit—Adam Müller—an entire province is sealed off.596

I replied:

Fine.

But that sealing-off produced the first map of the province.

28 October 1957

Three grim prophecies for the Germans:

  1. To reach your Reich, Germans, you struggle in vain.

  2. To form yourselves into a nation, Germans, you hope in vain.

    (With <Wilder>, the Jew has backing; see Karl Kraus.)597

  3. To become a people, Germans, you wish in vain.

  4. Like Rome.

  5. Like the French.

  6. Like the Poles and Czechs.598

29 October 1957

Why exactly did Ernst Bloch become so furious when I spoke of the “proletarian consciousness of having been cheated”?599

I said it as a proletarian myself.

Admittedly, a different kind of proletarian from his.

Not a proletarian hungry for loot.

All I have left is progress in the consciousness of having been cheated. From time to time I change the kind of person I allow to cheat me. Then the discarded swindler rages after me and calls me a characterless traitor.

31 December 1957

Good Werner Becker expects Rome to make a confession of guilt because of the Renaissance popes.

Rome will gladly give him one.

It does not matter anymore.

And are today’s dollar-and-rejuvenation popes really better and more Christian than those genuine sinners?

Those genuine sinners at least still held the trump card of pecca fortiter—sin boldly—and by their very existence could refute Luther eo ipso. Today’s popes, by contrast, are merely normativists and righteous peacemakers. Peacemakers with retirement insurance and a right to a long, edifying earthly life. That is: a right to die of old age.

We should not envy them for it. If I had the power, I would gladly guarantee every one of them death from old age.

4 January 1958

Today human beings use technology to create their own environment. They cease to be endangered living creatures and attain an improbably advanced age in complete security, with well-organized provision for every need. But in doing so, they cease to be the endangered living creature that remains “open” and is bound to no fixed environment. They become animals, like other animals.
