the impostor Lüth — Paul Lüth (1921–1986), who presented himself as a doctor despite not having completed his medical studies; author of writings on literary history and newspaper essays.

2 July 1949

Carrion-Comfort — Superficial, heartless consolation.

3 July 1940

Mahan — Alfred Thayer Mahan (1840–1914), American rear admiral and naval writer, an intellectual representative of US imperialism; his most important work was The Influence of Sea Power upon History (1890). See Maschke’s note in SGN, pp. 327–328 and 437.

“For Ahasuerus, who in 1933 …” — Ernst Jünger, Sämtliche Werke, vol. 8, p. 102.

4 July 1949

Hans Paeschke — (1911–1991), journalist and publisher. In 1947 he founded the monthly journal Merkur with Joachim Moras and remained its editor until 1978. Paeschke visited Schmitt in Plettenberg in July 1949; see his letters to Schmitt, RW 265, nos. 10756–10781.

Karl Löwith — (1897–1973), philosopher. Löwith emigrated in 1934 and, under the pseudonym “Hugo Fiala,” launched a sharp attack on Schmitt in 1935.

Schmitt responded to Löwith in 1944 in “Donoso Cortés in gesamteuropäischer Interpretation,” criticizing the fact that Löwith, in his book Von Hegel zu Nietzsche, “leaves essential questions in Bruno Bauer entirely out of account.” C. Schmitt, Donoso Cortés in gesamteuropäischer Interpretation, Cologne 1950, p. 99.

Löwith later acknowledged to Hanno Kesting that this criticism was justified. See H. Kesting’s letter to Schmitt of 22 September 1950, RW 265, no. 7467.

Schmitt also engaged with Löwith in his review of Meaning in History: C. Schmitt, “Drei Stufen historischer Sinngebung,” in Universitas 5, 1950, pp. 927–931. Under its original title, “Drei Möglichkeiten eines christlichen Geschichtsbildes,” it was reprinted in BW Blumenberg, pp. 161–166.

Schmitt gave the manuscript to Merkur editor Paeschke to read and suggested that he send it to Löwith without naming its author. Paeschke did so. The relevant letter survives in the papers of the Merkur editorial office at the German Literature Archive, HS 2274096.

For a German translation of Löwith’s book, Schmitt proposed Hanno Kesting, who completed it with substantial assistance from Reinhart Koselleck.

non possum scribere de eo qui potest proscibere — Correctly:

non est enim facile in eum scribere qui potest proscribere.

“It is not easy to write against someone who has the power to put you on a proscription list.”

Ambrosius Theodosius Macrobius, Saturnalia, II, 4/21.

Schmitt had already been fond of citing this sentence during the Nazi period—for example to Ernst Jünger; see Jünger’s Strahlungen, in E. Jünger, Sämtliche Werke, vol. 2, p. 265.

8 July 1949

Viennese émigré named Karpfen — Otto Maria Carpeaux, originally Otto Karpfen (1900–1978), Austrian journalist and literary critic. He converted from Judaism to Catholicism in 1932 and added “Maria” to his name. After the annexation of Austria he was forced into exile in Brazil, where he changed his name to Carpeaux.

See Mauro Souza Ventura, De Karpfen a Carpeaux. Formação política e interpretação literária na obra do crítico austríaco-brasileiro, Rio de Janeiro 2002.

On his dispute with Bernanos, see Andreas Pfersmann, “Carpeaux versus Bernanos. Eine literar. Fehde im brasilian. Exil,” in Gilbert Ravy, ed., Nouvelles recherches sur l’Autriche (Austriaca, 36), Rouen 1993.

Isidore Isou — Ioan-Isidor Goldstein (1925–2007), Romanian scandal-writer, artist, and philosopher who lived in France from 1945 onward and called himself Isidore Isou. His book L’Agrégation d’un nom et d’un messie, published by Gallimard in 1947, is an autobiographical novel.

9 July 1949

“Not willed, only faithful …” — From a poem by Konrad Weiß. In Weiß, p. 549:

“Deeply astonished, full of awe, I see how everything falls into place; nothing betrays me, not willed, only faithfully followed, […]”

See also BW Mohler, p. 141.

Bach is musical oratory — Arnold Schmitz (1893–1980), music historian and close friend of Carl Schmitt since 1922, had worked on this subject—for example in “Die Oratorische Kunst J. S. Bachs. Grundfragen und Grundlagen,” Kongreßbericht. Gesellschaft für Musikforschung. Lüneburg 1950, pp. 33–49; reprinted in Walter Blankenburg, ed., Johann Sebastian Bach, Darmstadt 1970, pp. 61–84.

Schmitz sent Schmitt an offprint bearing the dedication: “To Carl Schmitt, with respect, admiration, friendship, and gratitude — Arnold Schmitz.” The copy remains in private hands.

For decades the two men had discussed the specifically Western tradition of music tied to words. Arnold Schmitz’s monograph Die Bildlichkeit der wortgebundenen Musik Johann Sebastian Bachs, Mainz 1950, appeared with a printed dedication to Carl Schmitt.

12 July 1949

Donnedieu de Vabres — Henri Donnedieu de Vabres (1880–1952), French lawyer and judge at the Nuremberg trials.

14 July 1949

the Horkia — τὰ ὅρκια, the sacred rites connected with the taking of a solemn oath, especially in Homer.

17 July 1949

Tell it to no one but the wise — Correctly: “Tell it to no one, only to the wise.” Goethe, West-östlicher Divan, poem “Selige Sehnsucht,” Hamburg edition, vol. 2, pp. 18–19.

Maxima non curat praetor — Properly: Minima non curat praetor, “The praetor does not concern himself with trivial matters.” A maxim from Roman law.

Tempus docebit — “Time will tell.”

20 July 1949

the force with which Werner Weber criticizes the work — Werner Weber (1904–1976), a student of Schmitt and, from 1949 onward, professor of public and constitutional law at Göttingen. Between 1949 and 1951 he published three essays criticizing the Bonn Basic Law. They were later collected in W. Weber, Spannungen und Kräfte im westdeutschen Verfassungssystem, Stuttgart 1951.

Bella gerant alii — Bella gerant alii, tu, felix Austria, nube! “Let others wage wars; you, happy Austria, marry!” A couplet by an anonymous poet referring to the successful marriage policy of Maximilian I.

23 July 1949

**Kempner in Der Monat*** — Robert M. W. Kempner, “Der Kampf gegen die Kirche. Aus unveröffentlichten Tagebüchern Alfred Rosenbergs,” in *Der Monat 1, 1949, pp. 26–38.

Rosenberg’s diaries from the years 1934 to 1944 were believed to have disappeared after 1945. In fact, Robert Kempner had possession of the manuscript and took it with him to the United States. It was not rediscovered until 2013 and was published in 2015: A. Rosenberg, Die Tagebücher von 1934 bis 1944, ed. Jürgen Matthäus and Frank Bajohr, Frankfurt am Main 2015.

the Hochland high up in Bavaria — Refers to the journal Hochland, published in Munich. It was banned in 1941 and re-established in November 1946.

26 July 1949

Antiphon — Alternating or responsive chant.

28 July 1949

Maxime Leroy — (1873–1957), French lawyer and social historian; M. Leroy, La vie véritable du Comte Henri de Saint-Simon (1760–1825), Paris 1925. The following quotation is on p. 222.

4 August 1949

in the presence of Mr. Friesenhahn — Ernst Friesenhahn (1901–1984) had been Schmitt’s assistant at the University of Bonn from 1925 onward and received his doctorate under Schmitt in 1928. Their relationship broke down because of Schmitt’s involvement with National Socialism. From 1947 to 1948 Friesenhahn served as dean of the Faculty of Law and Political Science at the University of Bonn.

Kirchheimer — Otto Kirchheimer (1905–1965), a student of Schmitt who, like Friesenhahn, received his doctorate under Schmitt in 1928; see BW Forsthoff, p. 360.

6 August 1949

Reinach, Durkheim — Salomon Reinach (1858–1932), French art historian and scholar of religion. Émile Durkheim (1858–1917), French sociologist and ethnologist.

Reading Rudolf Diels — Rudolf Diels (1900–1957) entered the Prussian police service in 1930 and worked with Papen and Schleicher in 1932. Schmitt had known him since that time. When the Gestapa—the Prussian Secret State Police Office—was created, Diels became its first chief, but he was removed from the post by the end of 1933. He then went on to have a varied and ambiguous career under the Nazi regime, while also maintaining contacts with the resistance. After 1945 he worked for the American military government and appeared as a witness at the Nuremberg trials.

In his autobiography, Diels describes meeting Schmitt in Nuremberg just after Schmitt had been released from detention. Schmitt greeted him with Hutten’s exclamation: “It is a joy to be alive.” Rudolf Diels, Lucifer ante portas. Zwischen Severing und Heydrich, Zurich [1949], p. 322.

12 August 1949

as he appears in Shakespeare — In the note cited above (Leviathan, p. 40), Schmitt refers to Henry V, Act 3, Scene 3; A Midsummer Night’s Dream, Act 2, Scene 1; and The Two Gentlemen of Verona, Act 3, Scene 2.

14 August 1949

aeque enim transgredientes aequaliter puniri jubet aequitas naturalis — Thomas Hobbes, De cive, XIII.16. “For natural equity requires that those who break a law be punished equally.” Hobbes, M/B, p. 215.

20 August 1949

the fate of Miorița — A popular Romanian ballad. Three shepherds meet with their flocks. One of the sheep, named Miorița, tells its shepherd that the other shepherds are going to kill him. The shepherd then addresses the animal and says that, when he dies, he wants to be buried beside his sheep.

21 August 1949

Automatic < Arrest > — After the end of the war in 1945, the Allies placed political officials of the Nazi state under “automatic arrest.” Schmitt did not belong to the category of people covered by this policy, so his detention in 1945–46 was not, contrary to his repeated claims, an “automatic arrest.” See Quaritsch in Carl Schmitt – Antworten in Nürnberg, edited and annotated by Helmut Quaritsch, Berlin 2000, pp. 11–12.

22 August 1949

Aroneanu — Eugène Aroneanu (?–1960), jurist and Romanian resistance fighter. He emigrated to Paris in the 1930s, then to Switzerland in 1943, and prepared a list of Nazi war crimes for the Nuremberg trials. Schmitt is referring to Eugène Aroneanu, Das Verbrechen gegen die Menschlichkeit (excerpt from the Nouvelle Revue de droit internationale privé, no. 2, 1946), Baden-Baden 1947.

the figure of Scaeva — Schmitt is referring to Pharsalia, Book VI, where Scaeva turns against his own troops.

the Biedenhorns — Biedenhorn is a character in Ernst Jünger’s story On the Marble Cliffs: a mercenary commander who conducts himself with tactical skill during a civil war.

Compare my essay on Vitoria — Published anonymously: [C. Schmitt], “Francisco de Vitoria und die Geschichte seines Ruhmes,” in Die neue Ordnung 3 (1949), pp. 289–313. The essay was based on lectures delivered in Spain and Portugal in 1944 and was later included in Nomos, pp. 69–96.

Malraux — André Malraux (1910–1976), French existentialist writer and politician. His early novels deal with the human condition in revolution and civil war.

minor vobis causae vestrae amor quam mihi mortis — Correctly:

Pompei vobis minor est causaeque senatus / Quam mihi mortis amor.

“Pompey’s cause and the Senate’s mean less to you than death means to me.” Pharsalia, VI, 245–46.

23 August 1949

Nos actes nous suivent — “Our actions follow us.” Schmitt is probably referring to Revelation 14:13. He may also have had in mind the novel of the same title by the French Catholic writer Paul Bourget (1852–1935), published in Paris in 1927.

Non omnis moriar — “I shall not wholly die.” Horace, Carmina III.30.6.

Veit Valentin is right — Schmitt is referring to V. Valentin, Geschichte der Deutschen, Berlin 1947.

26 August 1949

excommunication of Communism — A decree of the Holy Office dated 1 July 1949, dealing with the attitude Catholics were to take toward the Communist Party, declared Catholic faith and Communism incompatible. See Acta Apostolicae Sedis 41 (1949), pp. 333–334; German translation in Herder-Korrespondenz 3 (1949), no. 11, p. 487.

liberation from the dreadful Cauchemaritain — A blend of cauchemar (“nightmare”) and “Maritain,” meaning Jacques Maritain. Maritain, who was accused by some of sympathizing with Communism, served as French ambassador to the Vatican from 1945 to 1948. His idea of “Integral Humanism” influenced the social teaching of Pope Pius XII. Schmitt apparently hoped that the decree would put an end to this influence.

27 August 1949

the return of Herr Hausenstein — Wilhelm Hausenstein (1882–1957), German cultural historian, writer, and diplomat. Schmitt had already met him in Munich in 1915; see Tb 1915. In 1950, Hausenstein was sent to Paris by the West German government, first as consul general and then as the Federal Republic’s first German ambassador there.

1 September 1949

Hans Peters — (1896–1966), constitutional lawyer and CDU politician. After 1945 he was one of the leading figures opposing Schmitt’s return to university teaching. See his report of 17 June 1946, Humboldt University of Berlin, University Archive, Faculty of Law, no. 524, fols. 5–6. He also opposed Schmitt’s admission to the Association of German Constitutional Law Teachers. See Levin von Trott zu Solz, Hans Peters und der Kreisauer Kreis. Staatslehre im Widerstand, Paderborn et al., 1997.

16 September 1949

as possessions lost, fermented into time — From a dedicatory poem for Carl Schmitt by Konrad Weiß:

“Our possessions are lost to us, fermented into the world we share.”

Weiß, p. 655.

21 September 1949

Omnis actio humana specificatur ex objecto — Correctly:

actus omnis habet speciem ab obiecto; et actus humanus, qui dicitur moralis, habet speciem ab obiecto relato ad principium actuum humanorum, quod est ratio.

“Every act takes its character from its object; and a human act, which is called moral, takes its character from the object as related to the principle of human action, namely reason.”

Thomas Aquinas, Summa theologiae, I–II, q. 18, a. 8, c.

23 September 1949

Sicilian Vespers — The name given to the uprising against the French occupation in Palermo on 30 March 1282. To stop disguised French soldiers from escaping, people were made to pronounce the words “cece, cici, ciceri.”

Hans Berger — (1909–1985), jurist and diplomat. At the time he was president of the Düsseldorf Regional Court. From 1954 onward he served in the diplomatic service of the Federal Republic of Germany and, beginning in 1959, as ambassador to various countries. He was also, for a period, head of the Office of the Federal President.

24 September 1948

Language is the house of Being. — Quotation from Martin Heidegger’s “Letter on Humanism.”

sustained by the inner image that cannot be possessed — An allusion to Konrad Weiß’s poem “Justitia,” dedicated to Carl Schmitt, which begins:

“In that confused age, the law no longer bent itself toward the inner image.”

Weiß, p. 665.

Jellinek — “Law, then, as the preserving element, will form the minimum of norms required by a particular state of society; in other words, it will include those norms that guarantee the continued existence of that society without fundamental change.” Georg Jellinek, Die sozialethische Bedeutung von Recht, Unrecht und Strafe, 2nd ed., Berlin 1908, p. 45.

25 September 1949

Grote — Manfred Grote, political scientist. In 1962 he wrote “Political ideas of Carl Schmitt and the ‘Nihilism of the 20th century’” (MA thesis, University of Kansas).

26 September 1949

numquid et vos vultis abire? — “Do you also want to leave?” Vulgate, John 6:68; Luther Bible, John 6:67.

1 October 1949

the Roman Church as a ghost — “And if a man considers the origin of this great ecclesiastical dominion, he will easily see that the Papacy is nothing other than the ghost of the deceased Roman Empire, sitting crowned upon its grave.” Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, trans. Jutta Schlösser, ed. Hermann Klenner, Hamburg 1996, p. 586.

Lenin’s ideal was the electrified earth — Schmitt quoting himself: “The great entrepreneur has no ideal other than Lenin’s, namely an ‘electrified earth.’” RK, p. 22; see also FoP, pp. 846–47, with note 24 on p. 861.

When someone suffers a defeat … — Schmitt is referring to the essay “Darf ein Mensch für die Wahrheit sich totschlagen lassen?” in the following edition: Søren Kierkegaard, Der Begriff des Auserwählten, translation and afterword by Theodor Haecker, Hellerau 1917; Schmitt’s copy survives in his papers, RW 265 no. 24274.

The passage on p. 295 reads:

“For when someone suffers a defeat, you do not fully see how weak he is; you see how strong the other man is. But when someone wins and then collapses helplessly, you see how weak he is and always was—and how strong the other man was: the man who tricked him into winning in such a way, who tricked him into being shattered by victory as no defeat could ever have shattered him.”

2 October 1949

Regnare enim dicitur non qui agendo … — “For we say that a man rules when he governs not through his actions but through his words, that is, through commands and threats.” Hobbes, M/B, p. 236.

proprie et accurate loquendo — “in the proper and exact meaning of the word”; the phrase belongs to the longer Hobbes quotation.

Rheema; rheemasin peithomenoi … — Rheema (ῥῆμα) means “command.” Schmitt is alluding to the famous epigram by Simonides of Ceos:

Ὦ ξεῖν’, ἀγγέλλειν Λακεδαιμονίοις, ὅτι τῇδε κείμεθα, τοῖς κείνων ῥήμασι πειθόμενοι.

In Schiller’s translation:

“Wanderer, if you come to Sparta, tell them there that you saw us lying here, as the law commanded.”

The best thing in the world is a command — See LuL, p. 13. Schmitt is freely translating Hobbes:

Tertio, quod imperare et imperata intelligere possimus, beneficium sermonis est, et quidem maximum.

“Third, that we are able to command and to understand commands is a benefit of language—and indeed its greatest benefit.”

Thomas Hobbes, Opera philosophica, ed. G. Molesworth, vol. II, London 1889, p. 91.

6 October 1949

Schmoller — Gustav von Schmoller (1907–1991), diplomat, formerly Schmitt’s doctoral student and assistant at Berlin University.

9 October 1949

a fine gloss of mine — st [= C. Schmitt], “Maritime Weltpolitik,” in Christ und Welt, 6 October 1949. Reprinted in SGN, pp. 478–480.

11 October 1949

Christinform — See Erich Schieweck, Christinform oder Kominform, das kommende Deutschland, Hamburg 1949.

27 October 1949

von der Heydte — Friedrich August von der Heydte (1907–1994), constitutional lawyer, soldier, and politician. The “desecration of asylum” refers to von der Heydte’s “reply” to Schmitt’s “Francisco de Vitoria und die Geschichte seines Ruhms,” published in Die Friedenswarte 49 (1949), pp. 190–197.

See also Schmitt to Forsthoff, 1 December 1949, in BW Forsthoff, pp. 59–60, and to E. R. Huber, 10 December 1949, in BW Huber, pp. 352 ff.

Klaus Mehnert — (1906–1984), political journalist and commentator.

Welty — Eberhard Welty (1902–1965), prior of the Dominican monastery at Walberberg. During these years he gave Schmitt opportunities to publish in the journal Die neue Ordnung, which Welty edited.

1 November 1949

Friedrich Ernst Peters — (1890–1962), German writer.

How beautiful and gratifying successful rhymes are — In 1950, Schmitt told Nicolaus Sombart that he wanted to write an essay about rhyme (BW Sombart, p. 36). He never did, but material for it survives among his papers: RW 265 no. 20801.

6 November 1949

Ernst Jünger’s miserable voice — At the beginning of November 1949, Jünger visited Schmitt. Anima Schmitt wrote about the visit to her mother on 7 November 1949:

“…Peter Heinrich, being a musical person, interpreted him [Jünger] entirely through his voice and shuddered at the thought of seeing his larynx.”

In Gerd Giesler, Carl Schmitt und die Künste der Plettenberger Nachkriegszeit (Plettenberger Miniaturen, 3), Plettenberg 2010, p. 26.

13 November 1949

Herr Jaspers’s … bacillophobia — Schmitt knew the expression “bacillophobia” through Gerhard Nebel. Jaspers had used it in conversation with Nebel, who reported this in a letter to Schmitt dated 7 October 1949 (RW 265 no. 10170).

Writing to Hannah Arendt on 19 October 1949 about Nazi crimes and the question of guilt, Jaspers said that he took “things in all their banality, all their nothingness—bacteria can cause epidemics that destroy entire peoples and yet remain nothing more than bacteria.”

Hannah Arendt/Karl Jaspers, Briefwechsel 1926–1969, ed. Lotte Köhler and Hans Saner, Munich 1985, p. 99.

15 November 1949

Walter Warnach — (1910–2000), writer and philosopher. The extensive correspondence between Warnach and Schmitt, covering 1948 to 1984, is forthcoming.

In a two-page letter dated 15 January 1949, Schmitt complains about attacks by Thieme and von der Heydte. He also suggests passing Warnach’s text on the Dominican priest R.-L. Bruckberger to Epting and contacting Father Laurentius Siemer in Cologne to arrange a meeting.

25 November 1949

un livre de Amédée Ponceau — A. Ponceau, Timoléon. Réflexions sur la Tyrannie, preface by Louis Lavelle, introduction by Raymond Aron (Pensée et civilisation), Paris 1950.

A. Ponceau (1884–1948) was a French existentialist philosopher. Schmitt was also in contact with his widow, Michelle Ponceau, whose favorable reaction to ECS pleased him; see BW Mohler, p. 85.

Maiwald — Serge Maiwald (1916–1952), formerly Schmitt’s doctoral student and habilitation candidate. In 1946 he founded the Schriftenreihe der Universitas. Zeitschrift für Wissenschaft, Kunst und Literatur, which provided Schmitt with a publishing forum.

Schmitt had a particularly close friendship with Maiwald and dedicated to him the only obituary he ever wrote: Carl Schmitt, “Zum Gedächtnis an Serge Maiwald,” in Zeitschrift für Geopolitik 7 (1952), pp. 447–448. See also Günter Maschke’s notes to the republication in FoP, pp. 872–876; and below, p. 271.

Someone puts on the cap of invisibility … — This refers to Ernst Jünger’s novel Heliopolis.

26 November 1949

Exposé by Father Bruckberger — Raymond-Léopold Bruckberger (1907–1998), French Dominican and member of the Resistance.

Laicus taceat in Ecclesia nisi clamat acclamationes praescriptas — “The layman is to remain silent in the Church except when uttering the prescribed acclamations.”

An allusion to 1 Corinthians 14:33–34: “As in all the congregations of the saints, women should remain silent in the churches; for they are not permitted to speak, but should be subordinate, as the law also says.”

30 November 1949

Prussia, then, has been destroyed — The history of Prussia formally ended with Allied Control Council Law No. 46 of 25 February 1947. See above, p. 38: “Il n’y a plus de Prusse”—“There is no longer a Prussia.”

3 December 1949

Dabitur donum fortitudinis — “The gift of courage will be given.” Refers to Thomas Aquinas; see Ulrich Horst, Die Gaben des Heiligen Geistes nach Thomas von Aquin, Berlin 2001, pp. 153 ff.

Father Franziskus Stratmann — (1883–1971), Dominican and representative of the Catholic peace movement.

6 December 1949

Nous ne comparons pas les victimes, nous ne comparons que les juges — “We are not comparing the victims; we are comparing only the judges.”

Schmitt quotes from Lucien Laberthonnière, Sicut ministrator. Critique de la notion de souveraineté de la loi (Œuvres), Paris 1947, p. 84. Schmitt’s annotated copy survives in his papers, RW 265 no. 27235.

On the importance of the Oratorian priest Laberthonnière (1860–1932) for Schmitt, see Schmitt’s essay “Das Problem der Legalität,” written around this time and originating in his interrogations by Kempner, in VA, pp. 440–451; first published in 1950 in Die neue Ordnung.

13 December 1949

Summa contra Gentiles III 93 — For this quotation, Schmitt was using the following edition: Thomas Aquinas, Summa contra gentiles divi Thomae Aquinatis Angelici et v. ecclesiae doctoris … quatuor tributa libris de veritate catholicae fidei … volumen primum [-alterum] … Editio recens Parthenopeia ceteris cunctis accuratius a mendis expurgata de veritate catholicae fidei, vols. 1–2, Naples 1773 (RW 265 nos. 24547, 24548).

Cum infidelibus nec nomina debemus habere communia … — “We should not even have names in common with unbelievers, lest sharing the same names create an opportunity for error.” Thomas Aquinas, as above.

quoted in Privilege and Liberty — Aurel Kolnai, “Privilege and Liberty,” in Laval théologique et philosophique, vol. 5 (1949), p. 109.

20 December 1949

Herr Ziemann’s idea — Ziemann was an editor at Heliopolisverlag in Tübingen.

Ernest Hello — (1828–1885), French writer and philosopher. The quotations can be found in E. Hello, Le siècle, les hommes et les idées, with a prefatory letter by Henri Lasserre, Paris 1896, pp. 365–367.

24 December 1949

the Hamburg judgment against the German general Manstein — Erich von Manstein (1887–1973), field marshal, was convicted as a war criminal in 1949 by a British military court in Hamburg.

30 December 1949

Causa victrix diis placuit — See above, note to p. 79.

9 January 1950

mortisque peribunt argumenta tuae —

Pulveris exigui sparget non longa vetustas / Congeriem, bustumque cadet, mortisque peribunt / Argumenta tuae.

“Before long, time will scatter the little heap of ashes; the tomb will collapse, and every sign of your death will disappear.”

Pharsalia, VI, 867 ff.

my edition of the Pharsalia by Cortius — Marcus Annaeus Lucanus, Pharsalia sive de Bello Civili libri X. [Also included:] Eidemque adscriptum Carmen ad Pisonem [= Laus Pisonis], edited and emended in many places by Gottlieb Cortius, Leipzig 1726. Schmitt’s copy survives in his papers, RW 265 no. 27049.

The summary containing the expression scelus infandum—“unspeakable crime”—comes from the editor Cortius. The concept became important to Schmitt in connection with his 1945 legal opinion; see above, note to p. 66.

10 January 1950

Smend wrote to me … — See BW Smend, pp. 123–124. Schmitt’s letter of 10 January 1950 appears there on p. 126.

To Ernst Jünger — See BW EJ, pp. 243 ff.

the review Karl Korn … — K. Korn, “Der Sprung ins Wunderbare. Zu Ernst Jüngers neuem Buch ‘Heliopolis’,” in FAZ, 24 December 1949.

the kind of distrust that animates Herr de Mendelssohn — Refers to Peter de Mendelssohn, “Gegenstrahlungen. Ein Tagebuch zu Ernst Jüngers Tagebuch,” in Der Monat 2 (1949/50), no. 14, pp. 149–174.

12 January 1950

“Then they remove them” — See above, note to p. 129.

Superos quid quaerimus ultra? — “Why look for the gods anywhere else?” Pharsalia, IX, 579.

Salus ex Judaeis? Perditio ex Judaeis? — “Salvation from the Jews? Destruction from the Jews?” Compare Vulgate, John 4:22. See also above, note to p. 153.

Spinoza was the first to slip himself in — See Leviathan, pp. 86 ff.

17 January 1950

opus operatum — A concept from the Catholic doctrine of the sacraments. For Catholics, a sacrament administered by an ordained priest works ex opere operato—by virtue of the rite having been performed—and therefore does not depend on the personal worthiness or unworthiness of the priest who administers it.

4 February 1950

favor victoris — “the favor of the victor.”

Forster — Not identified.

Porzia method — Refers to the Roman Lex Porcia; see above, note to p. 108.

Anyone who comments on himself falls below his own level — Quotation from Ernst Jünger’s Blätter und Steine (1934). See also BW EJ, p. 280.

5 February 1950

Jünger’s two letters — Not dated the 10th and 16th, but the 13th and 16th of January; see BW EJ, pp. 246 ff. See also below, note to p. 373.

Ch. Journet — Charles Journet (1891–1975), Swiss Catholic theologian and cardinal. Schmitt has the following title in mind: Charles Journet, L’Église du Verbe incarné. Essai de théologie spéculative. 1. La hiérarchie apostolique, [Paris] 1941.

Cum armis Jherusalem peregrinati sunt — “They went armed on pilgrimage to Jerusalem.” Quotation from the Gesta Francorum, an account of the First Crusade. See also Nomos, p. 27, note 2.

Bellorum quippe ac proeliorum certamina … — “The struggles of wars and battles are not merely the beginning of all deceptions; through deception they are also, in fact, discoveries of the arts of the devil.”

From Monumenta Germaniae historica inde ab anno Christi quingentesimo usque ad annum millesimum et quingentesimum: Epistolarum, vol. 6/1, Epistolae Karolini aevi, Berlin 1939, p. 585.

Il n’y a pas moyen d’expliquer comment … — Schmitt quotes from Joseph de Maistre, Les soirées de Saint-Pétersbourg, ou entretiens sur le gouvernement temporel de la providence. Suivis d’un traité sur les sacrifices, vols. 1–2, Paris 1821. The passage is in vol. 2, p. 2. Correctly:

“…il n’y a pas moyen d’expliquer comment la guerre est possible humainement.”

“…there is no way to explain how war is humanly possible.”

châtiment divin; divine au sens où l’enfer est divin — Quotation from Charles Journet, L’Église du Verbe incarné, vol. 1: La hiérarchie apostolique, 3rd ed., [Paris] 1962, p. 621. Correctly:

“la guerre apparaît comme un châtiment divin, elle est divine au sens où l’enfer est divin.”

“War appears as a divine punishment; it is divine in the sense that hell is divine.”

Deus indignatus —

Primo, quod ipsa peccata, quibus Deus indignatus implevit tantis calamitatibus mundum, humiliter cogitantes, quamvis longe absint a facinorosis, flagitiosis atque impiis, tamen non usque adeo se a delictis deputant alienos, ut nec temporalia pro eis mala perpeti se judicent dignos.

“First, when they humbly reflect on the sins because of which God, in his anger, has filled the world with so many calamities, they do not imagine themselves so free of fault that they believe they deserve no temporal suffering for their own sins—even though they are far removed from the criminal, vicious, and godless.”

Augustine, The City of God (De civitate Dei), trans. Wilhelm Thimme, introduction and commentary by Carl Andresen, vol. 1, Munich 1977, p. 15.

Après avoir lu cette description de la guerre juste … — Ch. Journet, op. cit., p. 623.

Carl Erdmann claims — In Die Entstehung des Kreuzzugsgedankens; see p. 223.

Batiffol — Pierre Batiffol, Le catholicisme de Saint Augustin, Paris 1920.

Gustave Schnürer — Gustav Schnürer, L’Église et la civilisation au Moyen-âge, vol. I, trans. G. Castella and Mme M.-Th. Burgard, preface by Édouard Jordan, Paris 1933.

8 February 1950

Godenholm — Ernst Jünger, Besuch auf Godenholm, Frankfurt am Main 1952.

21 March 1950

Not every kind of food is advisable for those who dream — In a letter to Nicolaus Sombart dated 2 May 1950, Schmitt gives the correct wording of this line from Georg Britting’s poem “Der Fasan”:

“About Sartre, only this line: Not every feast is advisable for those who dream.”

BW Sombart, p. 32.

23 March 1950

Son of this consecration … — Adapted from a line by Theodor Däubler in the poem “Am Meere,” from the collection Der sternhelle Weg. The original reads:

“Son of this consecration, you ought to tremble! Listen and suffer.”

24 March 1950

Rousseau speaks of the stake … — “The first man who fenced off a piece of land, thought of saying ‘This is mine,’ and found people simple enough to believe him was the true founder of civil society. How many crimes, wars, murders, miseries, and horrors might the human race have been spared by someone who pulled up the stakes or filled in the ditch and cried out to his fellow men: ‘Beware of listening to this impostor; you are lost if you forget that the fruits of the earth belong to everyone, and the earth itself to no one.’”

Jean-Jacques Rousseau, Diskurs über die Ungleichheit. Discours sur l’inégalité, critical edition of the complete text with all fragments and supplementary materials, newly edited, translated, and annotated by Heinrich Meier, Paderborn 1984, p. 173.

12 April 1950

In 1926 I wrote and published … — C. Schmitt, Die Kernfrage des Völkerbundes, Berlin 1926; reprinted in FoP, pp. 98–99, note 37.

the work by the young Hegel — See above, note to p. 50.

Ah, no bodily wing will join the wings of the spirit — Correctly:

“Ah! To the wings of the spirit no bodily wing will so easily be joined.”

Goethe, Faust, lines 1090–91.

3 May 1950

In the so-called Hochland it is getting more oppressive all the time — In the journal Hochland in 1950, Else Lasker-Schüler’s poem “Ich weiß” appears on p. 352, while Konrad Weiß’s meditation on Maria Caspar-Filser’s painting “Rosen in blauer Vase” appears after p. 568.

Weinreich — Paul Weinreich (1906–1974), editor at the Hanseatische Verlagsanstalt and, from 1946 onward, publisher of Deutsches Zeit-Archiv. Presseberichte und Zeitungsausschnittsdienst. Schmitt received Edition B, devoted to cultural news.

Vorwerk — Friedrich Vorwerk (1893–1969), journalist and publisher. Schmitt had known him since Vorwerk’s time as an editor of the journal Der Ring. See Schmittiana III (1991), pp. 159–162, and Tb 1930–34 (index).

Beste — Theodor Beste (1894–1973), born in Neheim-Hüsten. From 1939 onward, as professor of business administration, he was Schmitt’s colleague at the Friedrich Wilhelm University in Berlin.

4 May 1950

Welzel’s book — Hans Welzel, Vom irrenden Gewissen. Eine rechtsphilosophische Studie (Recht und Staat in Geschichte und Gegenwart, 145), Tübingen 1949.

The passage about the judge of heretics, for which Welzel gives no source, can be found in I. Kant, Die Religion innerhalb der Grenzen der bloßen Vernunft, in Werke in zehn Bänden, ed. W. Weischedel, Darmstadt 1975, vol. 7, pp. 860 ff.

5 May 1950

Brecht’s Threepenny Novel, Munich 1946? — Not 1946, but 1949.

“Brute force has had its day …” — B. Brecht, Dreigroschenroman, in Gesammelte Werke, vol. 13, Frankfurt am Main 1967, pp. 999–1000.

13 May 1950

Reading Ponceau — See above, note to p. 212.

19 May 1950

Found a note from 24 August 1915 — See Tb 1915, p. 116.

23 May 1950

And if it still has honor, it comes from me — Friedrich Hölderlin, The Death of Empedocles, Act 1, Scene 3:

The world is mine, and subject to me, serving me; all its powers are mine. Nature, which needs a master, has become my maid. And if it still has honor, it comes from me.

Just don’t write to this Dr. Lewald — Walter Lewald (1887–1986), jurist and co-editor of the Neue Juristische Wochenschrift, wrote in 1950 that Schmitt was a Luciferian spirit “who went astray into the worship of power and completed his work by deifying the Antichrist.” W. Lewald, “Carl Schmitt redivivus,” in Neue Juristische Wochenschrift 3 (1950), p. 377.

Non decet scribere ei qui vult proscribere — See above, note to p. 192. Here altered to mean: “It is not fitting to write to someone who wants to outlaw you.”

Hölderlin’s ode to Vanini — A counterpart to the ode “Empedokles,” stanza 3:

But sacred Nature, whom you loved while alive, who received you as you died, does not forget the deeds of men, and your enemies returned, like you, into the ancient peace.

Lucilio Vanini (1585–1619), philosopher and theologian, taught a pantheistic religion of nature and was tortured and burned at the stake in Toulouse in 1619.

28 May 1950

Letter from Álvaro d’Ors to Father Welty — Among Schmitt’s papers is a letter from Álvaro d’Ors dated 7 May 1950 to Father Eberhard Welty, who had invited him to give a lecture on Vitoria at Walberberg; RW 265 no. 10717.

making a tactless rogue like Erich Kaufmann the guiding spirit of international law — The constitutional and international lawyer Erich Kaufmann (1880–1972), with whom Schmitt initially had a very friendly relationship when they were colleagues in Bonn, became a bitter enemy around 1927.

On 6 April 1927 Schmitt first recorded a negative judgment of Kaufmann in his diary: “heard the unbelievable gossip and slander Kaufmann has been spreading about me in Berlin.” Publication forthcoming.

From 1950 onward Kaufmann served as an adviser to the Federal Chancellery and the Foreign Office. See Helmut Quaritsch, “Eine sonderbare Beziehung. Carl Schmitt und Erich Kaufmann,” in Bürgersinn und staatliche Macht in Antike und Gegenwart. Festschrift für Wolfgang Schuller, Konstanz 2000, pp. 71–87.

To Tüngel — Richard Tüngel (1893–1970), co-founder and editor-in-chief of the weekly newspaper Die Zeit. Because he gave Schmitt a platform there, he was dismissed in 1955 at the urging of Countess Dönhoff.

Tüngel’s article in Die Zeit of 25 May 1950 was entitled “Neues Biedermeier Bonner Staatsschutz” and criticized efforts by the federal cabinet to create new categories of political crime such as “betrayal of the peace.”

Schmitt’s letter to Tüngel survives in his papers, RW 265 no. 13580. It is published in K. Burkhardt, ed., Carl Schmitt und die Öffentlichkeit. Briefwechsel mit Journalisten, Publizisten und Verlegern aus den Jahren 1923 bis 1983, Berlin 2013, pp. 87–88.

31 May 1950

“Private property alienates …” — Karl Marx, Die deutsche Ideologie, in Karl Marx/Friedrich Engels, Werke, vol. 3, Berlin 1969, p. 212.

3 June 1950

Count Spee’s Cautio Criminalis of 1631 — Schmitt is referring to the following edition: Cautio criminalis oder Rechtliches Bedenken wegen der Hexenprozesse, German edition by Joachim-Friedrich Ritter (Forschungen zur Geschichte des deutschen Strafrechts, 1), Weimar 1939. Schmitt’s copy survives in his papers, RW 265 no. 27068.

7 June 1950

Mortisque peribunt / Argumenta tuae — See above, note to p. 219.

Gide: “c’était mettre le point d’honneur …” — See André Gide, Journal 1939–1949, Paris 1950, p. 44.

When one reads in André Gide that Hitler arose from Versailles — “Il n’y aurait jamais eu de Hitler sans le traité de Versailles.” — “There would never have been a Hitler without the Treaty of Versailles.” Gide, Journal, op. cit., p. 225.

8 June 1950

the argumentum ad canem — Hegel wrote against Schleiermacher’s definition of religion as a feeling of “absolute dependence”:

“If religion in man is based only on a feeling, then this feeling can properly have no further determination than the feeling of his dependence. In that case the dog would be the best Christian, because he possesses this feeling most strongly and lives above all in this feeling. The dog even has feelings of redemption when his hunger is satisfied with a bone.”

Schleiermacher wrote to Karl Heinrich Sack on 28 December 1822:

“But what do you say to Herr Hegel, who in his preface to Hinrichs’s philosophy of religion attributes to me the view that because of absolute dependence the dog is the best Christian, and accuses me of animal ignorance about God? Things like that must simply be passed over in silence.”

Quoted in F. Schleiermacher, Kritische Gesamtausgabe. Schriften und Entwürfe, vol. 7: Der christliche Glaube 1821–1822, part 1, Berlin/New York 1980, p. LVII. See also Tb 1930–34, p. 450, note 2059.

15 June 1950

With difficulty and complications … — Schmitt obtained the book through Peter Scheibert, who was traveling in the United States. See Schmitt to N. Sombart, 13 July 1950:

“What Peter Scheibert has brought me from the USA so far—for example Ernst Bloch’s Freiheit und Ordnung—has been disappointing.”

BW Sombart, p. 33.

23 June 1950

“C’est l’antisémite qui crée le juif” — “It is the antisemite who creates the Jew.” A. Gide, Journal, op. cit., p. 288.

“Les juifs sont les plus doux des hommes.” — “The Jews are the gentlest of men.” Ibid., p. 289.

Il est si doux — “He is so gentle.” See BW EJ, p. 154.

23 July 1950

Control Council Law No. 10 — The law enacted by the Allies on 20 December 1945 formed the legal basis for trials concerning war crimes, crimes against peace, and crimes against humanity. It was not incorporated into the law of the Federal Republic because of concerns about the prohibition on retroactive criminal laws.

1 August 1950

How proudly I wrote back then: Welcome, good and evil! — From the end of the preface to PuB, dated 20 August 1939.

11 August 1950

Again and again I fell for the deception; again and again I escaped it. — Schmitt quoting himself: ECS, p. 88.

29 August 1950

Only someone who knows his prey better than it knows itself can conquer it. — “The conquest of the disintegrated mass, its violent subjugation and reshaping by the army, is impossible—the army in its old organization no longer has the power to conquer, and the aristocracy of its commanders is no longer a historical force advancing into the future. For only someone who knows his prey better than it knows itself can conquer it, by subjugating it through his superiority in education and knowledge.”

Bruno Bauer, Die bürgerliche Revolution in Deutschland seit dem Anfang der deutsch-katholischen Bewegung bis zur Gegenwart, Berlin 1849, pp. 294–295.

Schmitt quoted this passage from Bruno Bauer frequently, and not only—as is sometimes claimed—after the defeat of 1945. See, for example, PuB, p. 333.

Monsieur Quine … — In Bernanos’s final novel, Monsieur Quine, the title character speaks on his deathbed of his “hunger for souls”:

“I took care not to change them. I revealed their own selves to them, with as much care as an entomologist needs to unfold the wings of a butterfly emerging from its chrysalis. Their Creator did not know them better than I did, and even through love one cannot possess anything as completely as I possessed those souls through this infallible act of possession, which does not wound the patient, leaves him undestroyed, and yet delivers him entirely into our hands, captured with all his most delicate shades, his iridescence, the whole color of life.”

Georges Bernanos, Monsieur Quine; here quoted from the German edition Die tote Gemeinde, Olten 1949, p. 284.

The time is coming, Nietzsche said … — See Friedrich Nietzsche, Werke in drei Bänden, ed. Karl Schlechta, 8th ed., Munich 1977, vol. 2, p. 672.

Heidegger, Holzwege, p. 205 — Schmitt quotes from Martin Heidegger, Holzwege, Frankfurt am Main 1950.

Lake Success — Village in the United States that served as the headquarters of the United Nations from 1946 to 1951.

1 September 1950

Nietzsche: “With firm shoulders …” — F. Nietzsche, Werke, ed. Giorgio Colli and Mazzino Montinari, Munich 1999, vol. 10, p. 207.

Nietzsche: “Look at the world …” — Correctly: “Look at the world as though time had passed away: then everything crooked will become straight for you.” Ibid., p. 216.

13 September 1950

Quid igitur lex? Propter transgressiones posita est — Vulgate, Galatians 3:19. “Why, then, the law? It was added because of transgressions.”

Τί οὖν ὁ νόμος; τῶν παραβάσεων χάριν προσετέθη — The same passage, Galatians 3:19, in the Greek New Testament.

Pros-etethe, that is, ex post? — προσετέθη means “was added.” The preposition πρός is primarily spatial in meaning but can also have a temporal sense.

for example in the Schott — In the Catholic missal known as the “Schott,” Galatians 3:19 reads: “Why, then, the law? It was established afterward because of transgressions.”

Anselm Schott, Das Meßbuch der heiligen Kirche lateinisch und deutsch, mit liturgischen Erklärungen und kurzen Lebensbeschreibungen der Heiligen, 36th ed., Freiburg im Breisgau 1932, p. 588.

30 September 1950

The jurisprudence I speak of at the end of “The Plight of European Jurisprudence” — “European jurisprudence does not have to die together with the myths of law and the lawgiver. Let us recall once again the history of our suffering, for our strength is rooted in our trust in suffering. Then the genius will not abandon us, and it will become clear that even the confusion of languages can be better than Babylonian unity.”

C. Schmitt, Die Lage der europäischen Rechtswissenschaft, Tübingen 1949, p. 32.

Rome n’est plus dans Rome, elle est toute où je suis. — “Rome is no longer in Rome; Rome is wherever I am.” Pierre Corneille, Sertorius, Act 3, Scene 1.

4 October 1950

Jürgen Rausch on Ernst Jünger — J. Rausch, “Ernst Jüngers Optik,” in Merkur 4 (1950), pp. 1069–1085; also published separately, Stuttgart 1951.

22 October 1950

the three righteous comb-makers — See above, note to p. 41.

and if we killed them all, we would all have to take their place — Schmitt quotes Bruno Bauer inaccurately. Bauer actually writes:

“Luther once said in his table talk: ‘If all the useless people had to die, then we ourselves would have to become useless; for the devil must have useless grounds. So let them go on living, since God allows them to live.’ Thus the lord of this world needs the Jews in order to carry out his finite and worldly purposes, and his need is so great that he is already recruiting part of his army from among the Christians as well. But if there were no Jews, then all of us would have to take their place.”

B. Bauer, Das Judenthum in der Fremde, Berlin 1863, p. 77. See also BW EJ, p. 190.

10 November 1950

A. Mitscherlich (Der Monat, issue 25, Oct. 1950) — Alexander Mitscherlich, “Ödipus und Kaspar Hauser. Tiefenpsychologische Probleme in der Gegenwart,” in Der Monat 2 (1950), pp. 11–18.

Verlaine’s Kaspar Hauser poem — “Gaspard Hauser chante” (1873/81); translated by Richard Dehmel as “Lied Kaspar Hausers” (1891) and by Stefan George as “Kaspar Hauser singt” (1915).

27 February 1951

Analyze that phonetically for once! — Schmitt is probably thinking of Ernst Jünger, “Lob der Vokale,” in Sämtliche Werke, vol. 12, Stuttgart 1979, pp. 40 ff.

Compare Jünger’s address for Schmitt’s ninetieth birthday:

“…I once made a note, on the occasion of one of the unpleasant incidents that befell you in your capacity as a professor of constitutional law: ‘Those are simply the misfortunes of the profession.’ You heard about this and remarked: ‘To understand that, one has to know the significance the vowel I has for Ernst Jünger.’”

Carl Schmitt und Plettenberg. Der 90. Geburtstag (Plettenberger Miniaturen, 1), Plettenberg 2008, p. 17.

28 February 1951

To Frau Jünger — See BW GJ, pp. 145–146.

Consolation is an absurd word — A line by Goethe that Schmitt occasionally quoted:

Yes, go on scolding, go on cursing; nothing better will ever come of it. For consolation is an absurd word: a man who cannot despair has no need to live.

Goethe, Werke (Weimar edition), I/2, p. 236.

4 March 1951

Distinguo ergo sum — “I distinguish, therefore I am.”

Schmitt also used this variation on Descartes as a dedicatory inscription to Ernst Jünger in the copy of Legalität und Legitimität that he sent him on 20 August 1932 in response to Jünger’s The Worker. See Martin Tielke, “Die Buchwidmung als hermeneutischer Schlüssel. Das frühe Verhältnis von Ernst Jünger und Carl Schmitt im Spiegel ihrer Widmungen,” in Das historische Erbe in der Region. Festschrift für Detlev Hellfaier, ed. Axel Halle et al., Bielefeld 2013, pp. 212–213.

6 March 1951

Aristotle’s refutation of “need” as the drive behind power — The quotation appears on p. 37 (Book II, Ch. IV/8) of the following edition: Aristotle, Aristotelis Politicorum libri octo. Ad recensionem Immanuelis Bekkeri recogniti … interpretatione germanica explanavit … Adolfus Stahr, Leipzig 1839.

The exact wording is:

οἷον τυραννοῦσιν οὐχ ἵνα μὴ ῥιγῶσιν

“For example, no one becomes a tyrant simply so that he will not be cold.”

7 May 1951

the 300th-anniversary celebration of Leviathan in Frankfurt — Apparently a rather unofficial celebration organized at Schmitt’s suggestion. See Schmitt to Nicolaus Sombart, 21 January 1951:

“How would it be if, on 5 April 1951—the birthday of Thomas Hobbes—we held a three-hundredth-anniversary celebration of the Leviathan in some little place with a proper name? I’m thinking of Werdohl, though it could just as well be somewhere else. Completely exclusive and esoteric.”

BW Sombart, p. 38; see also BW Forsthoff, p. 78.

For the occasion Schmitt published: C. Schmitt, “Dreihundert Jahre Leviathan. Zum 5. April 1951,” in Die Tat (Zurich), 5 April 1951.

the blind summons — See above, note to p. 18.

15 June 1951

Haec omnis, quam cernis, inops inhumataque turba est — “This is the multitude whom no grave has sheltered,” in Eduard Norden’s translation. In E. Norden, P. Vergilius Maro, Aeneis Buch VI, commentary by E. Norden, unchanged reprint of the 3rd ed. of 1927, 9th ed., Stuttgart 1995, p. 69.

Literally, inops inhumataque turba means “the powerless and unburied multitude.”

Etenim sacramentum regis abscondere bonum — “For it is good to keep a king’s secret hidden.”

16 June 1951

major academic honor from the University of Maryland — In May 1951 Ernst Friesenhahn received an honorary doctorate from the University of Maryland together with John McCloy, the American High Commissioner for Germany, and Federal President Theodor Heuss.

Sententiam eius quem contemnimus nostrae praelatam videre … — “…to have to watch the opinion of a man we despise being preferred to our own; to see our wisdom held in contempt before our very eyes; to begin an uncertain struggle for empty glory while being certain to make enemies, for this is unavoidable whether one wins or loses; to hate and be hated because of differences of opinion; to reveal one’s secret thoughts and wishes to everyone without necessity or benefit; to neglect one’s private affairs.”

Hobbes, M/B, p. 182.

Hobbes is speaking here about how man’s innate desire for honor is easier to satisfy in a republic than in a monarchy. Against this advantage, however, stand the disadvantages just listed.

catalogue from Hamlet’s soliloquy — Shakespeare, Hamlet, Act 3, Scene 1. The passage mentioned reads in Schlegel’s translation:

The oppressor’s wrong, the proud man’s insults, the pangs of despised love, the law’s delay, the insolence of office and the shame that worthless men inflict on patient merit, when he himself might bring it all to rest.

22 June 1951

Robert Mohl found it. — See above, note to p. 35.

24 June 1951

Tierno — Enrique Tierno Galván (1918–1986), Spanish jurist, opponent of Franco, and founder of Spain’s Socialist Party. He contributed in 1968 to the Festschrift for Carl Schmitt.

Truyol — Antonio Truyol y Serra (1913–2003), Spanish philosopher of law.

The names Tierno and Truyol do not appear in the mandatory reports Schmitt submitted to the Reich Ministry of Education about his lecture tours, published by Christian Tilitzki in Schmittiana VI (1994), pp. 191–270. This may have been because both men were opponents of Franco.

Hobbes (De Cive, II, §18) —

Praeterea, ei qui pacto tenetur, creditor: (pactorum enim vinculum sola fides est:) qui vero ad supplicium ducuntur, sive capital, sive capitali mitius, constringuntur vinculis, vel satellitibus custodiuntur.

“Moreover, the person who is bound by a contract is trusted, since trust alone is what binds contracts together; but those who are being led to punishment, whether death or some lesser penalty, are put in chains or guarded by officers.”

Hobbes, M/B, p. 94.

Ubi vero creditur … —

Ubi vero vel alteri vel utrique creditur, ibi is cui creditur, promittit se praestiturum postea, appellaturque hujusmodi promissum pacti.

“But where one party or both are trusted, the person who is trusted promises to perform later, and this kind of promise is called a contract.”

Hobbes, M/B, p. 90.

4 July 1951

Rhyme is to verse … — “La rime dans le vers, c’est la couleur dans la peinture.” — “Rhyme in verse is what color is in painting.” Ernest Hello, Le siècle. Les hommes et les idées, Paris 1928, pp. 366–367.

August Stramm — (1874–1915), pioneering Expressionist poet.

6 July 1951

Max Picard — (1888–1965), Swiss philosopher of culture.

Raum is the same word as Rom — See C. Schmitt, “Raum und Rom. Zur Phonetik des Wortes Raum,” in Universitas (1951), pp. 963–967; also in SGN, pp. 491–495. See Nicolaus Sombart, Jugend in Berlin, 6th ed., Frankfurt am Main 2001, p. 252.

13 July 1951

fallen for a Caliban — This refers to Gerhard Nebel; see below, notes to pp. 269 and 283.

14 July 1951

“Come to the bar with the green orchid …” — A parody of Gottfried Benn’s poem “Allerseelen,” which begins:

Put the fragrant mignonette on the table, bring out the last red asters, and let us speak once more of love, as we did that May.

19 July 1951

If you gave an answer, it would be deception — Correctly: “If you gave an answer, you would be deception.”

From Oskar Loerke’s poem “An meinen Dämon,” which Wilhelm Lehmann described as his “favorite poem” by Loerke; see W. Lehmann, Gesammelte Werke in acht Bänden, vol. 7, Stuttgart 2009, pp. 45–46.

Julius Bab — (1880–1955), writer, dramaturge, and theater critic. Bab was one of Schmitt’s early acquaintances; see Tb 1912–15. A letter from Schmitt to Bab dated 13 September 1914 was published by Piet Tommissen in Complexio Oppositorum. Über Carl Schmitt, ed. H. Quaritsch, Berlin 1988, pp. 92–94.

20 July 1951

If I cease to act, I am destroyed — F. Schiller, Wallenstein, Act 1, Scene 7:

Show me a way out of this pressure, helpful powers! Show me one that I am capable of taking—I cannot, like some hero of words, some prattler about virtue, warm myself with my own will and thoughts— I cannot proudly say to happiness when it turns its back on me: Go! I do not need you. If I cease to act, I am destroyed.

In the piercing awareness of my nothingness — F. Schiller, Don Carlos, Act 2, Scene 5:

Carlos: …Oh, I do not doubt that we shall soon hear of your victories. You will know how to prove yourself worthy of our gracious trust.

Alba, pointedly: Shall I indeed— in the piercing awareness of my nothingness?

5 August 1951

Fons turbatus pede & vena corrupta, est iustus cadens coram impio — Bacon is quoting the Vulgate, Proverbs 25:26: “Like a spring muddied by the foot and a corrupted fountain is the righteous man who gives way before the wicked.”

The Explicatio Bacon gives of this parable —

Praecipit Parabola, rebuspublicis ante omnia cavendum esse de iniquo et infami judicio, in causa aliqua celebri et gravi; praesertim ubi non absolvitur innoxius, sed condemnatur insons. Etenim injuriae inter privatos grassantes turbant quidem et polluunt latices justitiae, sed tanquam in rivulis: verum judicia iniqua, qualia diximus, a quibus exempla petuntur, fontes ipsos justitiae inficiunt et inquinant. Postquam enim tribunal cesserit in partes injustitiae, status rerum vertitur tanquam in latrocinium publicum: fitque plane, ut homo homini sit lupus.

“The parable teaches that, in public affairs, the greatest care must be taken to avoid an unjust and disgraceful judgment in any important and prominent case—especially when the innocent person is not acquitted but is instead condemned.

For injustices committed between private individuals certainly muddy and pollute the waters of justice, but only, so to speak, in the smaller streams. Unjust judgments of the kind we are discussing, however—judgments that become precedents—poison and pollute the very sources of justice themselves.

Once a court has gone over to the side of injustice, the whole condition of affairs changes into something like public robbery, and it becomes plainly true that man is a wolf to man.”

Francis Bacon, The Works of F. Bacon, ed. James Spedding, Robert Leslie Ellis, and Douglas Denon Heath, vol. 3, Boston 1862, pp. 79–80. See also Blumenberg, pp. 185–187.

24 August 1951

What can happen to me … — From Friedrich Schnack’s poem “Licht der Welt.” Schmitt owned several of Schnack’s books. The source here is F. Schnack, Das kommende Reich. Gedichte, Hellerau 1920, pp. 104–105.

The correct wording is:

Who can harm me, from all those evil hosts, when I am allowed to preserve You, tender, ancient spirit of flame?

Immediately before this:

I have been placed amid the enmity of enemies, amid the anger of cities, amid the breath of hatred from mouths. But I have lit the solemn lamp within me,

in the middle of the midnight hour: sweet light of the world.

26 August 1951

He is a Mal-Mann — French mal = bad, evil. A play on the name of Walter Mallmann (1908–1982), an editor at Mohr in Tübingen; see BW Forsthoff (index).

29 August 1951

Hegel, Phenomenology, p. 356 — Schmitt quotes from the following edition: Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel, Phänomenologie des Geistes (= Sämtliche Werke. Krit. Gesamtausgabe der Werke Hegels in zwölf Bänden, ed. and introduced by Otto Weiß), Leipzig 1909. Schmitt’s annotated copy survives in his papers, RW 265 no. 24638.

In the Suhrkamp edition the passage reads:

“The dead man whose right has been violated knows how to find instruments for his revenge that possess the same reality and force as the power that injured him. These powers are other communities, whose altars have been defiled by dogs or birds carrying the corpse that was denied its proper return to the elemental individual and therefore was not raised into unconscious universality, but remained above ground in the realm of actuality. As the power of divine law it now acquires a self-conscious and actual universality. These communities rise up as enemies and destroy the community that dishonored and shattered its own strength: the piety of the family.”

Hegel, Werke, ed. Eva Moldenhauer and Karl Markus Michel, vol. 3, Frankfurt am Main 1970, pp. 351–352.

See also the entries for 2 July 1948, 15 June 1951, and 2 July 1951.

The ashes will not let go … — See above, note to p. 93.

access to the summit of power — See Carl Schmitt, Gespräch über die Macht und den Zugang zum Machthaber, Pfullingen 1954 and later editions.

31 August 1951

Le secret de l’Église catholique — In Villiers de l’Isle-Adam’s novella “L’enjeu” (see above, note to p. 69), an abbé, having lost all his money gambling, stakes the “secret of the Church.” When he loses again and is asked to reveal the secret, he says:

“hélas! le grand secret de l’Église: Il n’y a pas de purgatoire”

“Alas! The great secret of the Church: there is no purgatory.”

See also Tb 1921–24, p. 530.

8 September 1951

Andersch — Alfred Andersch (1914–1980), writer and head of the evening studio at Hessischer Rundfunk, where he also introduced Carl Schmitt. Schmitt’s papers contain seven letters and one postcard from Andersch dating from 1951 to 1954; RW 265 nos. 389–396.

On Hannah Arendt … — Refers to H. Arendt, Elemente und Ursprünge totaler Herrschaft, Munich/Zurich 1986, pp. 108 ff., chapter “The Jews and Society.” This section also quotes Goethe’s review, mentioned below, of Gedichte von einem polnischen Juden, pp. 113–114.

Schmitt used the English edition, The Burden of Our Time, London 1951; his copy survives in his papers, RW 265 no. 22551.

Poems by a Polish Jew … — Isaschar Falkensohn Behr, Gedichte von einem polnischen Juden, Mitau/Leipzig 1772. This was the first collection of poetry by a German-language Jewish poet. See the modern edition by Andreas Wittbrodt, Göttingen 2002.

Goethe’s review can be found in J. W. Goethe, Gedenkausgabe der Werke, Briefe und Gespräche, ed. Ernst Beutler, 2nd ed., vol. 14, Zurich 1964, pp. 157–160; the quotations are on pp. 158 and 159.

Christianity is Judaism for the people — The sentence repeatedly quoted by Schmitt, “Christianity is Judaism for the multitude, but still it is Judaism,” appears in Benjamin Disraeli’s novel Tancred or the New Crusade.

Schmitt read the book in the abridged German translation by Julius Elbau, published in 1936 by the Jüdische Buchvereinigung Berlin. On p. 281 the line reads: “Christianity is Judaism for the general public.”

For Schmitt, this was the “key sentence” of the book. See Nicolaus Sombart, Jugend in Berlin, 6th ed., Frankfurt am Main 2001, pp. 260 ff.

Thomas Mann says: Christianity is the most beautiful flower of Judaism — “Say what you like: Christianity, this flower of Judaism, remains one of the two basic pillars on which Western civilization rests; the other is Mediterranean antiquity.”

Thomas Mann, Gesammelte Werke, vol. 9, 2nd revised ed., Frankfurt am Main 1974, p. 461.

Goethe says in 1824 — Not in the edition by Hesse cited there, but in J. W. Goethe, Sämtliche Werke nach Epochen seines Schaffens (Munich edition), vol. 13/1, Munich 1992, p. 403.

Stahl-Jolson as early as 1840 — Refers to Friedrich Julius Stahl, Die Kirchenverfassung nach Lehre und Recht der Protestanten, Erlangen 1840.

9 September 1951

sbirreria — Refers to the work of the sbirri, judicial and police officers in the Papal States who were militarily organized and armed.

Schmitt quotes from the following edition: Francis Bacon, Fr. Baconi De Verulamio Sermones fideles, Ethici, Politici, Œconomici: Sive Interiora Rerum. Accedunt Faber Fortunæ Colores Boni Et Mali …, Leiden 1644. Schmitt’s copy survives in his papers, RW 265 no. 23412.

The passage is not actually on p. 246, but on p. 240:

Cardinales Romani, (qui Theologi sunt, & Fratres & Scholastici,) verbum usurpant, extremi contemptus & convitii, erga negotia Civilia: Vocant enim negotia Civilia, (velut, Belli, Legationum, Iudiciorum, & hujusmodi,) Hispanico vocabulo, Sbirrarias; quod sonat, Munera Lictorum & Scribarum.

“The Roman cardinals, who are theologians, friars, and scholars, use a term of extreme contempt and disdain for civil affairs. They call such matters—war, diplomacy, judicial affairs, and the like—by the Spanish expression sbirreria, meaning work fit for bailiffs and clerks.”

10 September 1951

Otto Weininger claims … — Schmitt quotes from his copy of the following edition, inscribed “Carl Schmitt, Düsseldorf, May 1912”: Otto Weininger, Über die letzten Dinge, with a biographical foreword by Moritz Rappaport, 3rd ed., identical to the 2nd, Vienna et al. 1912, pp. 83 ff.

12 September 1951

draft of a project — See BW Mohler, p. 105.

If the religious laws of the Roman emperors … — Correctly: “Without the imperial legislation from Constantine through Theodosius, the Greco-Roman religion would still be alive today.”

Jacob Burckhardt, Weltgeschichtliche Betrachtungen (Kröner Taschenausgabe, 55), Stuttgart 1978, p. 57.

“Blind morsel arches without coarseness …” — R. M. Rilke, poem “Vasen-Bild (Toten-Mahl).” In: idem, Späte Gedichte, Leipzig 1934, p. 128. See Schmittiana VI, 1998, pp. 293–94; BW Mohler, pp. 104–5.

17 September 1951

“Everything here will find …” — Quotation from the poem “Die kleine Schöpfung” by Konrad Weiß. In: Weiß, p. 384:

The farmer came home with his hand, stopped and properly took his stand before our three travelers there, and asked: Child, companion, where are you from, where are you going, where is your home? The rooster said: All this will find its place within, and speak from the mind.

“The magnificent sentences in the Phenomenology of Spirit” — In the Moldenhauer and Michel edition of Hegel’s works, Frankfurt am Main 1970, the quotations can be found in vol. 3, pp. 365, 138, and 144.

19 September 1951

“The subject-object steamroller rolls …” — See also Schmitt’s ballad “Die Sub-stanz und das Sub-jekt.” In: Civis, 9 June 1955, pp. 29–30; now also in: Gedichte, pp. 16–21.

24 September 1951

“Let them mock us, so long as they spare us their pity.” — Walter Warnach, Die Welt des Schmerzes, Pfullingen 1952, p. 111.

25 September 1951

amor amaritudinis — “love of bitterness.” Used here as the opposite of amor fati, love of one’s necessary fate, in which Nietzsche saw human greatness.

26 September 1951

Peripsema — “scum”; see above, note to p. 23.

Congrua — the minimum income guaranteed to a clergyman from the revenues of his benefice.

5 October 1951

“The terror no one dares to name” — See C. Schmitt, “Gesang des Sechzigjährigen.” In: ECS, pp. 92–93; now in: Gedichte, pp. 5–7. Schmitt explains what he meant by this terror in the entry for 7 October 1951.

“A work by Montlosier” — François Dominique de Reynaud de Montlosier (1755–1835), French politician and opponent of ultramontanism. The work quoted was published not in 1826 but in 1827: F. D. de R. de Montlosier, Les Jésuites, les Congrégations et Le parti prêtre en 1827. Mémoire a M. le comte de Villèle …, Paris 1827, p. 65:

“I am well aware that there is a large class of people who do not want anyone concerning themselves with priests. For such people, religion is of no importance, and priests are of no more importance than religion. Their doctrine is this: criticize nothing the priests do, and believe nothing they say.”

7 October 1951

Max Nettlau — (1865–1944), historian of anarchism.

“Heidegger on thinking” — Correctly:

“The word of thinkers has no authority. The word of thinkers has no authors in the sense in which writers have authors. The word of thinking is poor in images and without charm. The word of thinking rests in a sobering return to what it says.”

Martin Heidegger, Gesamtausgabe, vol. 7, section 1, Frankfurt am Main 2000, p. 234.

“Poor in deeds and rich in thoughts” — See above, note to p. 127.

“Gliding on sultry dactyls …” — Published in: Die neue Gesellschaft. Bemerkungen zum Zeitbewußtsein, ed. Rüdiger Altmann and Johannes Gross, Stuttgart 1958, p. 99. Now also in: Gedichte, p. 26.

15 October 1951

“We arrive at the way we behave more by acting against ourselves than by acting out of ourselves.” — Quotation from Ludwig Raiser (1904–1980), jurist. In the Deutsche Universitätszeitung (1951, no. 9, p. 7), Raiser published an article entitled “Carl Schmitt — kein Bundesgenosse” (“Carl Schmitt — No Ally”).

“all righteous comb-makers” — See above, note to p. 41.

“I am trying to bring the accident of my own present into order through pure thought.” — See Schmitt’s letter to G. Jünger, 24 February 1948:

“I do not think about the future, because I know how powerless we are. Nor do I seek the past, because I do not want, by reflecting on myself, to outlive myself. So what am I looking for, and what am I doing? I am trying to bring the accident of my own present into order through pure thought.”

BW GJ, p. 105. Schmitt wrote something similar to E. R. Huber on 2 June 1948; BW Huber, p. 322. See also above, p. 73.

ἀναγκαζόμενος — See above, note to p. 18.

Rud. Fischer — Rudolf Fischer (1900–1961), journalist, who publicly but anonymously defended Schmitt. See X [= R. Fischer], “Hexenverfolgung. Der Fall Carl Schmitt. Charaktermord.” In: Der Fortschritt, 25 January 1952; see BW Mohler, pp. 115–16, 119; BW Forsthoff, pp. 84, 387.

Don Capisco (et obmutesco) — When Jünger criticized Schmitt for his conduct in 1933, Schmitt replied on 5 February 1950 with the sentence: “Capisco et obmutesco” — “I understand and fall silent.” BW EJ, p. 248. He later responded in the same way to criticism from Nicolaus Sombart; see Schmitt’s letter to Sombart of 7 January 1978, BW Sombart, p. 129.

“namesake of Carlo Schmid” — See above, note to p. 52.

17 October 1951

V. Leemans — Victor Leemans (1901–1971), social scientist and politician, author of Carl Schmitt. Bijdrage tot de sociologie van Staat en Politiek, Antwerp 1933; copy in the Schmitt papers, RW 265 no. 28380.

21 October 1951

“The body is the outward expression” —

“This outward element initially makes the inward visible only as an organ, or gives it a being for others at all; for the inward, insofar as it is in the organ, is the activity itself.”

G. W. F. Hegel, Phänomenologie des Geistes. In: idem, Werke, vol. 3, ed. Moldenhauer and Michel, Frankfurt am Main 1970, pp. 234–35.

23 October 1951

The character assassination as one of the fine arts — A reference to Thomas De Quincey, On Murder Considered as One of the Fine Arts, 1827 and later editions. See also the caption to the illustration on p. 257.

25 October 1951

“to Mohler, 12 November” — See BW Mohler, p. 108.

Lilian Winstanley — The English author Lilian Winstanley (1875–1960) made one of the first attempts, in her 1921 book Hamlet and the Scottish Succession, to interpret Shakespeare’s Hamlet against the political and historical background of the Elizabethan period. The book was translated into German by Anima Schmitt as L. Winstanley, Hamlet, Sohn der Maria Stuart, Pfullingen 1952. Carl Schmitt wrote a substantial foreword.

“to M. F.” — In his history of the English Revolution, Die große Revolution in England (1951), Michael Freund portrays James I as a grotesque figure. Schmitt commented on this in a letter to Freund dated 7 March 1953; RW 265 no. 13003. In March 2015, the antiquarian-book market ZVAB listed a copy of the 1956 edition of Hamlet oder Hekuba bearing a dedication to M. Freund.

6 November 1951

Forrestal — James Vincent Forrestal (1892–1949), United States Secretary of Defense. Doubts were raised about whether his death was really suicide.

28 November 1951

“Rest. Board at Herford” — The “Restitution Board” was an international court that decided claims for restitution arising from the period 1933–1945. It existed from 1955 to 1990 and was based in Herford until 1984. Schmitt must therefore have added this entry later, something also suggested by the different handwriting.

“Smend wrote this to me as early as 1938” — This refers either to Smend’s letter of 10 July 1938 or to a letter that has been lost; see BW Smend, pp. 99–100, note 333.

“the passages on p. 86 of my Leviathan” — Schmitt means Hobbes’s distinction between an outward “profession of the tongue” and inward belief, which Spinoza transfers from religion to philosophy:

“Only a few years after the publication of the Leviathan, the first liberal Jew fixed his attention on this barely visible fracture. He immediately recognized it as the great point through which modern liberalism could break in, and from which the entire relationship Hobbes had established and intended between outward and inward, public and private, could be turned into its opposite. Spinoza carried out this reversal in the famous chapter 19 of his Tractatus theologico-politicus, published in 1670.”

Leviathan, pp. 86–87.

Bakunin: il n’y a rien de plus borné … —

“Germany itself, moreover, cured me of the philosophical disease that prevailed there. After looking more closely into metaphysical problems, it did not take me long to become convinced of the emptiness and vanity of all metaphysics. I looked for life in it, but found only death and boredom. I looked for action, but found nothing but absolute inactivity. This discovery was greatly helped by my personal relations with German professors, because there is nothing more narrow-minded, more contemptible, or more ridiculous than the German professor — or the German in general!”

M. Bakounine, Confession (1857), reissue of the edition published in 1932, Paris 2001, pp. 61–62.

29 November 1951

Populus Romanus victam Pompejo … —

“Although, for example, the Roman people once governed the land of Judaea through a governor, Judaea was not therefore a democracy, because the people were not governed by an assembly that every one of them had a right to enter; nor was it an aristocracy, because they were not governed by an assembly that any elected person among them might enter.”

Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, trans. Jutta Schlösser, ed. Hermann Klenner, Hamburg 1996, p. 163.

22 December 1951

Ceterum censeo Romam esse liberandam (a Romanitate) — “For the rest, I believe that Rome must be liberated — from Romanness.” A variation on the famous sentence with which Cato the Elder was said to end his speeches in the Senate:

Ceterum censeo Carthaginem esse delendam.

“For the rest, I believe that Carthage must be destroyed.”

12 January 1952

Eulenburg Affair — The dispute between Philipp, Prince of Eulenburg-Hertefeld, and the journalist Maximilian Harden. Harden accused the circle around Eulenburg, which exercised considerable influence over the Kaiser, of homosexuality, and the affair grew into a major public scandal.

“Parallel: Kortner — W. Krauss” — The director Fritz Kortner considered Werner Krauss a great actor, but reproached him for his closeness to National Socialism. Schmitt said that he had once met Krauss on a train and spoken with him.

20 January 1952

“A professor, who was also a State Councillor, I think his name was Schmidt!” — From a note by Colonel General Werner von Fritsch dated 1 February 1938 concerning the Blomberg Affair, which led to his removal as commander-in-chief of the Army:

“In the autumn, the Party once again intensified its campaign against me. It was driven above all by the Gestapo and related circles. They succeeded in largely convincing Göring that I was planning a coup. Himmler claimed to know that this coup would be carried out on 10(?) January 1935, or on some other day in January 1935. For this reason, Blomberg invited the commanding generals and many other senior officers to an evening of beer at the Kaiser Wilhelm Academy on the first date in question, I believe 10 January 1935. Himmler gave a lecture.

“The incriminating point against me was supposedly that I had invited a professor, who was also a State Councillor, I think his name was Schmidt, to give a lecture on constitutional law on a Thursday at the Tirpitzufer. Göring claimed that the lecture was intended to prove that a coup was permissible under constitutional law. In the presence of the minister and numerous officers!

“The invitation had been issued by Department 4. The man was and remains completely unknown to me. The lecture was cancelled.”

Friedrich Hoßbach, Zwischen Wehrmacht und Hitler 1934–1938, 2nd rev. ed., Göttingen 1965, p. 61.

“Süsterhenn in the Parliamentary Council” — Correctly:

“We are not afraid of the danger of what has been called a ‘judicialized politics,’ which the namesake of our colleague Carlo Schmid — whose name is spelled with two t’s — has painted on the wall.”

See also VA, pp. 105–6.

3 February 1952

“This sentence by Karl Marx” —

“The Jew has emancipated himself in a Jewish manner, not only by acquiring the power of money, but because through him, and also without him, money has become a world power, and the practical Jewish spirit has become the practical spirit of the Christian peoples. The Jews have emancipated themselves to the extent that the Christians have become Jews.”

K. Marx, “Zur Judenfrage.” In: Marx/Engels, Werke, vol. 1, Berlin 1971, p. 373.

Blasius blessing — On 3 February, the feast day of St. Blaise, this blessing is given by holding two consecrated candles in the form of a St. Andrew’s cross before the face and throat.

5 February 1952

“everything becomes a set of brass knuckles in his hands” — An allusion to Gerhard Nebel’s boxing career and his fights; see above, p. 242.

Drath & Leibholz — The constitutional lawyer Martin Drath (1902–1976) dealt critically with Schmitt in his unpublished habilitation thesis at Jena in 1946. In 1951 he became a judge on the Federal Constitutional Court. See van Laak, pp. 166 ff.

The Schmitt critic Gerhard Leibholz (1901–1982) became a judge on the Federal Constitutional Court in 1951 and later one of the most influential judges in the Court’s history.

“poor Kriesenhahn” — Schmitt means Ernst Friesenhahn, who in the 1950 Festschrift for Richard Thoma had, in Ernst Forsthoff’s words, “perfidiously disowned” his teacher, and who criticized Schmitt when he took office as rector in Bonn in November 1950. See van Laak, pp. 154–55; BW Huber, pp. 331 and 377.

1 March 1952

quod licet Jovi, non licet bovi — “What Jupiter is allowed to do, the ox is certainly not allowed to do.” Roman saying.

6 March 1952

“Miorița fate” — See above, note to p. 201.

8 March 1952

animus procreandi — “the intention to procreate.”

In his essay “Die Einheit der Welt,” Schmitt writes:

“For in the end it would be a sorry state of affairs if the dualism of the present world amounted to nothing more than the contrast between birth control and animus procreandi, so that every newborn child entered the world as an aggressor and was immediately drawn into the modern system of criminalization.”

C. Schmitt, “Die Einheit der Welt.” In: Merkur 6, 1952, p. 8. Reprinted in SGN, pp. 496–512.

“Hans Peters, director of studies at the Nazi Academy of Administration …” — Although Peters was a member of the Kreisau Circle, before 1945 he published writings that conformed to the National Socialist regime. Schmitt wrote to Forsthoff about him on 3 September 1949:

“What you write about Hans Peters agrees with the experiences I have had with him since 1945: intellectually as well as morally, a specimen of the ruling third-rate set.”

BW Forsthoff, p. 53; see also BW Huber and above, note to p. 204.

9 March 1952

“Serge Maiwald died on 22 February …” — This note was expanded into the obituary; see above, note to p. 212.

20 March 1952

Miching mallecho — Shakespeare, Hamlet, Act 3, Scene 2. Hamlet to Ophelia:

“Marry, this is miching mallecho; it means mischief.”

See Schmitt’s reference in Hamlet oder Hekuba, Stuttgart 1985, p. 68, note 1, to Laura Bohannan, “Miching Mallecho. That Means Witchcraft.” In: The London Magazine 1, 1954, no. 5, pp. 51–60.

8 April 1952

“Power is evil in itself” and “God is dead” —

“And now power is evil in itself.”

Jacob Burckhardt, Weltgeschichtliche Betrachtungen, Kröners Taschenausgabe 55, Stuttgart 1978, p. 97.

“God is dead!”

Friedrich Nietzsche, The Gay Science, section 125.

“You, Earth, remained steadfast through this night as well” — Schmitt ended his 1955 radio “Conversation on the New Space,” broadcast by Hessischer Rundfunk, as follows:

“You surely know how the second part of Goethe’s Faust begins. Faust awakens after a night filled with terrible dreams and feels the happiness of a new earthly morning, which gives him comfort and strength, the happiness of a new beginning. And so he greets the new world now opening before him with the magnificent line:

You, Earth, remained steadfast through this night as well.

“In the same way, I believe that after a terrible night threatened by atomic bombs and similar horrors, mankind will one morning awaken and gratefully recognize itself once again as the child of the firmly grounded Earth.”

C. Schmitt, Gespräch über die Macht und den Zugang zum Machthaber. Gespräch über den neuen Raum, Berlin 1994, p. 64.

“Conclusion of my Duisburg lecture” — As part of the Lower Rhine University Weeks, Schmitt gave a lecture in Duisburg on 21 April 1952 entitled “Die Einheit der Welt.” It was largely identical to the essay of the same name published in Merkur, no. 47, 1952, pp. 1–11. It ends:

“But just as the Earth remains greater than the dilemma posed by this dualistic question, so history remains stronger than every philosophy of history. For that reason, I do not regard the present division of the world into two as a preliminary stage on the way to unity, but as a passage toward a new plurality.”

See also G. Maschke’s note to the republication in SGN, pp. 510–12.

27 April 1952

“Wonderful passage in Buffon” — Georges-Louis Leclerc de Buffon, Histoire naturelle, générale et particulière, avec la description du Cabinet du Roy, vols. 1–15, Paris 1749–1767.

The quotation in Rousseau reads, in Heinrich Meier’s German edition:

“Since plants draw far more of the substance they need for nourishment from air and water than from the earth, it follows that when they decay, they return more to the earth than they took from it …”

J. J. Rousseau, Diskurs über die Ungleichheit, ed. H. Meier, Paderborn 1984, p. 285.

renegatur et rejiciatur Norma — “The norm is denied and rejected.”

In his encyclical Summi Pontificatus of 20 October 1939, Pope Pius XII lamented the “denial and rejection of the norms of natural law,” which he identified as one of the causes of the war.

“Norma, Norma, you have vanished” — An allusion to Friedrich von Flotow’s opera Martha, oder der Markt zu Richmond. In Act 3, Scene 4, the aria “Ach! so fromm, Ach! So traut” contains the line:

“Martha! Martha! You have vanished.”

“Interjections by H. Heller and A. Arndt” — Hermann Heller, counsel for Prussia in the Prussia v. Reich case before the State Court in Leipzig in 1932, interrupted Schmitt’s plea by calling out “situational jurisprudence.” See Preußen contra Reich vor dem Staatsgerichtshof. Stenogrammbericht der Verhandlungen vor dem Staatsgerichtshof in Leipzig vom 10. bis 14. und vom 17. Oktober 1932, Berlin 1933, p. 464.

“CDU deputy Nellen” — On 3 July 1956, Bundestag deputy Peter Nellen raised objections to provisions governing conscientious objection in the Conscription Act, arguing that in his view they restricted a fundamental right.
